title: Practice set 1
desc: Mixed topics from the key notes, with 4 Ethics questions (48 questions, 2 h 24 min)

vignettes.body:
Marin compares exchange rate models and policy mixes.

Model 1: The pure monetary approach, in which PPP holds at all times.
Model 2: The Dornbusch model, in which prices are sticky in the short run.
Model 3: The portfolio balance approach, which focuses on long-run fiscal policy and government debt.

Country H has high capital mobility and adopts an expansionary monetary policy with a restrictive fiscal policy.

questions.q: After an unexpected monetary expansion, which model predicts that the domestic currency first depreciates by more than its long-run amount?
options: Model 2
Model 3
Model 1
questions.why: Dornbusch overshooting: with sticky prices, the currency initially depreciates more than PPP implies, then partly recovers. In the pure monetary approach, it depreciates in line with prices at once.

questions.q: Under the Mundell–Fleming model, Country H's currency will most likely:
options: appreciate
be unaffected
depreciate
questions.why: High capital mobility: expansionary monetary policy → lower rates → depreciation; restrictive fiscal policy → lower rates → depreciation. Both push the same way.

questions.q: Under Model 3, sustained fiscal deficits financed by rising government debt most likely cause the currency to:
options: depreciate in the long run, as investors demand a lower price or a higher return to hold more of the country's debt
stay unchanged, because in the long run only monetary policy affects the exchange rate
appreciate permanently, because higher interest rates keep attracting foreign capital
questions.why: Portfolio balance: short run, fiscal expansion may raise rates and the currency (Mundell–Fleming); long run, continuous deficits raise the supply of the country's bonds and investors require compensation → currency depreciates.

vignettes.body:
Hector Ruiz analyses Atlas Industrial, a US company, and its subsidiary in Mexico.

Transaction: On 1 November, Atlas sold goods to a German customer on credit for €1,000,000, when the exchange rate was $1.10/€. On 31 December, the rate was $1.15/€ and the receivable was still outstanding.

Subsidiary: The Mexican subsidiary earns all of its revenue and incurs most of its costs in Mexican pesos, buys some materials in US dollars and borrows in euros.

questions.q: Atlas's foreign currency transaction gain or loss at 31 December is closest to:
options: a gain of $50,000
a loss of $50,000
a gain of $1,150,000
questions.why:
Gain = foreign currency amount × (year-end rate − transaction-date rate) = 1,000,000 × (1.15 − 1.10) = $50,000.
A receivable in a currency that appreciates gives a gain (a payable would give a loss).

questions.q: The functional currency of the Mexican subsidiary is most likely the:
options: Mexican peso
euro
US dollar
questions.why: The primary indicators are the currency of revenues and the currency of operating costs; financing is a secondary indicator. Revenue and most costs are in pesos → peso is the functional currency.

vignettes.body:
Silva compares two option-adjusted spreads (OAS) calculated with the same interest rate tree. Bond T has an OAS of 85 bps and Bond U has an OAS of 60 bps. Both bonds are callable, have similar terms and have the same credit rating.

A junior analyst states: "The rates in the binomial tree are our forecasts of future interest rates."

questions.q: Based on the OAS, Silva should conclude that:
options: the OAS cannot be compared because the bonds are callable
Bond T is cheaper than Bond U
Bond U is cheaper than Bond T
questions.why: OAS can be compared only for bonds with the same credit rating (and the same tree). A larger OAS means the bond is cheaper (underpriced), so buy Bond T.

questions.q: The junior analyst's statement is:
options: incorrect, because the rates in the tree are not forecasts but stochastic paths consistent with the volatility assumption and current prices
correct, because each node gives the most likely rate at that date, based on the volatility assumption and economic forecasts
correct, because the tree is calibrated to the expected future short-term rates implied by analysts' forecasts
questions.why: The binomial tree's interest rate movements are not predictions: they are random (stochastic) paths calibrated to today's par curve and an assumed volatility, so the tree is arbitrage-free.

vignettes.body:
Jonas Weber is building trading models at Halcyon Quant.

Model X: Weber has 120 candidate features to predict monthly returns and wants an algorithm that shrinks the coefficients of unimportant features toward zero and removes some of them.

Model Y: Weber wants to sort companies into "likely default" and "unlikely default" using a linear boundary that separates the two classes with the widest margin.

Model Z: Weber wants to classify stocks as "buy" or "sell". The relationships between the features and the classification are non-linear and include interactions.

questions.q: The algorithm best suited to Model X is:
options: k-means clustering
LASSO, a penalised regression
principal components analysis
questions.why: LASSO (least absolute shrinkage and selection operator) is a penalised regression: it adds a penalty on the size of coefficients, shrinking some to zero and so selecting features. It is supervised.

questions.q: The algorithm best suited to Model Y is a:
options: hierarchical clustering algorithm
support vector machine
deep learning network with unlabelled data
questions.why: SVM = linear classification algorithm that separates the data into one of two classes with the widest margin. Logit/probit models are also classification models for two classes.

questions.q: The algorithm best suited to Model Z is:
options: principal components analysis (PCA)
LASSO (least absolute shrinkage and selection operator)
classification and regression tree (CART)
questions.why: Two classes (buy/sell) with non-linear relationships and interactions between features → CART.

vignettes.body:
Jonas Berg compares Norvik AB with its industry. Exhibit 1 gives selected data (in SEK millions).

Exhibit 1: Norvik Financial Data
# Item | Amount
Revenue | 4,800
EBIT | 720
Earnings before tax (EBT) | 600
Net income | 450
Average total assets | 6,000
Average equity | 2,500

Berg also notes:
Note 1: Norvik's ratio of operating cash flow before interest and taxes to operating income is well above 1.
Note 2: The Nordic segment accounts for 30% of total assets and 45% of total capital expenditures.
Note 3: Norvik's depreciable lives for PP&E are 20% longer than the industry average.

questions.q: Using the five-step DuPont analysis, Norvik's interest burden and ROE are closest to:
Note 1 most likely indicates that Norvik's earnings:
options: are inflated by accruals
include large one-time gains
are backed by cash flow
questions.why: Operating cash flow before interest and taxes ÷ operating income well above 1 → earnings are supported by cash (higher quality). When computing it, adjust for where interest and taxes paid are classified (IFRS allows CFO or CFF/CFI).

questions.q: Based on Note 2, the Nordic segment is most likely:
options: being run for cash
growing, because its capex share is greater than its asset share
shrinking, because it holds only 30% of assets
questions.why: Segment capex % ÷ segment asset % = 45/30 = 1.5 > 1 → the company is investing more there: growing. Below 1 → being reduced.

questions.q: If Berg adjusts Norvik's depreciation to the industry's shorter lives, Norvik's debt-to-equity ratio will most likely:
options: stay the same
decrease
increase
questions.why: Shorter lives → higher depreciation → lower net income → lower retained earnings and equity → higher D/E.

vignettes.body:
Tobias Weller values Grünwald AG with free cash flow models. Exhibit 1 shows data for the year (in € millions).

Exhibit 1: Grünwald AG Data
# Item | Amount
Net income | 420
Depreciation | 150
Fixed capital investment | 310
Increase in current assets (including a €30 million increase in cash) | 110
Increase in current liabilities | 40
Target debt ratio | 40%

Grünwald pays dividends that are far below its FCFE, and its dividends have little relation to its ability to pay.

questions.q: The investment in working capital used to calculate FCFE is closest to:
options: €150 million
€70 million
€40 million
questions.why: ΔWC = Δ current assets (excluding cash and cash equivalents) − Δ current liabilities = (110 − 30) − 40 = €40m.

questions.q: Grünwald's FCFE, assuming investment is financed at the target debt ratio, is closest to:
options: €260 million
€300 million
€236 million

questions.q: Weller should most likely value Grünwald with:
options: an FCFE model, because dividends differ greatly from the capacity to pay them
a residual income model, because FCFE is positive
a dividend discount model, because Grünwald pays dividends
questions.why: Use FCFE instead of DDM when dividends differ significantly from FCFE (dividend-paying capacity), when the company pays no dividends, or when an investor takes a control perspective.

vignettes.body:
Henrik Vass, CFA, is a research analyst at Brightwell Securities covering Kestrel Stores. Vass attends a private breakfast hosted by Kestrel's CFO for four analysts. The CFO says that next quarter's same-store sales will fall about 5%, against consensus expectations of growth of 2%. This has not been publicly announced. After the breakfast, Vass changes his recommendation to sell and first calls Brightwell's institutional clients, then emails the retail clients two hours later. The same afternoon he sells Kestrel shares in his personal retirement account.

Vass's brochure for new clients contains the statements listed in the last question of this vignette.

questions.q: Vass's actions after the breakfast most likely violated Standard:
options: II(A): Material Nonpublic Information.
II(B): Market Manipulation.
V(A): Diligence and Reasonable Basis.
questions.why: The CFO's statement was material and nonpublic, and Vass acted on it by changing his recommendation and trading. Standard II(A) prohibits acting on MNPI.

questions.q: Calling institutional clients before emailing retail clients most likely violated Standard:
options: III(B): Fair Dealing.
I(B): Independence and Objectivity.
III(A): Loyalty, Prudence and Care.
questions.why: Standard III(B) requires fair and equitable dissemination of recommendations to all clients, giving no group an advantage.

questions.q: After the breakfast, Vass should most appropriately have:
options: issued the recommendation without mentioning the source.
traded only in his clients' accounts.
encouraged the CFO to make the information public and refrained from acting on it.
questions.why: When a member receives MNPI he should encourage the issuer to disclose it publicly and not act on it or cause others to act.

questions.q: Which statement in Vass's brochure complies with Standard VII(B): Reference to CFA Institute, the CFA Designation and the CFA Program?
options: "As a CFA charterholder, Henrik Vass will earn you higher returns."
"Henrik Vass passed all three CFA exams on his first attempt, which makes him a better analyst."
"Henrik Vass is a CFA charterholder."
questions.why: Stating that one holds the designation is acceptable. Implying superior skill or promising better performance because of the designation is not.

vignettes.body:
Elena Vidal, an options strategist at Bruma Capital, presents three charts of implied volatility for options on the Iberia 35 index.

Chart 1 plots implied volatility against both exercise price and time to expiration.
Chart 2 shows that implied volatility is higher for deep in-the-money and deep out-of-the-money options than for at-the-money options.
Chart 3 shows implied volatility falling steadily as the exercise price rises, and Vidal notes that the slope became steeper during last month's sell-off.

questions.q: Implied volatility is best described as the volatility that:
options: the dealer sets so that all exercise prices have the same option price
is backed out of market option prices and reflects expected future volatility
is measured from past returns of the underlying index
questions.why: Implied volatility = the volatility that makes the model price equal the market option price. It is forward-looking (expected future volatility), unlike historical volatility.

questions.q: Chart 1 is best described as a volatility:
options: smile
surface
skew
questions.why: Volatility surface = implied volatility across both exercise prices and maturities (a 3-D plot).

questions.q: Which statement about Charts 2 and 3 is most accurate?
options: Chart 2 is a volatility skew; Chart 3 is a smile, which flattens when demand for hedging rises
Both charts show a smile, because implied volatility varies with exercise price
Chart 2 is a volatility smile; Chart 3 is a skew, which steepens when demand for downside hedging rises
questions.why:
Smile = implied volatility higher for ITM and OTM than ATM (U shape).
Skew = implied volatility varies with exercise price in one direction (higher for low strikes); it steepens when demand for protective puts rises, so it does not have the shape of a smile.

vignettes.body:
Charlotte Reyes, a fixed-income analyst at Penrose Capital, uses the arbitrage-free framework. Exhibit 1 shows the current par curve for annual-pay government bonds.

Exhibit 1: Par Curve
# Maturity (years) | Par rate
1 | 2.00%
2 | 2.50%
3 | 2.90%

Reyes is asked whether a three-year, 4.0% annual-coupon government bond trading at 102.60 is mispriced. Her steps are: (1) bootstrap spot rates from the par curve; (2) discount the bond's cash flows at the spot rates; (3) compare the value with the market price.

questions.q: The three-year spot rate is closest to:
The arbitrage-free value of the bond is closest to:
questions.why:
Value = 4/1.02 + 4/(1 + 2.5063%)² + 104/(1 + 2.9167%)³ = 103.13
Each cash flow is discounted at its own spot rate, not at one rate.

questions.q: Based on Reyes's analysis, the bond is:
options: fairly priced, because its coupon is above the par rate
overvalued, so it should be sold
undervalued, so it should be bought
questions.why: Arbitrage-free value 103.13 vs market price 102.60. Value > price → undervalued → buy.

questions.q: The bond's yield to maturity at its arbitrage-free value is closest to:
questions.why:
N = 3, PMT = 4, FV = 100, PV = −103.1344 → I/Y = 2.894%
The YTM is a single blended rate, slightly below the 3-year spot rate for a coupon bond on an upward-sloping curve.

questions.q: The one-year forward rate two years from now, f(2,1), is closest to:

vignettes.body: Ten months ago, Marco Bellini entered a long 14-month forward contract on one share of Lumen Foods, a stock that pays no dividends, at a forward price of €88.40. Today Lumen's share price is €94.10, so four months remain until expiration. The risk-free rate is 2.2% a year with annual compounding.

questions.q: The current value of Bellini's forward position is closest to:
questions.why:
Value (long) = (FPt − FP0) / (1 + r)^(T−t), with T − t = 4/12.
FPt = 94.10 × 1.022^(4/12) = 94.7851
Value = (94.7851 − 88.40) / 1.022^(4/12) = 6.34
Equivalently S − F0/(1+r)^(T−t). €5.70 forgets discounting F0; €6.39 is not discounted to today.

vignettes.body:
Nora Lindahl screens companies for earnings quality.

Company P: revenue growth well above peers; receivables growing faster than revenue; a rising share of revenue booked in the fourth quarter; net income greater than cash flow from operations for three years. Its receivables turnover has fallen, and Lindahl suspects bill-and-hold sales and channel stuffing.
Company Q: an Altman Z-score of 3.4 and a Beneish M-score of −2.6.
Company R: a Beneish M-score of −1.2 and a high level of accruals. Lindahl separates accruals into normal accruals explained by a regression on business activity, and the residual.

Company S reports under IFRS and classifies interest paid in financing activities. To compare it with peers, Lindahl reclassifies interest paid into operating activities.

questions.q: Company P's pattern is most consistent with:
options: aggressive revenue recognition that inflates receivables
conservative accounting that defers revenue to later periods
high-quality earnings that are well supported by operating cash flow
questions.why: Warning signs: revenue growth above peers, receivables growing faster than revenue, high share of revenue in the final quarter, net income > CFO. Bill-and-hold and channel stuffing raise receivables and lower receivables turnover.

questions.q: Which company is most likely to be manipulating earnings?
options: Company R
Neither, because both M-scores are negative
Company Q
questions.why: M-score above −1.78 → higher probability of manipulation: R (−1.2) is above, Q (−2.6) below. A higher Altman Z-score means lower bankruptcy risk.

questions.q: The residual from Lindahl's accruals regression represents:
options: discretionary accruals, which may signal earnings manipulation
cash earnings
non-discretionary accruals, which arise from normal operations
questions.why: Non-discretionary accruals come from normal business activity (explained by the regression). Discretionary accruals (the residual) come from unusual choices and can signal manipulation; high accruals mean lower earnings quality.

questions.q: After Lindahl's reclassification, Company S's CFO and CFF will be, respectively:
options: unchanged and lower
lower and higher
higher and lower
questions.why: Interest paid is a cash outflow. Moving it from CFF to CFO lowers CFO and raises (makes less negative) CFF.

vignettes.body:
Diego Navas, a fixed-income analyst, computes forward prices. The three-year forward rate two years from now, f(2,3), is 3.2% (annual compounding).

Navas also comments on interest rate volatility: "Volatility of short-term rates is driven mainly by monetary policy, while volatility of long-term rates is driven mainly by expectations for the economy and inflation."

questions.q: The forward price, two years from now, of a zero-coupon bond paying 1 at year 5 is closest to:
questions.why:
Forward price F(j,k) = 1 / (1 + f(j,k))^k = 1 / 1.032³ = 0.9098
The exponent is k (the 3-year length of the forward period), not j or j + k.

questions.q: Regarding Navas's comment, short-term rates are generally:
options: less volatile than long-term rates, because monetary policy is predictable
more volatile than long-term rates, and the drivers he names are correct
equally volatile, and the drivers he names are reversed
questions.why: Short-term volatility comes from monetary policy and is usually higher; long-term volatility reflects the economy and inflation expectations.

vignettes.body:
Harlow Utilities has issued fixed-rate bonds. Its CFO, Lena Brandt, says: "I want our debt to behave like floating-rate debt so that the market value of our liabilities is less sensitive to changes in interest rates."

Separately, Harlow's pension consultant, Omar Haddad, expects interest rates to rise sharply over the next year and wants a position that gains if they do, while limiting the loss if he is wrong.

questions.q: To meet Brandt's objective, Harlow should enter into a swap in which it:
options: pays fixed and receives an equity return
pays floating and receives fixed
pays fixed and receives floating
questions.why:
Harlow pays fixed on its bonds. Receiving fixed and paying floating on a swap cancels the fixed payments and leaves floating-rate debt, whose value is much less sensitive to rate changes.
To reduce interest rate risk of fixed-rate debt: pay-floating interest rate swap.

questions.q: Haddad's view is best expressed with a:
options: receiver swaption
payer swaption
receive-fixed interest rate swap
questions.why:
If rates rise, the right to PAY fixed (and receive floating) at the old, lower rate becomes valuable: payer swap or payer swaption.
The swaption limits the loss to the premium if rates do not rise.

vignettes.body:
Emil Varga trains analysts at Corvus Partners on multifactor models.

Model 1 uses surprises in GDP growth, inflation and credit spreads as factors.
Model 2 uses company attributes such as P/E, market capitalisation and leverage as factors.
Model 3 uses principal components analysis to find the factors that best explain historical return covariances.

Varga notes that arbitrage pricing theory (APT) assumes that returns are generated by a factor model, that asset-specific risk can be diversified away in a portfolio, and that no arbitrage opportunities exist.

questions.q: Which statement about APT is most accurate?
options: APT does not specify the number or the identity of the factors
APT assumes investors hold the market portfolio
APT requires a market portfolio factor, like the CAPM
questions.why: APT says returns follow a factor model but does not say how many factors there are or what they are.

questions.q: Which statement about how the models are estimated is most accurate?
options: In Model 2 the factor sensitivities (standardised attributes) are specified first and factor returns are estimated; in Model 1 the factor surprises are specified first and sensitivities are estimated
In both models the factor sensitivities are estimated first by time-series regression, and the factor returns are then observed directly
In Model 1 the factor sensitivities are specified first from company data; in Model 2 the sensitivities are estimated last by regression
questions.why:
Fundamental models: sensitivities come first (from attributes), factor returns are estimated by cross-sectional regression.
Macroeconomic models: factor surprises are observed first, sensitivities are estimated by time-series regression.

questions.q: Compared with Models 1 and 2, Model 3 most likely:
options: is the model most used by active equity managers
has factors that are easy to interpret economically
makes minimal assumptions, but its factors are hard to interpret
questions.why:
Statistical factor models: advantage = minimal assumptions; disadvantage = factors (principal components) are hard to interpret, harder than fundamental or macro factors.
Active equity managers mostly use fundamental models.

vignettes.body:
Weller values a small private company, Hallberg GmbH, for a minority investor. A controlling interest would command a control premium of 25%, and the discount for lack of marketability is 20%.

Weller also computes the residual income for a public company with net income of €80 million, beginning equity of €600 million, ending equity of €640 million and a cost of equity of 10%.

questions.q: The total discount applied to a controlling value to value Hallberg's minority, non-marketable stake is closest to:
questions.why:
DLOC = 1 − 1/(1 + control premium) = 1 − 1/1.25 = 20%.
Total discount = 1 − (1 − DLOC)(1 − DLOM) = 1 − 0.80 × 0.80 = 36% (the discounts multiply, they are not added).

questions.q: Residual income for the year is closest to:
options: €18 million
€20 million
€16 million
questions.why: RI = NI − r × beginning book value of equity = 80 − 0.10 × 600 = €20m. Use beginning equity, not ending or average.

vignettes.body:
Quiroga needs the swap spread for a corporate bond that matures in 3.40 years. Exhibit 1 gives the data she has.

Exhibit 1: Yields and Swap Rates (%)
# | 3 years | 4 years
Off-the-run government yield | 0.70 | 0.86
On-the-run government yield | 0.62 | 0.78
Swap rate | 1.38 | 1.51

questions.q: Using linear interpolation, the swap spread for 3.40 years is closest to:
options: 75 bps
143 bps
67 bps
questions.why:
Swap spread = swap rate − on-the-run government yield, both interpolated to 3.40 years.
Swap rate = 1.38 + 0.40 × (1.51 − 1.38) = 1.432%
On-the-run = 0.62 + 0.40 × (0.78 − 0.62) = 0.684%
Spread = 1.432 − 0.684 = 0.748% ≈ 75 bps
67 bps uses the off-the-run yield; 143 bps is the swap rate, not the spread.

vignettes.body:
Arjun Mehta reviews three regressions built by junior analysts at Kittering Partners.

Regression 1 explains bank loan growth. A Breusch–Pagan test is significant at the 1% level.
Regression 2 explains housing starts with five macroeconomic variables. Its R² is 0.91 and the F-statistic is significant at the 1% level, but none of the five t-statistics is significant at the 5% level.
Regression 3 is a time-series regression of monthly sales. A Breusch–Godfrey test is significant. Mehta also reports a Durbin–Watson statistic of 1.20; with this sample size, the lower and upper critical values are 1.39 and 1.60.

questions.q: In Regression 1, the most likely consequence of the test result is that the t-statistics are:
options: unaffected, because only the F-test is affected
too low, so significant variables look insignificant; adding variables fixes this
too high, so the analyst may wrongly reject true null hypotheses; robust (White) standard errors fix this
questions.why:
Breusch–Pagan significant → conditional heteroskedasticity.
Standard errors too low → t-statistics too high → Type I errors. The F-test is unreliable.
Fix: robust (White-corrected) standard errors.

questions.q: Regression 2 most likely suffers from:
options: heteroskedasticity, which can be checked with the Breusch–Pagan test
serial correlation, which can be checked with the Durbin–Watson test
multicollinearity, which can be checked with variance inflation factors
questions.why:
Signals of multicollinearity: large R², significant F, but low or insignificant t-statistics (inflated standard errors).
Detect with VIF; fix by dropping or combining variables or increasing the sample.

questions.q: Based on the Durbin–Watson statistic, Regression 3 shows:
options: no serial correlation
positive serial correlation
an inconclusive result
questions.why:
Zones: 0 to dl = reject, positive serial correlation; dl to du = inconclusive; du to 4 − du = no serial correlation; then inconclusive; 4 − dl to 4 = negative serial correlation.
1.20 < dl = 1.39 → positive serial correlation.

questions.q: The most appropriate correction for Regression 3 is to use:
options: a smaller number of independent variables
White standard errors only
Newey–West (serial-correlation consistent) standard errors
questions.why: Serial correlation: test with Breusch–Godfrey (or DW), correct with robust Newey–West standard errors. White standard errors correct heteroskedasticity only.

title: Practice set 2
desc: Mixed topics from the key notes, with 4 Ethics questions (48 questions, 2 h 24 min)

vignettes.body: Tanaka compares unconstrained and constrained versions of a strategy. The unconstrained information ratio is 0.40. Long-only constraints give a transfer coefficient of 0.6. The benchmark has a Sharpe ratio of 0.35 and a standard deviation of 16%.

questions.q: The optimal amount of active risk for the constrained portfolio is closest to:
questions.why:
Unconstrained: σA* = IR/SR_B × σ_B. Constrained: σA* = TC × (IR/SR_B) × σ_B (IR here = IC√BR)
= 0.6 × (0.40/0.35) × 16% = 10.97%

questions.q: The maximum Sharpe ratio of the constrained portfolio is closest to:
questions.why:
Constrained: SR_P = √[SR_B² + TC² × IR²] = √[0.35² + 0.6² × 0.40²] = 0.424
Unconstrained would be √(SR_B² + IR²) = 0.532.

questions.q: If the optimal active risk is 9.6% and the active portfolio's active risk is 12%, the weight in the active portfolio (the rest in the benchmark) is:
options: 125%, borrowing 25% from the benchmark
20%, with 80% in the benchmark
80%, with 20% in the benchmark
questions.why: Optimal weight in active portfolio = optimal active risk / active risk of the portfolio = 9.6/12 = 0.80; benchmark weight = 1 − 0.80 = 0.20.

questions.q: The transfer coefficient best measures:
options: the number of independent active decisions the manager makes per year on different securities
how well the manager's anticipated risk-adjusted returns are translated into risk-adjusted active weights
the manager's ability to forecast returns, measured as the correlation between forecast and actual active returns
questions.why: TC = correlation between forecast (risk-adjusted) returns and risk-weighted active weights; constraints lower it. IC = forecasting skill; BR = number of independent decisions.

vignettes.body:
Tobias Lang evaluates a single-A rated corporate bond for Ostend Fixed Income Fund. The bond has a yield to maturity of 4.30% and a modified duration of 5.2. Exhibit 1 shows one-year rating transition probabilities for an A-rated bond and the change in credit spread if the rating changes.

Exhibit 1: One-Year Transition Probabilities and Spread Changes
# New rating | Probability | Change in spread
AA | 4% | −45 bps
A | 90% | 0 bps
BBB | 5% | +60 bps
BB | 1% | +200 bps

questions.q: The expected percentage price change from credit migration over the year is closest to:
questions.why:
Each rating: probability × (−modified duration × change in spread).
Upgrade (spread falls) → positive; downgrade → negative.
AA: 0.04 × (−5.2 × −0.0045) = +0.0936%
BBB: 0.05 × (−5.2 × 0.0060) = −0.1560%
BB: 0.01 × (−5.2 × 0.0200) = −0.1040%
Sum = -0.166%

questions.q: Taking credit migration into account, the bond's expected one-year return is closest to:
questions.why:
Expected return ≈ yield + expected migration effect = 4.30% + (-0.17%) = 4.13%
Credit migration usually lowers the expected return, because downgrades are larger and more likely than upgrades.

vignettes.body:
Ravi Kapoor evaluates the Orion Equity Fund against its benchmark using a three-factor model. Last year the fund returned 11.2% and the benchmark returned 8.1%.

Exhibit 1: Factor Sensitivities and Factor Returns
# Factor | Fund sensitivity | Benchmark sensitivity | Factor return
Market | 1.15 | 1.00 | 6.0%
Size | 0.40 | 0.10 | 2.0%
Value | -0.10 | 0.20 | 4.0%

questions.q: The fund's return from factor tilts is closest to:
questions.why:
Factor tilt = Σ (fund sensitivity − benchmark sensitivity) × factor return
Market: 0.15 × 6% = 0.90%
Size: 0.30 × 2% = 0.60%
Value: −0.30 × 4% = -1.20%
Total = 0.30%

questions.q: The fund's return from security selection is closest to:
questions.why:
Active return = 11.2% − 8.1% = 3.1%
Security selection = active return − factor tilt = 3.1% − (0.30%) = 2.80%

questions.q: Which factor tilt added the most to the fund's active return?
options: Value
Size
Market
questions.why: Compare the tilt contributions: market 0.90%, size 0.60%, value -1.20%. Market is the largest; value detracted.

questions.q: Based on its sensitivities, the fund's style relative to the benchmark is best described as:
options: high beta, small-cap and growth
high beta, large-cap and value
low beta, large-cap and value
questions.why: Positive active market sensitivity → beta > benchmark; positive size → small-cap tilt; negative value → growth tilt. (Momentum: positive = momentum, negative = contrarian.)

vignettes.body:
Gabriela Silva, a portfolio manager at Tamsin Fixed Income, compares bonds with embedded options. All bonds have the same issuer, maturity and coupon unless stated otherwise.

Bond P is a floating-rate note whose coupon resets once a year; the next reset is in one year.
Bond Q is callable, Bond R is putable and Bond S is an option-free (straight) bond.

Silva expects interest-rate volatility to rise. She also expects the upward-sloping yield curve to flatten while the level of rates is unchanged.

questions.q: The effective duration of Bond P is closest to:
options: the bond's years to maturity
questions.why: A floating-rate bond's effective duration is close to the time to the next reset. With annual resets and the next reset in one year, effective duration ≈ 1.

questions.q: If interest rates fall sharply, compared with Bond S, Bond Q's effective duration most likely:
options: rises and its convexity stays positive
falls and its convexity becomes negative
stays the same as Bond S's duration
questions.why:
Callable bond when rates fall: the call is likely to be exercised, so duration falls below that of the straight bond and convexity becomes negative (price compression).
When rates rise, the callable behaves like the straight bond.

questions.q: Which ordering of prices is most likely correct?
options: Bond R < Bond S < Bond Q
Bond Q < Bond S < Bond R
Bond S < Bond Q < Bond R
questions.why:
Callable = straight − call option (investor is short the call) → cheapest.
Putable = straight + put option (investor is long the put) → most expensive.

questions.q: If interest-rate volatility rises, the values of Bond Q and Bond R most likely:
options: fall and rise, respectively
rise and fall, respectively
both rise
questions.why:
Higher volatility raises the value of both options.
Callable = straight − call → falls. Putable = straight + put → rises.

questions.q: If the upward-sloping yield curve flattens, the value of the call option in Bond Q and the value of Bond R most likely:
options: fall and rise, respectively
both rise
rise and fall, respectively
questions.why:
Upward-sloping curve flattens → long-term forward rates fall → the call is more likely to be exercised: call value rises and the callable bond falls.
The put is less likely to be exercised: put value falls, so the putable bond falls.

vignettes.body:
Kenji Arai is building a sentiment model from 50,000 web news articles at Okubo Advisors. The steps of a text project are text problem formulation, data curation, text preparation and wrangling, text exploration, and model training.

Arai's raw text contains HTML tags, punctuation, numbers and extra white space. He then applies four wrangling steps to the cleansed tokens: converting to lower case, removing words such as "the" and "is", reducing "integrated", "integrating" and "integration" to "integr", and converting "better" to "good" using a dictionary.

After wrangling, Arai builds a bag of words and computes document frequency (DF) and mutual information (MI) for each token. He also converts the categorical feature "sector" into binary columns.

questions.q: Removing HTML tags, punctuation, numbers and white space is part of:
options: text cleansing
text wrangling (preprocessing)
text exploration
questions.why:
Text cleansing: remove HTML tags, punctuation (keeping meaningful symbols such as % or $, replaced with tokens), numbers and white spaces.
Text wrangling (preprocessing) then works on tokens: lowercasing, stop-word removal, stemming, lemmatisation.

questions.q: Reducing words to "integr" and converting "better" to "good" are, respectively:
options: stemming and lemmatisation
lemmatisation and stemming
tokenisation and stemming
questions.why:
Stemming cuts words to a common base ("integr"), which may not be a real word.
Lemmatisation uses morphology and a dictionary to get the real base word (lemma): "better" → "good". It is more computationally expensive.

questions.q: Converting "sector" into binary columns is called:
options: bag of words
one-hot encoding
n-gram creation
questions.why: One-hot encoding turns a categorical feature into binary dummy variables.

questions.q: Which statement about DF and MI is most accurate?
options: Stop words have a low DF, and MI measures the number of documents in the corpus
Rare names have a high DF, and MI measures how often a token appears in a document
Stop words have a high DF, and MI measures how much a token contributes to identifying a class
questions.why:
DF = number of documents containing the token ÷ total documents. Stop words → high DF; important words → medium DF; rare words such as names → low DF.
MI = how much a token contributes to a class (0 = not informative, 1 = strongly linked to one class).

questions.q: Arai's four wrangling steps are completed. The next step is most likely to:
options: create a bag of words from the normalised tokens
return to text problem formulation
remove HTML tags from the tokens
questions.why: After cleansing and wrangling (normalisation), the tokens are collected into a bag of words (BOW), and then a document term matrix is built.

vignettes.body:
Bettina Kral, a fixed-income analyst, shows one interest rate path generated from a calibrated binomial tree. The tree has nodes at times 0, 1, 2 and 3. Along the path the one-year rates are 2.0% (time 0 to 1), 3.1% (time 1 to 2), 3.8% (time 2 to 3) and 4.4% (time 3 to 4).

She values a three-year, 4% annual-coupon, option-free bond along this path using the pathwise method.

questions.q: The value of the bond along this path is closest to:
questions.why:
Pathwise: discount each cash flow by the product of the one-year rates along the path (not by spot rates).
4/1.020 + 4/(1.020 × 1.031) + 104/(1.020 × 1.031 × 1.038) = 103.00
A three-year bond needs only the first three rates; the 4.4% rate (time 3 to 4) is not used.
100.68 wrongly treats the path rates as spot rates.

questions.q: For an option-free bond, the value found by discounting at spot rates compared with the value from a calibrated binomial tree is:
options: lower when the assumed volatility is higher
higher when the assumed volatility is higher
the same, whatever volatility is assumed
questions.why: A calibrated tree reprices the benchmark bonds, so an option-free bond has the same value from the tree as from spot rates, regardless of the volatility used. Volatility matters only for bonds with embedded options.

vignettes.body:
Mei Tanaka analyses the record of a quantitative manager who makes 100 independent-looking stock decisions a year.

Fact 1: The manager's forecasts of whether stocks outperform are correct 56% of the time.
Fact 2: The decisions are not truly independent: the average correlation between decisions is 0.05 because of cross-sectional and time-series dependency.
Fact 3: Each decision has an active risk of 3%.

Tanaka also analyses a sector rotation strategy that switches between two sectors X and Y each month. The monthly standard deviations are 5.0% for X and 4.0% for Y, and their correlation is 0.80.

questions.q: The manager's information coefficient is closest to:
The manager's effective breadth is closest to:
questions.why: With correlated decisions: BR = N / [1 + (N − 1) r] = 100 / (1 + 99 × 0.05) = 100 / 5.95 = 16.8

questions.q: Using the effective breadth, the manager's expected annual active return is closest to:
questions.why:
Annualised active risk σA = σ per decision × √BR = 3% × √16.81 = 12.30%
E(RA) = IC × √BR × σA = 0.12 × 4.100 × 12.30% = 6.05%

questions.q: The monthly active risk of the sector rotation strategy is closest to:

vignettes.body:
Anika Feld is a fixed-income derivatives trader at Rhinebeck Capital. She and her colleague Tomas Lindgren review two Treasury note futures contracts.

Five-Year Note Futures
The underlying 2.0% semi-annual Treasury note is quoted at a clean price of 100.80. It has been 50 days since the last coupon payment and the next coupon is payable in 130 days. Feld asks Lindgren to calculate the full spot price of the note.

Ten-Year Note Futures
The underlying 2.5% semi-annual Treasury note has a dirty price of 105.20. It has been 40 days since the last coupon payment, and the futures contract expires in 90 days. No coupon is paid before expiration. The quoted futures price is 136.00, the annualised three-month risk-free rate is 1.80%, and the conversion factor is 0.7550.

questions.q: The full spot price of the five-year note is closest to:
questions.why:
Accrued interest uses the days since the last coupon over the 180-day period.
AI = 50/180 × 1.00 = 0.2778
Full price = 100.80 + 0.2778 = 101.08
101.52 wrongly uses the 130 days to the next coupon; 100.80 is the clean price.

questions.q: The equilibrium quoted futures price of the ten-year note is closest to:
questions.why:
Everything is measured at expiration.
FV of full price = 105.20 × 1.018^(90/360) = 105.6702
Accrued interest at expiration = (40 + 90)/180 × 1.25 = 0.9028
QFP = (105.6702 − 0.9028) / 0.755 = 138.76
139.59 subtracts today's accrued interest (0.2778) instead of the accrued interest at expiration; 139.96 subtracts no accrued interest.

questions.q: Based on the equilibrium price, the arbitrage strategy for the ten-year note futures is to:
options: take no position, because the contract is fairly priced
buy the futures, short sell the note and lend the proceeds
sell the futures, buy the note with borrowed funds
questions.why:
Market price 136.00 < model price 138.76, so the futures is undervalued.
Undervalued → reverse cash-and-carry: Buy futures, Short the bond, Lend (BSL).
Overvalued (market > model) would be cash-and-carry: Sell futures, Buy bond, Borrow (SBB).

vignettes.body:
Ines Moreau compares money market and swap spreads for Galloway Treasury Services.

Exhibit 1: Selected Rates
# Instrument | Rate
Three-year swap fixed rate | 3.45%
Three-year government bond yield | 3.10%
Three-month MRR | 2.95%
Three-month Treasury bill yield | 2.60%

questions.q: The three-year swap spread is closest to:
options: 35 bps
50 bps
85 bps
questions.why: Swap spread = swap fixed rate − government bond yield of the same maturity = 3.45% − 3.10% = 0.35% = 35 bps.

questions.q: The TED spread is closest to:
options: 85 bps (three-year swap rate minus the three-month T-bill yield)
15 bps (three-year swap rate minus three-month MRR)
35 bps (three-month MRR minus the three-month T-bill yield)
questions.why: TED spread = three-month MRR − three-month Treasury bill yield = 2.95% − 2.60% = 35 bps. It reflects credit and liquidity risk in the banking system.

vignettes.body:
Leah Morgan, an insurance analyst, analyses Harbour Mutual, a property and casualty (P&C) insurer, for the year (in $ millions).

Exhibit 1: Harbour Mutual Underwriting Data
# Item | Amount
Net premiums written | 1,250
Net premiums earned | 1,200
Claims paid | 690
Increase in loss reserves | 90
Underwriting expenses, including commissions | 350

Morgan notes that after several years of intense competition and weak pricing, many P&C insurers have lost capital and some have left the market.

questions.q: Harbour's loss ratio and expense ratio are closest to:
questions.why:
Loss ratio = (claims paid + increase in loss reserves) / net premiums earned = (690 + 90)/1,200 = 65.0% (efficiency of underwriting standards).
Expense ratio = underwriting expenses incl. commissions / net premiums written = 350/1,250 = 28.0% (efficiency of operations).

questions.q: Based on Morgan's note, the P&C cycle is most likely moving into a:
options: hard market, with reduced competition and higher premiums
soft market, because capital is shrinking
soft market, with more competition and lower premiums
questions.why: Cycle: soft market (high competition, weak prices) → capital shrinks and firms exit → reduced competition and higher prices (hard market) → higher profits attract new entrants → soft market again.

vignettes.body:
Felix Arnaud gives the investment committee three points on active management.

Point 1: An index fund that meets its objective exactly.
Point 2: A manager with a very low information coefficient.
Point 3: A change of the manager's benchmark to an index with a different risk profile.

questions.q: The information ratio of the index fund in Point 1 is most likely:
options: indeterminate but positive
equal to its Sharpe ratio
zero
questions.why: An index fund that tracks its benchmark exactly has zero active return, so its IR is zero.

questions.q: For the manager in Point 2, it will most likely be:
options: easy to add value if the manager overweights the securities with the best forecasts
hard to add value, even with many independent decisions or a high transfer coefficient
irrelevant, because IR depends only on breadth
questions.why: IR = TC × IC × √BR: a low IC (poor forecasting) makes it hard to add value. Managers should overweight securities with the best forecast relative returns, but this helps only if the forecasts are good.

questions.q: The change in Point 3 most likely affects:
options: the information ratio only, because the Sharpe ratio does not use the benchmark
both the Sharpe ratio and the information ratio
the Sharpe ratio only, because active risk does not change
questions.why: The Sharpe ratio, (Rp − Rf) ÷ σp, does not involve the benchmark, while the information ratio is built on active return and active risk measured against the benchmark. Changing the benchmark therefore changes the IR but not the Sharpe ratio.

vignettes.body:
Rosa Delgado leads a big data project at Calloway Credit to predict loan defaults from structured borrower data. Her team follows five steps but has written them in the wrong order: data exploration; data collection; model training; conceptualisation of the modelling task; data preparation and wrangling.

During data preparation the team finds the following problems in the raw data:
Problem 1: Some borrowers have no income recorded.
Problem 2: Dates of birth are recorded as DD/MM/YYYY for some borrowers and as YYYY-MM-DD for others.
Problem 3: The same borrower appears twice with identical records.

The team then transforms the data. It creates an "age" variable from date of birth and replaces extreme income values with the value at the 99th percentile. Finally it rescales income so that its values lie between 0 and 1.

questions.q: The correct order of the five steps for a structured data project is:
options: conceptualisation, data exploration, data collection, model training, data preparation and wrangling
data collection, conceptualisation, data exploration, data preparation and wrangling, model training
conceptualisation, data collection, data preparation and wrangling, data exploration, model training
questions.why: Structured data: conceptualisation of the modelling task → data collection → data preparation and wrangling → data exploration → model training.

questions.q: Problems 1, 2 and 3 are, respectively, examples of:
options: missing values, non-uniformity and duplication errors
invalid values, inaccuracy and duplication errors
missing values, invalid values and non-uniformity errors
questions.why: Data cleansing deals with errors in raw data: missing values, invalid values, inaccurate values, non-uniformity (same data in different formats) and duplicates.

questions.q: Creating age from date of birth and replacing extreme incomes with the 99th-percentile value are best described as:
options: aggregation and trimming
extraction and winsorisation
selection and standardisation
questions.why:
Data wrangling transformations: extraction (create a new variable from an existing one), aggregation, filtration (remove rows), selection (remove columns).
Outliers: trimming removes them; winsorisation replaces them with the value at a set percentile.

questions.q: The final rescaling of income is best described as:
options: winsorisation, which removes outliers
standardisation, which centres the variable at a mean of 0
normalisation, which is sensitive to outliers
questions.why:
Normalisation rescales to the range 0 to 1 (sensitive to outliers).
Standardisation centres at mean 0 with standard deviation 1 (assumes roughly normal data).

vignettes.body: Castell compares a REIT with a real estate operating company (REOC) for a client.

questions.q: Compared with a REOC, a REIT most likely:
options: can freely reinvest earnings and develop properties for sale, but pays corporate tax
has more flexible capital structure and lower dividend yields
must distribute most of its taxable income and is exempt from corporate income tax, which limits its ability to reinvest
questions.why: REIT: tax exempt if it distributes most income → high dividend yield, less retained capital, limits on development. REOC: ordinary taxable company, more freedom to reinvest, develop and use leverage; lower yield.

vignettes.body:
Aalto computes Kiruna's diluted shares. Basic weighted-average shares are 5,000,000 and the average share price is $30.

Exhibit 1: Potentially Dilutive Securities
# Security | Number | Exercise price | Average unrecognised compensation expense
Stock options | 200,000 | $18 | $600,000
Unvested RSUs | 60,000 | – | $900,000

Average unrecognised expense is the average of the beginning and ending unrecognised compensation expense.

questions.q: Kiruna's diluted shares are closest to:
questions.why:
Treasury stock method: dilutive shares = number − (cash proceeds + average unrecognised expense) / average price
Options: 200,000 − (200,000 × 18 + 600,000)/30 = 200,000 − 140,000 = 60,000
RSUs (no cash proceeds): 60,000 − 900,000/30 = 30,000
Diluted = 5,000,000 + 60,000 + 30,000 = 5,090,000

vignettes.body: Ana Petrova trades standardised CDS contracts at Vistula Bank. The Lark Corp. CDS has a standard coupon of 1%, and its current spread is 1.8%. The Mosel Inc. CDS has a standard coupon of 5%, and its current spread is 3.6%.

questions.q: If Petrova buys protection on Lark Corp., at initiation she will most likely:
options: pay nothing upfront, because standard contracts trade at par
receive an upfront premium from the protection seller
pay an upfront premium to the protection seller
questions.why: Spread > coupon → the coupon is too low for the risk → the protection buyer pays the difference upfront (CDS price below 100).

questions.q: If Petrova sells protection on Mosel Inc., at initiation she will most likely:
options: receive the full 5% coupon in advance
pay an upfront premium to the protection buyer
receive an upfront premium from the protection buyer
questions.why: Spread < coupon → the buyer pays a coupon that is too high → the protection seller pays the buyer upfront (CDS price above 100).

vignettes.body:
Ethics: Standards of Professional Conduct
Four independent questions. Each one can be answered on its own.

questions.q: Which procedures does VI(B), Priority of Transactions, recommend for personal trades?
options: No pre-clearance, but a quarterly review of all trades
Annual holdings reports only
Pre-clearance of trades (compliance approval) and duplicate trade confirmations or statements sent by the broker to the employer
questions.why: VI(B) recommends pre-clearance and having the broker send copies of personal trade confirmations or account statements to the employer.

questions.q: New laws took effect before the firm's policies were updated. The best fix is to:
options: Review all compliance policies once a year
Set up a process to learn about legal changes promptly
Train client service staff on the new laws
questions.why: Procedures must be updated before laws take effect, so the firm needs timely information on legal changes. An annual review can miss mid-year laws.

questions.q: Client information is confidential for:
options: Current clients only
Current and prospective clients, not former ones
Former, current and prospective clients
questions.why: III(E) covers all client information, whatever the status of the relationship.

questions.q: Insider trading is legal where a member works. Under I(A), the member must:
options: Follow local law, since it applies there
Follow the stricter rule: the CFA Standards
Follow whichever rule the employer picks
questions.why: I(A) Knowledge of the Law: when local law and the Standards differ, follow the stricter one.

title: Practice set 3
desc: Mixed topics from the key notes, with 4 Ethics questions (52 questions, 2 h 36 min)

vignettes.body:
Priya Natarajan uses equity index forwards at Kestrel Advisors. She enters a long nine-month forward on the Alba 100 index when the index is at 4,250. The index has a continuously compounded dividend yield of 1.8% and the continuously compounded risk-free rate is 3.5%.

Three months later the index is at 4,410. Rates and the dividend yield are unchanged.

questions.q: The initial forward price is closest to:
Three months after initiation, the value of the long forward is closest to:

vignettes.body:
Navas considers rolling down the yield curve. He would buy a five-year zero-coupon government bond and sell it after two years. The five-year spot rate is 3.0% and the three-year spot rate is 2.4%. He assumes the yield curve stays stable, so when he sells, the bond (then a three-year bond) is priced at today's three-year spot rate.

Navas also compares his projected spot curve with the current forward curve. For a two-year bond, he expects future spot rates to be below the current forward rates.

questions.q: Navas's annualised return from rolling down the curve is closest to:
questions.why:
Buy price = 100 / 1.030⁵ = 86.2609
Sell price after 2 years (now a 3-year bond) = 100 / 1.024³ = 93.1323
Annualised return = (sell / buy)^(1/H) − 1 with H = 2 = (93.1323/86.2609)^(1/2) − 1 = 3.91%
7.97% is the two-year total return, not annualised.

questions.q: If the projected spot curve is below the current forward curve, the bond is:
options: overvalued, so Navas should sell it
fairly valued, because forward rates are unbiased
undervalued, so Navas should buy it
questions.why:
Projected spot below forward → future prices higher than the forward prices imply → bond undervalued → buy.
Projected spot above forward → overvalued → sell.

vignettes.body: Castell analyses commodity futures. The spot price of crude oil is $82.00 per barrel. Storage costs are $2.50 per barrel for the period, and the convenience yield is $4.00 per barrel (expressed in the same terms). Ignore financing costs.

questions.q: The futures price is closest to:
questions.why: Futures price = spot + storage costs − convenience yield = 82.0 + 2.5 − 4.0 = $80.50

questions.q: The oil futures market is most likely in:
options: contango, because storage costs are positive
contango, because the convenience yield is high
backwardation, because the convenience yield exceeds storage costs
questions.why: Convenience yield > storage cost (low inventories) → futures below spot → backwardation. Storage costs > convenience yield (ample inventories) → contango.

vignettes.body:
Ethics: Standards of Professional Conduct
Four independent questions. Each one can be answered on its own.

questions.q: A supervisor spots suspicious activity by a team member. Which response is most appropriate?
options: Report it to the upper supervisor immediately, before any other step
Limit the member's trading and increase monitoring while looking into it
Meet the member in person to warn them
questions.why: IV(C): act to prevent further violation by limiting trading and monitoring more closely while the facts are investigated.

questions.q: Using third-party research is:
options: Not a violation, but the member must make reasonable efforts to determine whether the research is sound
A violation unless the third party is a charterholder
Fine without checks if the source is well known
questions.why: V(A): third-party information may be used, but the member needs diligence and a reasonable basis.

questions.q: Scott works for a regional brokerage firm. He estimates that Walkton Industries will increase its dividend by US$1.50 a share during the next year. He realizes that this increase is contingent on pending legislation that would, if enacted, give Walkton a substantial tax break. The US representative for Walkton’s home district has told Scott that, although she is lobbying hard for the bill and prospects for its passage are favorable, concern of the US Congress over the federal deficit could cause the tax bill to be voted down. Walkton Industries has not made any statements about a change in dividend policy. Scott writes in his research report, “We expect Walkton’s stock price to rise by at least US$8.00 a share by the end of the year because the dividend will increase by US$1.50 a share. Investors buying the stock at the current time should expect to realize a total return of at least 15% on the stock.” According to the Standards:
options: Scott violated the Standards because he used material inside information.
Scott violated the Standards because he failed to separate opinion from fact.
Scott violated the Standards by basing his research on uncertain predictions of future government action.
questions.why: This question relates to Standard V(B) Communication with Clients and Prospective Clients. Scott has issued a research report stating that he expects the price of Walkton Industries stock to rise by US$8 a share “because the dividend will increase” by US$1.50 per share. He has made this statement knowing that the dividend will increase only if Congress enacts certain legislation, an uncertain prospect.

questions.q: Which fee arrangement for issuer-paid research best supports independence?
options: Full disclosure of the arrangement and a flat fee, with no bonus, regardless of the conclusion or recommendation
A fee that is higher if the report is favourable
Payment partly in the issuer's shares
questions.why: Compensation must not depend on the conclusion (I(B), VI(A)). Disclose the arrangement and use a flat fee without bonus.

vignettes.body: Montclair and Quint Corp. each own 50% of a joint venture. Montclair's analyst compares reporting the joint venture with the equity method and with proportionate consolidation, and then compares these with the acquisition method used for a controlled subsidiary.

questions.q: Compared with the equity method, proportionate consolidation of the joint venture reports:
options: higher revenue, net income and equity
the same revenue, but higher net income
higher revenue and assets, but the same net income and equity
questions.why: Proportionate consolidation adds the venturer's share of revenues, expenses, assets and liabilities line by line. Net income and equity are the same as under the equity method.

questions.q: Ranking the three methods for total assets, liabilities and revenue gives:
options: equity method > proportionate consolidation > acquisition
proportionate consolidation > acquisition > equity method
acquisition > proportionate consolidation > equity method
questions.why: Acquisition adds 100% of the subsidiary; proportionate adds only the owned share; the equity method adds one line (investment) and one income line. Net income (to the parent) is the same under all three.

vignettes.body: Brenner values a three-year, 4% annual-coupon bond issued by Harrow Logistics. The value of the bond assuming no default (VND), using the benchmark government spot curve, is 104.20. His credit valuation adjustment (CVA), computed with risk-neutral probabilities of default, is 3.10. The bond trades at 102.40.

questions.q: Based on Brenner's analysis, the Harrow bond is:
options: overvalued, because its price is above VND − CVA
fairly valued, because the CVA uses risk-neutral probabilities
undervalued, because its price is below VND
questions.why:
Fair value = VND − CVA = 104.2 − 3.1 = 101.10
Price 102.4 > 101.10 → overvalued (sell).
Price < VND − CVA would mean undervalued.

questions.q: The credit spread on the Harrow bond implied by Brenner's fair value is closest to:
options: 62 bps
361 bps
108 bps
questions.why:
Credit spread = YTM of the credit-risky bond − YTM of the benchmark.
Benchmark YTM: N = 3, PMT = 4, FV = 100, PV = −104.2 (use VND, not the market price) → 2.529%
Risky YTM: PV = −101.10 → 3.607%
Spread = 108 bps. 62 bps uses the market price instead of the fair value.

vignettes.body:
Marin explains growth theory to junior staff.

Statement 1: "In the neoclassical model, in the steady state, growth of output per worker equals the rate of technological progress divided by labour's share, and total output grows at that rate plus labour force growth."
Statement 2: "In the steady state, the marginal product of capital equals the real interest rate, and MPK = α × Y/K."
Statement 3: "Capital deepening raises output per worker but runs into diminishing returns, so it cannot raise growth permanently."
Statement 4: "In the neoclassical model, capital flows from rich to poor countries, helping convergence."

questions.q: Which of Marin's statements are correct?
options: All four
Statements 1 and 3 only
Statements 2 and 4 only
questions.why: Neoclassical steady state: growth per capita = θ/(1 − α); total output growth = θ/(1 − α) + labour force growth. Steady state: MPK = r = αY/K. Capital deepening has diminishing returns. Open-economy neoclassical model: capital flows to poorer, capital-scarce countries with higher returns → convergence.

vignettes.body:
Petra Lindgren, CFO of Halvard Industries, reviews payout policy. Halvard's net income is SEK 900 million, its share price is SEK 120 and its EPS is SEK 9. It has 100 million shares and total equity of SEK 4,800 million.

Proposal 1: Borrow SEK 1,200 million at an after-tax cost of 5% and use it to repurchase shares at the market price.
Proposal 2: Pay a 10% stock dividend instead of cash.
Proposal 3: Raise the cash dividend from SEK 3.00 to SEK 3.60 per share.

A board member says Halvard's payout ratio is low because the company has high growth prospects, high flotation costs on new equity and shareholders face high tax rates on dividends.

questions.q: Based on Proposal 1, the debt-financed repurchase will most likely:
options: increase EPS, because the earnings yield is higher than the after-tax cost of debt
leave EPS unchanged, because shareholder wealth is unchanged
decrease EPS, because the earnings yield is lower than the after-tax cost of debt
questions.why:
Earnings yield = E/P = 9/120 = 7.5% (or 1 ÷ P/E). 7.5% > 5% after-tax cost of debt → EPS rises.
Check: new EPS = (900 − 0.05 × 1,200)/90 = 840/90 = 9.33 > 9.00. If earnings yield < cost of debt, EPS falls.

questions.q: After the repurchase in Proposal 1, Halvard's book value per share is closest to:
questions.why:
Shares bought = 1,200/120 = 10 million → 90 million left.
Equity = 4,800 − 1,200 = 3,600
BVPS = equity ÷ shares = 3,600/90 = SEK 40.00 (it falls because the price paid, 120, is above BVPS of 48).

questions.q: After the stock dividend in Proposal 2, Halvard's share price is most likely closest to:
questions.why: New price = old price / (1 + stock dividend %) = 120/1.10 = SEK 109.09. A scrip (stock) dividend does not change shareholder wealth.

questions.q: The market will most likely interpret Proposal 3 as:
options: a positive signal, because managers raise dividends only when they expect to sustain them
a negative signal, because cash leaves the company instead of funding growth
no signal, because dividend policy is irrelevant to firm value
questions.why: Initiating or increasing a dividend → positive signal; cutting or omitting → negative signal. Firms avoid raising dividends they cannot maintain.

questions.q: Which of the board member's reasons is consistent with a low payout ratio?
options: High tax rates on dividends only
High growth prospects only
All three
questions.why: Low payout is consistent with high growth opportunities, high flotation costs of new issues and high taxes on dividends.

vignettes.body:
Castell values Alpenhaus REIT. Next year's net operating income is CHF 32 million and the market capitalisation rate for similar properties is 6.4%. Alpenhaus also holds CHF 18 million of cash and other tangible assets, and has CHF 290 million of debt. It has 10 million shares.

Castell notes that Alpenhaus is highly leveraged and trades at a large discount to NAVPS, and that its debt matures next year.

questions.q: Alpenhaus's NAVPS is closest to:
questions.why:
Property value by direct capitalisation (not depreciated book cost) = NOI / cap rate = 32.0/0.064 = CHF 500.0m
NAV = 500.0 + 18 − 290 = 228.0m
NAVPS = 228.0/10 = CHF 22.80

questions.q: Castell's concern about Alpenhaus most likely relates to:
options: an advantage, because the discount to NAVPS makes it cheap to issue new equity
refinancing risk, because a highly leveraged REIT trading below NAVPS may struggle to raise new capital
inflation risk, because its long leases have fixed rents that do not rise with prices
questions.why: High leverage plus a deep discount to NAVPS signals market concern; issuing equity below NAV is dilutive and lenders are cautious, so refinancing maturing debt is hard.

vignettes.body:
Sanne de Vries, a credit analyst, reviews retail and securitised credit.

Applicant 1 has a long credit history, no late payments, low use of available credit, few recent credit enquiries and uses many types of credit.
Bond 2 is a subordinated bond of a company whose senior unsecured debt is rated A.
Pool 3 is a large pool of short-term, homogeneous and granular credit card receivables.
Pool 4 is a pool of medium-term, homogeneous and granular auto loans.

questions.q: Applicant 1 most likely has a high credit score, and Bond 2 is most likely rated:
options: below A, because ratings are notched down for lower-priority debt
above A, because subordinated bonds pay higher coupons
A, because all debt of an issuer has the same rating
questions.why:
Credit scores rise with long histories, no delinquencies, low utilisation, few enquiries and a wide variety of credit.
Ratings apply to senior unsecured debt; other classes are notched (lower priority → higher loss given default → lower rating).

questions.q: The most appropriate approaches to analyse Pools 3 and 4 are, respectively:
options: loan-by-loan analysis for both
statistical and portfolio approaches
portfolio and statistical approaches
questions.why:
Short-term, homogeneous and granular (e.g. credit cards) → statistical approach.
Medium-term, homogeneous and granular (e.g. auto loans) → portfolio approach.
Non-granular pools need loan-by-loan analysis.

vignettes.body:
Lindgren compares dividend policies and repurchase methods.

Company A pays a dividend of SEK 2.00 per share every year, whatever its earnings.
Company B pays out 40% of earnings every year.

Method 1: Buy shares in the open market over time.
Method 2: A fixed-price tender offer or Dutch auction.
Method 3: A direct negotiation with a large shareholder.

A hedge fund has bought a large stake in Halvard and threatens a takeover unless Halvard buys its shares back at a premium.

questions.q: The dividend policies of Companies A and B are, respectively:
options: constant payout and stable
residual and stable
stable and constant payout
questions.why: Stable dividend: the amount stays the same (or grows smoothly). Constant payout: the percentage of earnings stays the same (sometimes a target range).

questions.q: Which statement about the repurchase methods is most accurate?
options: Method 1 usually buys at a premium; Method 2 is the most flexible; Method 3 is always done at a premium
Method 1 is the most flexible; Methods 2 usually buy at a premium; Method 3 may be done at a discount
Method 1 is the least flexible; Method 2 always buys at a discount; Method 3 is done at the market price
questions.why: Open market = flexible. Fixed-price tender / Dutch auction → premium to market. Negotiated (direct) → can be at a discount, or at a premium in greenmail.

questions.q: The hedge fund's demand is best described as:
options: greenmail
a liquidating dividend
a Dutch auction
questions.why: Greenmail = buying back a hostile bidder's shares at a premium to stop a takeover.

questions.q: Compared with paying the same amount as a cash dividend, a share repurchase leaves shareholder wealth:
options: lower, because the shares are bought at market price
higher, because the share count falls
the same, unless taxes or signalling differ
questions.why: With equal amounts and no taxes or signalling effects, shareholders' wealth is the same under a repurchase and a cash dividend.

vignettes.body: Felix Arnaud examines an active equity portfolio to which the manager adds cash.

questions.q: Adding cash to an active portfolio most likely:
options: changes neither ratio
changes the Sharpe ratio but leaves the information ratio unchanged
leaves the Sharpe ratio unchanged but changes the information ratio
questions.why: Mixing with cash scales excess return and risk equally → Sharpe ratio unchanged. But the cash creates active weights against the benchmark, changing active return and active risk, so the IR changes (falls).

vignettes.body: An analyst invests a fixed amount of money each month in a fund (cost averaging). Over five months the fund's unit price changes each month. She computes the arithmetic, geometric and harmonic means of the unit prices.

questions.q: For a set of positive unit prices that are not all equal, the relationship between the three means is:
options: harmonic < geometric < arithmetic
arithmetic < geometric < harmonic
geometric < harmonic < arithmetic
questions.why: For positive values that are not all equal: harmonic mean < geometric mean < arithmetic mean. They are equal only if all values are the same. The harmonic mean gives the average cost per unit under cost averaging.

vignettes.body:
Brenner models default risk for two issuers over three years.

Issuer 1 has a constant annual hazard rate of 2.0%.
Issuer 2 has hazard rates of 1.5% in year 1, 2.5% in year 2 and 3.5% in year 3. Brenner notes that hazard rates that change every year are more realistic.

questions.q: For Issuer 1, the probability of default in year 3 (PD3) is closest to:
questions.why:
PD_t = PS_(t−1) × hazard rate, with PS_t = (1 − h)^t
PS2 = 0.98² = 0.9604
PD3 = 0.9604 × 0.02 = 1.921%
5.881% is the cumulative PD over three years.

questions.q: For Issuer 2, the probability of survival to the end of year 3 is closest to:

vignettes.body:
Lucia Ferrante, an economist at Banca Orsini, explains the links between the economy and asset prices.

Point 1: The price of an asset equals E(CF) / (1 + Rf + π + θ + φ), where π is expected inflation, θ is the premium for inflation uncertainty and φ is the premium for other risks such as default and illiquidity.
Point 2: A one-year default-free zero-coupon bond with par of 100 trades at 95.77. The real risk-free rate is 1.5% and expected inflation over the next year is 2.5%.
Point 3: Country 1 has nominal GDP growth of 8.5% and inflation of 3.0%, with low volatility of growth. Country 2 has nominal GDP growth of 6.0% and inflation of 0.5%, with high volatility of growth.
Point 4: The inter-temporal rate of substitution (ITRS) is the marginal utility of consuming one unit in the future divided by the marginal utility of consuming one unit now.

questions.q: Based on Point 2, the inflation uncertainty premium is closest to:
Based on Point 3, real interest rates are most likely higher in:
options: Country 2, because real growth is the same but growth is more volatile
Country 1, because nominal growth is higher
neither country, because real growth is the same
questions.why: Real GDP growth = nominal − inflation: Country 1 = 8.5 − 3.0 = 5.5%; Country 2 = 6.0 − 0.5 = 5.5%. Equal real growth, so compare volatility: higher volatility → investors demand higher real rates.

questions.q: If investors expect to be much better off in the future, the ITRS and real interest rates most likely:
options: rise and fall, respectively
fall and rise, respectively
both rise
questions.why: Better off later → future consumption worth less at the margin (numerator falls) → ITRS falls → investors save less → real rates rise. If they expect to be worse off, ITRS rises and real rates fall.

vignettes.body:
Sofia Greco, an analyst at Aurelio Research, regresses the monthly excess return of a consumer-goods portfolio on three factors (market, size and value) using 60 monthly observations. Exhibit 1 shows the ANOVA results.

Exhibit 1: ANOVA for the Three-Factor Model
# Source | Degrees of freedom | Sum of squares
Regression | 3 | 0.0770
Error | 56 | 0.0480
Total | 59 | 0.1250

Greco then estimates a restricted model that drops the size and value factors. Its sum of squared errors is 0.0560.

Greco also compares two candidate models. Model A has AIC −310 and BIC −298. Model B has AIC −314 and BIC −296.

Greco's colleague states: "Adding another factor will always increase the adjusted R², so we should keep adding factors."

questions.q: The standard error of estimate of the three-factor model is closest to:
questions.why:
SEE = √MSE = √(SSE / (n − k − 1)) = √(0.048 / 56) = 0.0293
0.000857 is the MSE (no square root).

questions.q: The adjusted R² of the three-factor model is closest to:
The F-statistic for testing whether size and value are jointly zero is closest to:
questions.why:
Nested F = [(SSE_R − SSE_U)/q] / [SSE_U/(n − k − 1)] with q = 2
= [(0.056 − 0.048)/2] / [0.048/56] = 4.67
29.94 is the overall F-test (RSS/k ÷ SSE/(n−k−1)), which asks whether at least one factor explains Y.

questions.q: Based on AIC and BIC, which model is preferred for forecasting and which for goodness of fit?
options: Model A for forecasting; Model B for goodness of fit
Model B for forecasting; Model A for goodness of fit
Model B for both
questions.why:
Lower is better for both.
AIC (better forecast): Model B (−314 < −310).
BIC (better goodness of fit, heavier penalty for extra variables): Model A (−298 < −296).

questions.q: Greco's colleague's statement is:
options: correct, because adjusted R² always lies between 0 and 1
correct, because R² never falls when a variable is added
incorrect, because adjusted R² can fall when a variable is added and can even be negative
questions.why: R² never falls when a variable is added, but adjusted R² penalises extra variables: it falls when the new variable adds little, and it can be negative.

vignettes.body:
Lucia Ferrante makes three further observations.

Observation 1: The economy has a positive output gap.
Observation 2: Credit spreads between government and corporate bonds, and between higher- and lower-rated corporate bonds, are narrowing.
Observation 3: An investor compares a building leased to a government agency with a similar building leased to commercial tenants.

questions.q: Observation 1 most likely means that:
options: the economy is growing at its sustainable rate
actual GDP is above potential GDP, with rising inflation pressure and low unemployment
actual GDP is below potential GDP, with high unemployment
questions.why: Positive output gap: producing beyond sustainable capacity → high inflation and low unemployment.

questions.q: Based on Observation 2, which is most likely to perform best?
options: Lower-rated corporate bonds
Government bonds
Higher-rated corporate bonds
questions.why: Narrowing spreads: corporate bonds beat government bonds, and lower-rated bonds beat higher-rated bonds (their spreads fall most).

questions.q: For Observation 3, the commercial building's rental income should most likely be discounted at:
options: a higher rate, because it includes a credit risk premium for the tenants
the same rate, because both include inflation and inflation uncertainty premiums
a lower rate, because commercial rents rise faster
questions.why: Value = net rental income / (1 + r)^t, where net rental income = rental payments − rental expenses. Both rates include inflation (π) and inflation uncertainty (θ); the commercial lease also includes a credit risk premium (φ), so its discount rate is higher.

vignettes.body:
One year ago, Aldren Manufacturing entered a four-year interest rate swap with annual payments to pay a fixed rate of 2.10% and receive MRR on a notional principal of $60 million. Aldren's treasurer, Gwen Ashby, wants to know the swap's value today, exactly one year after initiation, just after the first settlement. Exhibit 1 shows current present value factors.

Exhibit 1: Present Value Factors
# Maturity (years) | Present value factor
1 | 0.9732
2 | 0.9441
3 | 0.9135
4 | 0.8820

questions.q: The fixed rate on a new swap that matches the remaining term of Aldren's swap is closest to:
questions.why:
Three annual payments remain, so use only Z1, Z2 and Z3.
SFR = (1 − Z3) / (Z1 + Z2 + Z3) = (1 − 0.9135) / 2.8308 = 3.0557%
3.18% wrongly uses all four factors.

questions.q: The value of the swap to Aldren (the fixed-rate payer) is closest to:
questions.why:
Value (pay fixed) = ΣZ × (SFRnew − SFRold) × NP (annual payments, so the period factor is 1)
= 2.8308 × (3.0557% − 2.10%) × 60,000,000 = $1,623,192
Rates rose above the old fixed rate, so the payer of fixed gains.

vignettes.body:
Ilse Brandt, a portfolio strategist, describes three past changes in the yield curve.

Episode 1: Short-term yields fell much more than long-term yields during a recession.
Episode 2: During an economic expansion, short-term yields rose more than long-term yields as the central bank tightened.
Episode 3: During a market panic, long-term yields fell much more than short-term yields as investors rushed into long-dated government bonds.

questions.q: Episode 1 is best described as a:
options: bullish flattening
bullish steepening
bearish flattening
questions.why: Bullish = yields fall (prices rise). Short yields fall more → curve steepens → bullish steepening (typical in recessions when the central bank cuts).

questions.q: Episode 2 is best described as a:
options: bullish flattening
bearish flattening
bearish steepening
questions.why: Bearish = yields rise. Short yields rise more than long → curve flattens → bearish flattening (expansion, tightening).

questions.q: Episode 3 is a bullish flattening, also called a flight to quality. A manager who expected it should have:
options: bought short-term bills only
shortened duration and used a bullet
extended duration and used a barbell
questions.why: Long yields fall most → long bonds gain most → extend duration, using a barbell with long bonds.

vignettes.body:
Helena Dvorak is a fixed-income portfolio manager. Pavel Kuiper, a junior analyst, and Dvorak meet to review several positions in Dvorak's portfolio.

Dvorak begins the meeting by discussing credit rating migration. Dvorak asks Kuiper to estimate the expected return over the next year on a bond issued by Halden Group. The BBB rated bond has a yield to maturity of 5.10% and a modified duration of 7.25. Kuiper calculates the expected return on the bond over the next year given the partial credit transition and credit spread data in Exhibit 1. Kuiper assumes that market spreads and yields will remain stable over the year.

Exhibit 1
One-Year Transition Matrix for BBB Rated Bonds and Credit Spreads
# Rating | AAA | AA | A | BBB | BB | B | CCC, CC, C
Probability (%) | 0.05 | 0.55 | 6.20 | 83.45 | 7.40 | 2.00 | 0.35
Credit spread | 0.45% | 0.70% | 0.95% | 1.30% | 3.00% | 5.80% | 8.60%

Dvorak next asks Kuiper to analyze a three-year bond, issued by Estrava S.A., using an arbitrage-free framework. The bond's coupon rate is 3.5%, with interest paid annually and a par value of 100. In the analysis, Kuiper makes the following three assumptions:
The annual interest rate volatility is 12%.
The recovery rate is one-third of the exposure each period.
The annual probability of default each year is 1.20%.

Selected information on benchmark government bonds for the Estrava bond is presented in Exhibit 2, and the relevant binomial interest rate tree is presented in Exhibit 3.

Exhibit 2
Par Curve Rates for Annual Payment Benchmark Government Bonds
# Maturity | Coupon rate | Price | Discount factor | Spot rate | Forward rate
1 | 2.20% | 100 | 0.978474 | 2.2000% | 2.2000%
2 | 2.90% | 100 | 0.944241 | 2.9102% | 3.6254%
3 | 3.50% | 100 | 0.901164 | 3.5298% | 4.7802%

Exhibit 3
One-Year Binomial Interest Rate Tree for 12% Volatility (risk-neutral probability of 50% on each branch)
# Date | 0 | 1 (top) | 1 (bottom) | 2 (top) | 2 (middle) | 2 (bottom)
Rate | 2.2000% | 4.0604% | 3.1940% | 6.0010% | 4.7205% | 3.7133%

Kuiper estimates the value of the Estrava bond assuming no default (VND) as well as the fair value of the bond. Kuiper then estimates the bond's yield to maturity and the bond's credit spread over the benchmark in Exhibit 2. Kuiper asks Dvorak, "What might cause the bond's credit spread to decrease?"

Dvorak and Kuiper next discuss the drivers of the term structure of credit spreads. Kuiper tells Dvorak the following:

Statement 1:
