The credit term structure for the most highly rated securities tends to be either flat or slightly upward sloping.

Statement 2:
The credit term structure for lower-rated securities is often steeper, and credit spreads widen with expectations of strong economic growth.

questions.q: Based on Exhibit 1, the one-year expected return on the Halden Group bond is closest to:
questions.why:
A. Correct. Expected return = YTM + expected percentage price change from migration. For each rating the price change = −modified duration × (new spread − 1.30%) × probability:
AAA: −7.25 × (0.45% − 1.30%) × 0.05% = +0.0031%
AA: −7.25 × (0.70% − 1.30%) × 0.55% = +0.0239%
A: −7.25 × (0.95% − 1.30%) × 6.20% = +0.1573%
BB: −7.25 × (3.00% − 1.30%) × 7.40% = -0.9121%
B: −7.25 × (5.80% − 1.30%) × 2.00% = -0.6525%
CCC, CC, C: −7.25 × (8.60% − 1.30%) × 0.35% = -0.1852%
BBB: no change = 0
Sum = -1.5655%. Expected return = 5.10% − 1.57% = 3.53%.
B. Incorrect. 5.10% is the yield to maturity only; it ignores the negative effect of migration.
C. Incorrect. 6.67% adds the absolute size of the migration effect (5.10% + 1.57%), treating it as a gain; downgrades have a larger price effect than upgrades, so migration lowers the expected return.

questions.q: Based on Kuiper's assumptions and Exhibits 2 and 3, the credit spread on the Estrava bond is closest to:
questions.why:
B. Correct. Step 1: VND from the tree (discount at the tree rates, probability 0.5 on each branch, coupon 3.5) = 100.0000.
Step 2: CVA = sum of DF × probability of default × LGD × expected exposure. Expected exposures 102.2000, 102.2760, 103.5000; LGD = 2/3 of exposure (recovery one-third); probabilities of default in each year 1.2000%, 1.1856%, 1.1714%; benchmark discount factors 0.978474, 0.944241, 0.901164. CVA = 0.8000 + 0.7633 + 0.7284 = 2.2917.
Step 3: Fair value = 100.0000 − 2.2917 = 97.7083. The yield to maturity that prices the bond at 97.7083 is 4.3310%.
Step 4: Credit spread = 4.3310% − 3.5000% (3-year benchmark coupon) = 0.8310%.
A. Incorrect. 0.6208% results from using a loss given default of 50% of exposure instead of 2/3.
C. Incorrect. 1.2565% results from assuming no recovery (loss given default of 100%).

questions.q: The most appropriate response to Kuiper's question relating to the credit spread is:
options: a decrease in the risk-neutral probability of default.
an increase in the loss given default.
an increase in the probability of default.
questions.why:
A. Correct. A lower risk-neutral probability of default lowers the CVA, raises the fair value and lowers the yield and the credit spread.
B. Incorrect. A higher loss given default raises the CVA and widens the credit spread.
C. Incorrect. A higher probability of default raises the CVA, lowers the fair value and widens the credit spread.

questions.q: Which of Kuiper's statements regarding the term structure of credit spreads is correct?
options: Only Statement 1
Only Statement 2
Both Statements 1 and 2
questions.why:
A. Correct. For the highest-rated issuers spreads are very low (with a floor at zero), so the credit term structure is flat or slightly upward sloping (Statement 1 is correct).
B. Incorrect. Lower-rated issuers are more sensitive to the credit cycle, but their credit spreads narrow (not widen) with expectations of strong economic growth, so Statement 2 is incorrect.
C. Incorrect. Statement 2 is incorrect.

title: Practice set 4
desc: Mixed topics from the key notes, with 4 Ethics questions (54 questions, 2 h 42 min)

vignettes.body:
Lukas Brenner, a credit analyst at Alder Bank, values short-term debt of Fenwick Ltd. A one-year Fenwick zero-coupon bond trades at 95.80 per 100 of par. The one-year risk-free rate is 2.0%, and the recovery rate if Fenwick defaults is 40%.

Brenner also values a Fenwick bond that matures in one year and pays a final coupon of 5 with the principal of 100. He estimates the hazard rate for the year at 3% and the same 40% recovery rate on the amount owed.

questions.q: The risk-neutral probability of default implied by the zero-coupon bond is closest to:
The expected value at maturity of the coupon bond is closest to:
questions.why:
Expected value = (principal + coupon) × (1 − hazard rate) + (principal + coupon) × recovery rate × hazard rate
= 105 × 0.97 + 105 × 0.40 × 0.03 = 101.85 + 1.26 = 103.11

questions.q: If the risk-neutral probability of default on Fenwick debt falls, Fenwick's credit spread will most likely:
options: increase
decrease
not change, because the spread includes only liquidity risk
questions.why: A lower risk-neutral PD means lower expected loss, so the credit spread falls. In practice, the observed spread over the risk-free yield also includes liquidity and tax effects, not only credit risk.

vignettes.body:
Leah Morgan, a bank analyst, compares two banks. Exhibit 1 shows selected ratios for the last two years.

Exhibit 1: Selected Ratios
# Ratio | Bank X last year | Bank X this year | Bank Y last year | Bank Y this year
Allowance for loan losses / net charge-offs | 2.8 | 3.4 | 2.6 | 2.1
Provision for loan losses / net charge-offs | 1.0 | 1.3 | 1.0 | 0.8
Allowance for loan losses / nonperforming loans | 1.1 | 1.3 | 1.2 | 0.9
Liquid assets / total assets | 0.18 | 0.21 | 0.20 | 0.17
Loans / total assets | 0.62 | 0.60 | 0.61 | 0.66
Trading revenue / total revenue | 0.08 | 0.07 | 0.15 | 0.24

Bank X funds itself mainly with long-term consumer deposits; Bank Y relies on short-term interbank borrowing. Morgan expects the yield curve to invert next year.

questions.q: Based on the loan loss ratios, which bank is accounting more conservatively and building a larger cushion?
options: Neither, because both provision ratios equal 1 last year
Bank X
Bank Y
questions.why: Allowance/charge-offs rising → bigger cushion. Provision/charge-offs > 1 → conservative; = 1 → flat allowance; < 1 → aggressive. Allowance/NPLs rising → sufficient provisioning. All three improve for Bank X and worsen for Bank Y.

questions.q: Based on asset quality and earnings quality, which statement is most accurate?
options: Bank X is better: higher liquid assets, lower loans to assets and a smaller share of volatile trading revenue
Bank Y is better, because a higher loans-to-assets ratio means more interest income
Bank Y is better, because higher trading revenue means more diversified earnings
questions.why: Liquid assets/total assets ↑ = good; loans/total assets ↑ = more credit risk (bad). Trading revenue is volatile and not sustainable, so a lower share of revenue is better.

questions.q: Which bank has the more stable funding, and what effect would an inverted yield curve most likely have on bank net interest revenue?
options: Bank X; net interest revenue would rise
Bank X; net interest revenue would fall
Bank Y; net interest revenue would rise
questions.why:
Stable funding: longer-term and consumer (retail) deposits are stickier than short-term interbank funding.
Banks borrow short and lend long (maturity transformation). An inverted curve raises short-term funding costs relative to long-term lending rates → lower net interest revenue.

questions.q: Which item is included in Common Equity Tier 1 capital?
options: Retained earnings
Preferred stock with discretionary dividends
Subordinated convertible bonds
questions.why:
CET1: common stock, additional paid-in capital, retained earnings, OCI, less intangibles and deferred tax assets.
Other Tier 1: preferred stock with discretionary dividends. Tier 2: subordinated debt such as convertible bonds.

vignettes.body:
Tobias Weller values the preferred shares and estimates growth for Ostmark AG.

Ostmark's non-callable, non-convertible perpetual preferred shares pay €4.50 a year. The risk-free rate is 3.0% and the equity risk premium applicable to the preferred shares is 4.5%.

Ostmark expects EPS of €6.00 next year with a target payout of 45%. Its most recent dividend was €2.40, and it expects to move to the target payout over three years in equal annual steps.

Ostmark's ROE is 12% and its retention ratio is 55%.

questions.q: The value of Ostmark's preferred shares is closest to:
questions.why:
Preferred value = D / r, with r = Rf + ERP = 3.0% + 4.5% = 7.5% (check whether you are given r or only the ERP).
Value = 4.50 / 0.075 = €60.00. (€100 uses only the ERP; €150 uses only Rf.)

questions.q: Next year's expected dividend is closest to:
questions.why:
Expected growth in dividend = [(expected EPS × target payout) − previous dividend] / n = (6.00 × 0.45 − 2.40)/3 = (2.70 − 2.40)/3 = 0.10
Next dividend = 2.40 + 0.10 = €2.50

questions.q: Ostmark's sustainable growth rate is closest to:
questions.why: g = b × ROE = 0.55 × 12% = 6.6%, where b = retention ratio = 1 − payout ratio (payout = DPS/EPS).

vignettes.body:
Varga gives the class a two-factor model for Stock K:
R(K) = a(K) + b1 F1 + b2 F2 + e(K)
where F1 and F2 are surprises in the two factors (expected value zero).

He also gives an APT-type equation for Portfolio M: the risk-free rate is 3%, the portfolio's sensitivities to factors 1 and 2 are 1.2 and −0.4, and the factor risk premiums are 4% and 2%.

questions.q: The expected return of Stock K equals:
options: b1 F1 + b2 F2
a(K) + b1 + b2
a(K) only
questions.why: With factors measured as surprises, E(F1) = E(F2) = 0, so E(R) = a(K). a(K) is the expected return only because the other terms have zero expected value.

questions.q: The expected return of Portfolio M is closest to:

vignettes.body:
Montclair Holdings acquires 80% of Tessaro SpA for €800 million in cash. The fair value of Tessaro's identifiable net assets is €850 million. Montclair's analyst compares the full goodwill and partial goodwill methods.

The analyst also considers a different deal in which the entire excess of the purchase price over book value is allocated to identifiable assets.

questions.q: Goodwill under the full goodwill method is closest to:
options: €50 million
€120 million
€150 million
questions.why: Full goodwill = purchase price / % owned − FV of identifiable net assets = 800/0.80 − 850 = 1,000 − 850 = €150m.

questions.q: Under the partial goodwill method, goodwill and the non-controlling interest are closest to:
options: €120 million and €170 million
€150 million and €200 million
€120 million and €200 million
questions.why:
Partial goodwill = 800 − 0.80 × 850 = €120m.
NCI (partial) = % not owned × identifiable net assets = 0.20 × 850 = €170m.
(Full method: NCI = 0.20 × 1,000 = €200m.)

questions.q: Compared with the full goodwill method, the partial goodwill method most likely reports:
options: the same ROE and ROA
lower ROE and lower ROA
higher ROE and higher ROA
questions.why: Partial goodwill gives smaller goodwill (lower assets) and smaller NCI (lower equity), with the same net income → higher ROA and ROE.

questions.q: In the deal where the entire excess is allocated to identifiable assets, goodwill is:
options: positive under the full method only
equal to the excess of fair value over book value
zero under both the full and partial goodwill methods
questions.why: If all of the excess goes to identifiable assets, nothing is left for goodwill under either method.

vignettes.body: Ruth Okafor supervises the options desk at Tellis Securities. She reviews four positions: a long call, a short call, a long put and a short put, all on Ardent Mining shares. A client who owns 50,000 Ardent shares asks Okafor how buying put options on Ardent would change the risk of the client's position.

questions.q: Which of the four positions has negative gamma and positive theta?
options: Short put
Long put
Long call
questions.why:
Long options (call or put): gamma +, vega +, theta −.
Short options (call or put): gamma −, vega −, theta +.
So the short put (and the short call) has negative gamma and positive theta.

questions.q: Compared with holding the shares alone, the client's position after buying the puts will most likely have:
options: lower delta and positive gamma
lower delta and negative vega
higher delta and negative gamma
questions.why:
Long stock delta = +1. A long put has delta between −1 and 0, so total delta falls.
A long put has gamma + and vega +, and the stock has none, so the position gains positive gamma and positive vega.

questions.q: Which Greeks are negative for a long put?
options: Delta and rho
Delta and gamma
Gamma and vega
questions.why:
Long put signs: delta −, gamma +, vega +, theta −, rho −.
Higher rates lower put values, so rho is negative.

vignettes.body:
Bettina Kral, a fixed-income analyst, gives the class a two-asset example. Both assets are risk free and mature at time 1.

Exhibit 1: Two Risk-Free Assets
# Asset | Price today | Payoff at time 1
A | 500 | 520
B | 1,000 | 1,060

questions.q: Based on the dominance principle, the arbitrage strategy and its profit at time 1 are:
options: buy one unit of A, short sell one unit of B: profit of 60
buy two units of A, short sell one unit of B: profit of 20
short sell two units of A, buy one unit of B: profit of 20
questions.why:
Price per 1 of payoff: A = 500/520 = 0.9615; B = 1,000/1,060 = 0.9434. B is cheaper.
Buy the cheap asset, sell the expensive one at zero net cost: short 2 A (+1,000), buy 1 B (−1,000).
Time 1: receive 1,060 from B, pay 2 × 520 = 1,040 on A → profit 20.

vignettes.body:
Sven Aalto analyses the share-based compensation of Kiruna Tech, a US GAAP reporter with a 25% tax rate.

During the year 30,000 RSUs vested. They were granted at the start of the year with a grant-date fair value of $24 per RSU, and Kiruna's share price on the vesting date was $31. In the same year, 2,000 unvested RSUs from an earlier grant (grant-date fair value $22) were forfeited, and the full expense previously recognised for them ($22 per RSU) is reversed this year.

Kiruna also grants stock options. Aalto considers how changes in valuation inputs affect the options' fair value and Kiruna's reported earnings.

questions.q: Kiruna's RSU compensation expense for the year is closest to:
questions.why:
RSU expense = vested × grant-date FV − forfeited × their FV = 30,000 × 24 − 2,000 × 22 = 720,000 − 44,000 = $676,000.
The vesting-date price ($31) does not affect the expense.

questions.q: The tax effect of the RSU vesting and its accounting under US GAAP is closest to:
options: a $52,500 shortfall that increases income tax expense
a $52,500 windfall that reduces income tax expense
a $52,500 windfall recorded in equity
questions.why:
Tax effect = units vested × (settlement price − grant-date value) × tax rate = 30,000 × (31 − 24) × 25% = $52,500.
Positive → windfall. US GAAP: through the income statement (lower tax expense). IFRS: excess goes to equity.

questions.q: Because of the windfall, Kiruna's effective tax rate under US GAAP compared with what it would be under IFRS is:
options: lower
higher
the same
questions.why: US GAAP: the windfall reduces income tax expense → lower effective tax rate. IFRS: excess goes to equity → no effect on the rate, so IFRS shows a higher rate for a windfall (and a lower one for a shortfall).

questions.q: The vesting of the RSUs increases Kiruna's basic shares outstanding by:
options: 28,000 shares
30,000 shares
0 shares, because RSUs are only potentially dilutive
questions.why: Once RSUs vest they become common shares: basic shares rise by the number vested (30,000). Unvested RSUs are potentially dilutive.

questions.q: Holding other inputs constant, which change in the option valuation inputs would increase Kiruna's reported net income?
options: A higher risk-free rate
A longer expected option life
A higher expected dividend yield
questions.why:
Option value ↑ with higher risk-free rate, longer life and higher volatility → higher compensation expense → lower net income (bad for the company).
Higher dividend yield → lower call value → lower expense → higher net income.

questions.q: If expected share price volatility rises, the fair value of RSUs and of stock options at grant will most likely:
options: increase for RSUs and stay the same for options
increase for both
stay the same for RSUs and increase for options
questions.why: RSU fair value = share price at grant, not affected by volatility. Option value rises with volatility → higher expense and lower net income.

vignettes.body:
Kaito Mori, a treasury analyst at Shirane Bank, entered a long 6 × 9 FRA (pay fixed, receive three-month MRR) on a notional of €25 million at an FRA rate of 2.40%. The FRA is settled in advance: the settlement amount is paid at FRA expiration, discounted at the three-month MRR.

Situation 1: Ninety days after initiation, the rate on a new 3 × 6 FRA is 2.70% and the 180-day discount rate is 2.60%.
Situation 2: At FRA expiration (month 6), three-month MRR is 2.85%.

questions.q: In Situation 1, the value of Mori's FRA is closest to:
questions.why:
Value (pay fixed) = (FRAg − FRA0) × tm × NP / (1 + D(T−g) × t(T−g))
= (2.70% − 2.40%) × 90/360 × 25,000,000 / (1 + 0.026 × 180/360)
= 18,750 / 1.013 = €18,509
Rates rose, so the fixed payer (long FRA) has a positive value.

questions.q: In Situation 2, the settlement amount Mori receives at FRA expiration is closest to:
questions.why:
Interest difference paid at T (month 9) = (2.85% − 2.40%) × 90/360 × 25,000,000 = €28,125
Settled at month 6, so discount for 90 days at MRR: 28,125 / (1 + 0.0285 × 90/360) = €27,926

vignettes.body:
Maya Lindqvist explains unsupervised and deep learning methods to new hires at Fjord Analytics.

Method 1 groups 2,000 stocks. It starts with each stock as its own cluster and repeatedly merges the two closest clusters until one cluster remains.
Method 2 also groups stocks, but the analyst must choose the number of clusters, k, before running it.
Method 3 is a neural network with many hidden layers that learns to recognise patterns in satellite images.

Lindqvist warns that including a very large number of features can cause the model to fit noise. She plots a learning curve to check the problem.

questions.q: Method 1 is best described as:
options: k-means clustering
divisive (top-down) hierarchical clustering
agglomerative (bottom-up) hierarchical clustering
questions.why:
Agglomerative = bottom-up: start with each observation as its own cluster and merge similar clusters over time.
Divisive = top-down: start with one cluster and split it over time.
k-means needs k (a hyperparameter) chosen in advance: that is Method 2.

questions.q: A neural network such as Method 3 is classified as a deep learning network when it has:
options: no hidden layers but many input nodes
at least two hidden layers (often more than 20)
exactly one hidden layer
questions.why: Deep learning nets (DLNs) have at least 2 hidden layers, and in practice often more than 20.

questions.q: Which statement about Lindqvist's warning is most accurate?
options: Overfitting is mainly a concern for unsupervised learning; a learning curve plots the number of clusters against accuracy
Overfitting is a concern for supervised learning; a learning curve plots accuracy in the validation or test sample against the size of the training sample
Overfitting cannot occur when many features are used; a learning curve plots training time against the number of features
questions.why:
Overfitting (fitting noise, often with too many features) is a problem for supervised learning, not unsupervised learning.
Learning curve: accuracy in the validation/test sample versus the size of the training sample.

vignettes.body:
Kovacs evaluates a merger between Danubia's client Velkor and a competitor. Velkor expects (1) revenue gains from cross-selling, (2) cost savings from closing duplicate offices, (3) some customers leaving because of overlap and (4) one-time integration costs.

To value the competitor she gathers the P/E ratios of five comparable companies: 14, 16, 18, 21 and 31. The competitor's EPS is €2.50.

questions.q: Which items increase the combined company's operating income?
options: Items 1, 2 and 3
Items 1 and 2 only
Items 3 and 4 only
questions.why: Revenue synergies and cost synergies raise operating income. Revenue dis-synergies (lost customers), cost dis-synergies and one-time integration costs reduce it. Think of where each hits operating income.

questions.q: Using comparable companies, the competitor's value per share is closest to:
questions.why: Use the median P/E, not the mean: median of 14, 16, 18, 21, 31 = 18. Value = 18 × 2.50 = €45.00. (Mean = 20 → €50; the outlier 31 distorts it.)

vignettes.body:
Ravi Kapoor, a portfolio analyst, gives the investment committee three notes on the Orion Equity Fund.

Note 1: Orion's active specific risk has risen sharply this year.
Note 2: A comparison table of macroeconomic and fundamental factor models.
Note 3: The risk team's VaR model, and a backtest that needs a covariance matrix for 12 factors.

questions.q: Note 1 most likely indicates that:
options: Orion's factor tilts relative to the benchmark have grown
a larger share of Orion's active risk now comes from stock selection
Orion has become more diversified across individual securities
questions.why: Active specific risk = security-specific risk. Higher → more active risk from stock selection; low active specific risk suggests a well-diversified portfolio.

questions.q: Which statement in Note 2 is most accurate?
options: In a macroeconomic model the intercept is the stock's expected return when all factor surprises are zero; in a fundamental model the intercept has no economic meaning
In a macroeconomic model the factors are estimated from cross-sectional regressions, and the intercept has no economic meaning
In a fundamental model the sensitivities are regression slope estimates, and the intercept is the expected return when factors are zero
questions.why:
Macroeconomic: sensitivities = regression slopes; factors = surprises in macro variables; intercept = expected return.
Fundamental: sensitivities calculated directly from data (standardised attributes); factor returns estimated from multiple regression; intercept has no meaning.

questions.q: Regarding Note 3, which statement is most accurate?
options: VaR does not capture liquidity risk, and the covariance matrix has 132 distinct covariances
VaR does not capture liquidity risk, and the covariance matrix has 66 distinct covariances
VaR fully captures liquidity risk, and the covariance matrix has 144 distinct covariances
questions.why:
VaR ignores liquidity risk (it assumes positions can be sold at market prices).
Distinct covariances = n(n − 1)/2 = 12 × 11/2 = 66.

vignettes.body: Yusuf Demir analyses a callable, putable convertible bond issued by Ostrava Motors. The conversion price is well above Ostrava's current share price. Over the next month Ostrava's share price rises 6% but remains below the conversion price.

questions.q: The value of the callable, putable convertible bond is best expressed as:
options: straight bond + call option on the stock + call option on the bond − put option on the bond
straight bond + call option on the stock − call option on the bond + put option on the bond
straight bond − call option on the stock − call option on the bond + put option on the bond
questions.why:
Investor owns the conversion option (call on stock) and the put on the bond, and is short the issuer's call on the bond:
straight + call(stock) − call(bond) + put(bond).

questions.q: After the 6% rise in Ostrava's share price, the convertible's price most likely:
options: rises only slightly, because the conversion option is still out of the money
rises by about 6%, because it tracks the share price
falls, because the issuer is more likely to call the bond
questions.why: With the share price below the conversion price the bond behaves like a straight bond, so share price moves pass through only weakly. Only when the share price exceeds the conversion price does the bond start to track the stock.

vignettes.body:
Ruiz compares two foreign subsidiaries of Atlas. Both have net monetary liabilities and positive net assets.

Subsidiary A's functional currency is the US dollar (the parent's presentation currency), so it is remeasured with the temporal method.
Subsidiary B's functional currency is its local currency, so it is translated with the current rate method.

During the year both local currencies appreciate against the dollar. Prices in both countries are rising, and Subsidiary B uses FIFO.

Ruiz notes that in both cases the translated balance sheet does not balance until a plug figure is added. He also wants to reduce Atlas's balance sheet translation exposure for Subsidiary B.

questions.q: Which statement about the plug figure is most accurate?
options: For A the plug is translation gain or loss in net income; for B it is the cumulative translation adjustment in equity
For A the plug is the cumulative translation adjustment; for B it is a gain or loss in net income
For both subsidiaries the plug is recorded in net income
questions.why:
Temporal method: remeasurement gain/loss goes to net income (and so to retained earnings).
Current rate method: the translation adjustment goes to OCI as the CTA in equity. Both are the balancing (plug) figures.

questions.q: Because the local currency appreciated, Subsidiary A's remeasurement result and Subsidiary B's CTA are most likely:
options: a loss for both
a gain in income for A and a negative CTA for B
a loss in income for A and a positive CTA for B
questions.why:
A: exposure = net monetary liabilities; foreign currency ↑ → liabilities worth more in dollars → loss in net income.
B: exposure = net assets (positive); foreign currency ↑ → positive translation adjustment (CTA ↑).

questions.q: For a subsidiary with an appreciating local currency and rising prices, which choices give the higher translated gross margin?
options: Temporal method and LIFO
Temporal method and FIFO
Current rate method and LIFO
questions.why:
Temporal method: COGS at older (lower) historical rates while sales are at the average rate → higher margin when the foreign currency appreciates (current rate method is better when it depreciates).
Rising prices: FIFO uses older, cheaper costs → higher margin (LIFO when prices fall).

questions.q: To reduce the balance sheet exposure of Subsidiary B, Atlas should most likely:
options: increase B's local currency receivables, for example by extending longer credit terms to local customers
reduce B's net assets, for example by paying B's local cash to the parent as a dividend
convert B's local currency borrowings into equity issued to the parent, reducing its local liabilities
questions.why: Find the net exposure under the method used, then choose the action that moves it toward zero. B's exposure is net assets (positive), so reduce exposed assets without reducing liabilities (for example a dividend paid out of local cash) or increase exposed liabilities. Paying down local liabilities with local cash leaves net assets unchanged, and converting debt to equity would increase net assets.

vignettes.body:
Ethics: Standards of Professional Conduct
Four independent questions. Each one can be answered on its own.

questions.q: Pietro, president of Local Bank, has hired the bank’s market maker, Vogt, to seek a merger partner. Local is currently listed on a stock exchange and has not reported that it is seeking strategic alternatives. Vogt has discussed the possibility of a merger with several firms, but they have all decided to wait until after the next period’s financial data are available. The potential buyers believe the results will be worse than the results of prior periods and will allow them to pay less for Local Bank. Pietro wants to increase the likelihood of structuring a merger deal quickly. Which of the following actions would most likely be a violation of the Code and Standards?
options: After confirming with Local’s chief financial officer, Pietro could instruct Local to issue a press release reaffirming the firm’s prior announced earnings guidance for the full fiscal year.
Pietro could place a buy order for 2,000 shares (or four times the average weekly volume) through Vogt for his personal account.
Pietro could instruct Local Bank to issue a press release announcing that it has retained Vogt to find a merger partner.
questions.why: Through placing a personal purchase order that is significantly greater than the average volume, Pietro is violating Standard II(B) Market Manipulation. He is attempting to manipulate an increase in the share price and thus bring a buyer to the negotiating table.

questions.q: When a firm holds material nonpublic information (MNPI) about an issuer, a required control is:
options: Relying on a ban on discussing the issuer, with no extra monitoring
Suspending all trading in every security the firm covers
Heightened review of all trading, which helps restrict the flow of confidential information
questions.why: II(A): the firm should closely review trading while it holds MNPI so that the information cannot leak into trades. It does not need to halt all trading.

questions.q: A complete ban on staff investing in private placements is:
options: Required by law under the Standards for every firm
A violation, because staff have a right to invest
Consistent with VI(B), which recommends strict limits
questions.why: VI(B) recommends strict limits on private placements and IPOs; a full ban goes further but is allowed.

questions.q: An analyst receives a company's unannounced earnings warning from the CFO, who says he has told several visiting analysts. Trading on it is:
options: Allowed, since it was freely given and shared with others
Allowed if insider trading is legal locally
A violation of II(A), because the information is material and not yet public
questions.why: Selective disclosure to a few analysts does not make information public. Even where local law permits, the Standards (stricter) prohibit acting on MNPI (I(A) also applies).

vignettes.body:
Silva values a two-year floating-rate note with an annual coupon equal to the one-year reference rate set at the start of each year, paid at the end of the year. The coupon is capped at 4.8%. Exhibit 1 shows the calibrated binomial interest rate tree (equal probabilities).

Exhibit 1: One-Year Rates
# Node | Rate
Time 0 | 3.20%
Time 1, upper node | 5.40%
Time 1, lower node | 3.80%

questions.q: The value of the capped floater is closest to:
questions.why:
Time 1 upper: rate 5.40% > cap → coupon 4.8: value = 104.80/1.054 = 99.4307
Time 1 lower: coupon = rate 3.80%: value = 103.80/1.038 = 100.0000
Time 0: coupon 3.20 (below cap): value = [0.5 × (99.4307 + 3.20) + 0.5 × (100.0000 + 3.20)] / 1.032 = 99.72
An uncapped floater would be worth 100.

questions.q: The cap in this note most likely benefits:
options: the investor, because a floor also applies
the investor, and the value of the cap is about 0.28 per 100
the issuer, and the value of the embedded cap is about 0.28 per 100
questions.why:
A cap limits the coupon the issuer pays when rates rise, so it benefits the issuer; the investor is short the cap.
Cap value = straight floater − capped floater = 100 − 99.72 = 0.28
A floor (minimum coupon) would benefit the investor.

vignettes.body:
Orchard Packaging Group (OPG) had total assets of $2,400,000, financed with three times as much debt capital as equity capital.

OPG's pretax cost of debt is 7% and its cost of equity capital is 11%.

OPG had EBIT of $280,000 and was taxed at a rate of 30%. EBIT is expected to continue at $280,000 indefinitely.

OPG's book value per share is $15 and it has 40,000 shares of common stock outstanding.

questions.q: Using the method that deducts an equity charge, OPG's residual income is closest to:
questions.why:
Debt = 3/4 × $2,400,000 = $1,800,000 and equity = $600,000. Interest = $1,800,000 × 7% = $126,000.
Pretax income = 280,000 − 126,000 = $154,000; tax = 30% = $46,200; net income = $107,800.
Equity charge = $600,000 × 11% = $66,000.
Residual income = 107,800 − 66,000 = $41,800.
$107,800 is net income (no equity charge deducted). $130,000 = EBIT × (1 − 30%) − 66,000 ignores the interest on the debt.

questions.q: Using the residual income model, with the residual income expected to continue indefinitely, OPG's intrinsic value per share is closest to:
questions.why:
Residual income per share = 41,800 / 40,000 = $1.045.
Because EBIT stays at $280,000 indefinitely, the residual income is a perpetuity: PV = 1.045 / 0.11 = $9.50.
Intrinsic value = book value per share + PV of residual income = 15.00 + 9.50 = $24.50.
$9.50 leaves out the book value. $16.05 = 15.00 + 1.045 counts only one year of residual income instead of the perpetuity.

vignettes.body:
Lisa Parker is a junior analyst with a long-only equity investment manager. Parker is asked to value several stocks on a watch list. During a weekly meeting to discuss her approach, Parker and Russell Stark, the firm's director of research, review the residual income model and its characteristics. Stark begins by explaining how to calculate the intrinsic value of Company A's common stock using the residual income model. Stark provides Parker with the following data to calculate Company A's residual income for the year.

Beginning book value per share is $10.00.
Expected net income per share is $2.00.
Expected dividends per share is $0.40.
Required rate of return on equity is 10%.

Stark asks Parker to calculate the intrinsic value of Company B's common stock using a single-stage residual income model. Parker assumes that Company B has a constant ROE and a constant earnings growth rate through time. For her analysis, Parker uses the following inputs.

Current book value per share is $10.00.
Expected long-term ROE is 6.5%.
Expected long-term growth rate is 4%.
Cost of equity is 5%.

Stark asks Parker to compare residual income models to dividend discount models and free cash flow models. Parker recognizes that valuation models based on discounting dividends or discounting free cash flows are as theoretically sound as the residual income model. While investigating the relationship of the residual income model to other valuation models, Parker makes the following statements.

Statement 1: Residual income valuations recognize value later than different present value approaches.

Statement 2: In theory, residual income valuations are mutually consistent with other present value approaches.


Stark asks Parker to evaluate whether the common stock of Company D is undervalued, fairly valued, or overvalued based on a residual income model. Parker uses the two-stage residual income model to value Company D’s share. For her analysis, she assumes the following:

Current market price is $24.00.
Beginning book value per share is $20.00.
Earnings per share will be 32% of beginning book value for the next year.
Cash dividends will be 50% of earnings per share for the next year.
At the end of the year, the stock's P/B ratio will be 1.1.
Required rate of return on equity is 10%.

questions.q: Based on the information given, the residual income of Company A’s common shares is closest to:
questions.why: C is correct. Equity charge = 10 × 10% = $1; residual income = net income − equity charge = 2.00 − 1.00 = $1.00 (use beginning book value and net income, not retained earnings).

questions.q: Based on the given information, the intrinsic value of Company B's stock is closest to:
Are Parker's statements comparing residual income models with different present value approaches both correct?
options: Yes
No, only statement 1 is correct
No, only statement 2 is correct
questions.why: C is correct. RI models recognize value EARLIER, not later (Statement 1 wrong); in theory they are mutually consistent with other approaches (Statement 2 correct).

questions.q: Based on the information given, Parker should conclude that Company D’s share is:
options: undervalued.
fairly valued.
overvalued.

title: Practice set 5
desc: Mixed topics from the key notes, with 4 Ethics questions (54 questions, 2 h 42 min)

vignettes.body:
Sanne de Vries compares credit models at Kestrel Bank.

Model M treats a company's equity as a long call option on the company's assets, and its debt as a riskless bond plus a short put option on the assets. It uses balance sheet data and option pricing.
Model N uses historical variables, financial ratios and macroeconomic data. Its key input is the default intensity: the probability of default over the next period, estimated with regression.

questions.q: A strength of Model M is that it:
options: allows default intensity to change with the economy
does not require the company's assets to be traded
provides an economic explanation of why default happens
questions.why:
Structural model strengths: economic rationale for default; uses option pricing to value risky debt.
Weaknesses: assumes assets are traded, hard for complex balance sheets, burdensome to implement, default barrier hard to measure.

questions.q: A weakness of Model N is that it:
options: cannot use macroeconomic variables
does not explain why default happens and treats default as a random event
assumes the company's assets trade in the market
questions.why:
Reduced-form strengths: no need for traded assets; default intensity can vary with company fundamentals and the economy.
Weaknesses: does not explain the cause of default; treats it as a surprise.

questions.q: In Model M, the value of risky debt equals:
options: the value of riskless debt minus the value of a put option on the company's assets
the value of riskless debt plus a call option on the company's assets
the value of the company's assets plus a put option
questions.why: Debt = riskless bond − put on assets (bondholders are short the put). Equity = call on assets.

vignettes.body:
Brandt summarises theories of the term structure for clients.

Theory A: Long-term rates are the average of expected future short-term rates; there is no risk premium. It applies only to risk-free assets.
Theory B: Over short holding periods all bonds earn the same return, but long holding periods include a risk premium.
Theory C: Investors demand a premium for holding longer maturities, and the premium rises with maturity.
Theory D: Investors and borrowers stay in their own maturity segments and never move to other maturities.
Theory E: Investors prefer certain maturities but will move to another maturity if the extra yield is large enough.

questions.q: Theory B is best described as the:
options: unbiased (pure) expectations theory
local expectations theory
liquidity preference theory
questions.why: Local expectations: short-term holding returns are the same for all bonds (the risk-free rate); a risk premium appears only over longer holding periods. Theory A is the unbiased (pure) expectations theory.

questions.q: Theory C is best described as the:
options: preferred habitat theory
segmented markets theory
liquidity preference theory
questions.why: Liquidity preference: a liquidity (term) premium that increases with maturity.

questions.q: Which theory says investors leave their preferred maturity when they are paid enough to do so?
options: Theory A, the pure expectations theory
Theory D, the segmented markets theory
Theory E, the preferred habitat theory
questions.why: Preferred habitat: investors have favourite maturities but move if compensated. Segmented markets: they never move.

vignettes.body:
Felix Arnaud reviews three managers for Sienne Pension Fund.

Exhibit 1: Manager Results
# Manager | Portfolio return | Benchmark return | Active risk
A | 8.80% | 8.75% | 3.06%
B | 9.40% | 8.75% | 3.32%
C | 10.50% | 8.75% | 9.46%

Manager D runs a balanced fund: 70% fixed income (return 10%, benchmark 8%) and 30% equity (return 12%, benchmark 10.5%). The benchmark weights are 60% fixed income and 40% equity.

Arnaud adds: (1) "Manager A has very low active risk, a Sharpe ratio close to the benchmark's and an indeterminate information ratio, like a closet index fund." (2) "If Manager B doubled all active weights, its information ratio would not change." (3) "Changing the benchmark would change the managers' Sharpe ratios."

questions.q: Which manager has the highest information ratio?
options: Manager A
Manager C
Manager B

questions.q: Manager D's return from security selection is closest to:
questions.why:
Security selection = Σ portfolio weight × (portfolio return − benchmark return) = 0.7 × (10 − 8) + 0.3 × (12 − 10.5) = 1.40 + 0.45 = 1.85%.
(Asset allocation = Σ benchmark return × (portfolio weight − benchmark weight) = 8 × 0.10 + 10.5 × (−0.10) = −0.25%.)

questions.q: Which of Arnaud's statements is incorrect?
options: Statement 1
Statement 2
Statement 3
questions.why:
The Sharpe ratio (Rp − Rf)/σp does not involve the benchmark, so the benchmark choice affects the IR but not the Sharpe ratio.
Scaling active weights (aggressiveness) does not change the IR. Closet index funds have low active risk, Sharpe near the benchmark and an indeterminate IR.

questions.q: Active return is most accurately described as:
options: the portfolio return minus the benchmark return, which is not the same as alpha
the same as alpha in all cases, because both measure the return above the benchmark
the return from security selection only, after removing the effect of asset allocation
questions.why: Active return = Rp − RB. Alpha is the return beyond what the portfolio's risk exposures explain (for example, beyond beta × market premium), so the two are not the same unless the portfolio's beta equals the benchmark's.

vignettes.body: Ferdinand Osei analyses a convertible bond issued by Brightwater Energy for Cathay Ridge Capital. Each bond has a par value of $1,000 and can be converted into 25 Brightwater shares. The convertible trades at $1,080, Brightwater shares trade at $38.00, and the value of an otherwise identical straight bond is $960.

questions.q: The conversion price of the bond is closest to:
questions.why:
Conversion price = par value of the convertible ÷ conversion ratio = 1,000 / 25 = $40.00 (fixed at issue).
$43.20 is the market conversion price (market price ÷ conversion ratio).

questions.q: The minimum value of the convertible bond is closest to:
questions.why:
Conversion value = share price × conversion ratio = 38.00 × 25 = $950
Minimum value = max(conversion value, straight value) = max(950, 960) = $960

questions.q: The market conversion premium ratio is closest to:
questions.why:
Market conversion price = 1080 / 25 = $43.20
Market conversion premium per share = 43.20 − 38.00 = $5.20
Premium ratio = 5.20 / 38.00 = 13.68%

questions.q: The premium over straight value is closest to:
questions.why: Premium over straight value = (market price of convertible / straight value) − 1 = 1080/960 − 1 = 12.50%

vignettes.body: Yusuf Demir measures the interest rate risk of three bonds with the same issuer and maturity: Bond X (option free), Bond Y (callable, with the call option near the money) and Bond Z (putable, with the put option near the money). He computes one-sided durations (up = rates rise, down = rates fall) and key rate durations.

questions.q: Which statement about one-sided durations is most accurate?
options: For all three bonds the up- and down-durations are equal
For Bond Y the down-duration is greater than the up-duration; for Bond Z it is the reverse
For Bond Y the one-sided up-duration is greater than the down-duration; for Bond Z it is the reverse
questions.why:
Callable near the money: when rates fall the call caps the price, so down-duration is small → up > down.
Putable near the money: when rates rise the put floors the price, so up-duration is small → up < down.
Option-free: up ≈ down.

questions.q: Compared with Bond X, the one-sided down-duration of Bond Y is most likely:
options: lower
higher
the same
questions.why: When the call is at or near the money, a fall in rates barely raises the callable bond's price, so its down-duration is lower than that of the comparable option-free bond.

questions.q: For Bond X, the key rate duration is most likely highest at:
options: the first coupon date
the bond's maturity
the one-year key rate
questions.why: An option-free bond's largest key rate duration is at its maturity, where the principal is paid. For a callable or putable bond, the key rate near the likely exercise date can be the largest.

questions.q: The effective durations of Bonds Y and Z compared with Bond X are:
options: greater for Bond Y and less for Bond Z
less than or equal to that of Bond X
greater than or equal to that of Bond X
questions.why: Both embedded options shorten the effective duration: effective duration of a callable or putable bond ≤ effective duration of the option-free bond.

vignettes.body:
Bettina Kral teaches a term structure workshop at Danube Fixed Income. She describes four models of the short-term interest rate r:

Model 1 (Cox–Ingersoll–Ross): dr = a(b − r)dt + σ√r dz
Model 2 (Vasicek): dr = a(b − r)dt + σ dz
Model 3 (Ho–Lee): dr = θ(t)dt + σ dz
Model 4 (Kalotay–Williams–Fabozzi): d ln(r) = θ(t)dt + σ dz

A participant asks which models are calibrated so that they reproduce current market prices of benchmark bonds.

questions.q: Which of Models 1 and 2 can produce negative interest rates?
options: Model 2 only
Model 1 only
Both Model 1 and Model 2
questions.why:
In CIR, volatility is σ√r, so it shrinks to zero as r approaches zero: rates cannot become negative.
In Vasicek, volatility σ is constant and does not depend on r, so rates can become negative.

questions.q: In which model does interest rate volatility increase as the level of rates rises?
options: Model 3
Model 1
Model 2
questions.why: CIR: the volatility term σ√r grows with r. Vasicek and Ho–Lee have constant volatility σ.

questions.q: Models 3 and 4 are best described as:
options: equilibrium models, which are built from macroeconomic assumptions and need fewer parameters
equilibrium models that allow rates to drift to a long-run level b
arbitrage-free models, which take current bond prices as given and assume they are correctly priced
questions.why:
Arbitrage-free models (Ho–Lee, KWF) use a time-dependent drift θ(t) calibrated to market prices, assuming those bonds are correctly priced.
Equilibrium models (CIR, Vasicek) describe the economy, mean-revert to b and need fewer parameters to estimate.

questions.q: Compared with Model 3, a key feature of Model 4 is that:
options: volatility rises with the level of rates through √r
rates cannot become negative, because the model describes the logarithm of r
the model is an equilibrium model with mean reversion
questions.why: KWF models ln(r), so r = e^(ln r) is always positive (log-normal rates). Ho–Lee models r itself with constant volatility, so rates can go negative.

vignettes.body:
Sofia Marin, a currency strategist at Iberia Capital, reviews FX positions.

Position 1: Three months ago Iberia sold EUR 10 million forward against USD for six months at USD 1.1050/EUR. Today the three-month forward rate is USD 1.0950/EUR and the three-month USD interest rate is 4.0% (annualised).
Position 2: A client wants a one-year forward on USD/MXN. Spot is 17.20 MXN/USD and the dealer quotes forward points of +850 (in units of 0.0001).

questions.q: The mark-to-market value of Position 1 to Iberia is closest to:
options: USD 99,010 gain
USD 99,010 loss
USD 100,000 gain
questions.why:
Iberia sold EUR forward at 1.1050. To close, it buys EUR forward at 1.0950: gain = (1.1050 − 1.0950) × 10m = USD 100,000 at settlement.
Discount for 3 months: 100,000 / (1 + 0.04 × 90/360) = 100,000 / 1.01 = USD 99,010.

questions.q: The all-in one-year forward rate for Position 2 is closest to:
options: 18.0500 MXN/USD
17.1150 MXN/USD
17.2850 MXN/USD
questions.why: All-in forward = spot + forward points/10,000 = 17.2000 + 0.0850 = 17.2850 MXN/USD.

vignettes.body:
Hana Novak explains exchange-traded funds (ETFs) to clients of Tatra Wealth.

Point 1: The Tatra Europe ETF has a NAV of €24.80 per share and trades at €25.10.
Point 2: Novak lists components of an ETF's bid–ask spread: creation/redemption fees and other direct costs; the bid–ask spread of the underlying securities; compensation for the risk of hedging or carrying positions for the rest of the day; the market maker's desired profit; and a discount for the chance of receiving an offsetting order soon.
Point 3: A client plans to buy €100,000 of the ETF and hold it for 9 months. The round-trip commission is 0.10%, the bid–ask spread is 0.12% and the annual management fee is 0.20%.

questions.q: Based on Point 1, authorised participants are most likely to:
options: do nothing, because the difference is within the ETF's bid–ask spread and cannot be arbitraged
create ETF shares by delivering the underlying securities, then sell the ETF shares
buy ETF shares in the market and redeem them for the underlying securities, then sell those securities
questions.why: ETF price > NAV → premium → authorised participants (market makers) buy the basket, create ETF shares and sell them, pushing the price down. Price < NAV → redemption.

questions.q: For a highly liquid ETF, which components of the spread in Point 2 matter least?
options: The first three: direct costs, the underlying spread and hedging compensation
All components matter equally
The market maker's profit and the offsetting-order discount
questions.why: For very liquid ETFs, market makers rarely need to create/redeem or hedge, so the first three components hardly affect the spread; it reflects mainly the market maker's profit less the discount for offsetting orders. The ETF spread is at most the sum of these components.

questions.q: The client's total expected holding cost in Point 3 is closest to:
questions.why: Total cost = round-trip commission + spread + management fee × (months/12) = 0.10% + 0.12% + 0.20% × 9/12 = 0.10 + 0.12 + 0.15 = 0.37%.

questions.q: Which statement about ETF types and risks is most accurate?
options: Synthetic ETFs carry no counterparty risk; leveraged and inverse ETFs deliver their stated multiple over any holding period
Synthetic ETFs and ETNs carry counterparty risk; leveraged and inverse ETFs aim to deliver their multiple only over very short periods
ETNs have no counterparty risk because they hold physical assets; synthetic ETFs carry only settlement risk
questions.why: Synthetic ETFs use swaps → counterparty risk. ETNs are unsecured notes of the issuer → counterparty risk (no settlement/tracking of a basket). Leveraged/inverse funds reset daily, so long-horizon returns differ from the multiple. Other risks: expectation-related risk (investors misunderstanding the ETF) and fund closure risk (regulation, competition, corporate actions).

questions.q: A manager uses an ETF to keep market exposure while a new sub-manager is being hired for an asset class. This use is best described as:
options: portfolio completion
portfolio liquidity management
portfolio rebalancing
questions.why: Liquidity management: equitise cash quickly. Rebalancing: move back to target asset-class weights cost-efficiently (ETFs can also be shorted). Completion: fill temporary gaps in allocation, such as during a manager transition.

vignettes.body:
Montclair creates a special purpose entity (SPE) and sells it $200 million of receivables. The SPE pays for the receivables with money borrowed from an outside bank. Montclair absorbs the SPE's losses, so it must consolidate the SPE.

Montclair also holds bonds classified at amortised cost and equity securities at fair value through OCI. Management plans to change its business model for the bonds and asks whether they can be reclassified.

questions.q: Because Montclair consolidates the SPE, the sale of receivables most likely:
options: leaves consolidated cash unchanged, because intercompany sales are eliminated
increases consolidated cash, because the money came from outside the group
reduces consolidated debt
questions.why: The intercompany sale is eliminated, but the bank loan is new money from outside the group: consolidated cash and debt both rise. If the SPE had been funded by Montclair itself, consolidated cash would be unchanged.

questions.q: Which statement about IFRS 9 and the reclassification is most accurate?
options: FVPL securities are carried at amortised cost; reclassification of financial assets is never allowed under IFRS 9
Amortised-cost securities are carried at historical cost; reclassification is allowed after a significant change in the business model and prior statements are not restated
FVOCI securities are carried at historical cost; reclassification is allowed at any time but requires restating prior periods
questions.why:
FVPL and FVOCI → carried at fair (market) value; amortised cost → historical cost.
Reclassification of debt securities is allowed only when the business model changes significantly; it applies prospectively, with no restatement.

vignettes.body:
Nadia Rahman manages credit strategies at Belcourt Partners and discusses five trade ideas with her analyst, Leo Fischer.

Idea 1: Fischer expects the credit quality of Varga Steel to improve.
Idea 2: The CDS curve of Delmont Telecom is upward sloping, and Fischer expects it to steepen.
Idea 3: Rahman expects the economy to strengthen. She wants to trade high-yield and investment-grade CDS indexes against each other.
Idea 4: Hollis Retail's bonds yield a spread over MRR that is larger than its CDS spread for the same maturity.
Idea 5: Fischer believes Pratt Foods will be taken over in a leveraged buyout financed mostly with new debt.

questions.q: For Idea 1, Belcourt should:
options: buy protection on a CDS index that includes Varga Steel
buy protection on Varga Steel
sell protection on Varga Steel
questions.why:
Credit improves → CDS spread falls → protection seller gains: sell protection = long credit.
Credit deteriorates → buy protection = short credit.

questions.q: For Idea 2, the most appropriate trade is to:
options: buy protection on short-maturity CDS and sell protection on long-maturity CDS
sell protection on short-maturity CDS and buy protection on long-maturity CDS
buy protection at both maturities
questions.why:
Steepening = long-maturity spreads rise relative to short-maturity spreads.
Buy protection (short credit) at the long end, sell protection (long credit) at the short end.

questions.q: For Idea 3, Rahman should:
options: buy protection on both indexes
sell protection on the high-yield index and buy protection on the investment-grade index
buy protection on the high-yield index and sell protection on the investment-grade index
questions.why:
A stronger economy narrows high-yield spreads more than investment-grade spreads.
High yield: sell protection. Investment grade: buy protection.

questions.q: For Idea 4, the basis trade is to:
options: sell the bond and sell CDS protection
buy the bond and sell CDS protection
buy the bond and buy CDS protection
questions.why:
Bond spread > CDS spread (negative basis) → buy the bond and buy protection (earn the bond spread, pay the smaller CDS spread).
Bond spread < CDS spread → sell the bond and sell protection.
Bond spread = bond yield − MRR, a credit risk premium.

questions.q: For Idea 5, the most appropriate strategy is to:
options: buy Pratt Foods shares and buy CDS protection on Pratt Foods
buy Pratt Foods shares and sell CDS protection on Pratt Foods
sell Pratt Foods shares and sell CDS protection on Pratt Foods
questions.why: In an LBO the target's shares usually rise (takeover premium), while its heavy new debt weakens its credit, so its CDS spread widens: buy shares and buy protection.

vignettes.body:
Before valuing callable bonds, Danube's analysts calibrate a binomial interest rate tree. A trainee lists the inputs he thinks are needed:

Input 1: An assumed interest rate volatility.
Input 2: An interest rate model, such as a log-normal model.
Input 3: The observed market values of benchmark bonds.
Input 4: Analysts' forecasts of future interest rates.

questions.q: Which inputs are needed to calibrate the tree?
options: Inputs 1, 2, 3 and 4
Inputs 1, 2 and 3 only
Inputs 1 and 4 only
questions.why: Calibration needs volatility, an interest rate model (for example log-normal rates) and the market values of benchmark bonds. Rates in the tree are not forecasts; they are random (stochastic) paths consistent with today's prices.

vignettes.body:
Clara Weiss, CFA, analyses the investments of Montclair Holdings, which reports under IFRS.

Investment 1: On 1 January, Montclair bought 12% of Pell Foods for $66 million and classified it at fair value through profit or loss (FVPL). On 31 December, the fair value of 100% of Pell's equity was $610 million. Pell reported net income of $45 million and paid dividends of $25 million during the year.

Investment 2: On 1 January, Montclair bought 30% of Rosen AG for €360 million and uses the equity method. Rosen's book value of net assets was €900 million. The fair value of Rosen's plant and equipment exceeded its book value by €100 million; the plant has a remaining life of 10 years (straight line). Any remaining excess is goodwill. Rosen reported net income of €120 million and paid dividends of €50 million.

During the year Rosen also sold inventory to Montclair at a profit; half of that inventory was still held by Montclair at year-end.

questions.q: The pre-tax income Montclair reports from Investment 1 is closest to:
options: $10.2 million
$3.0 million
$7.2 million
questions.why:
FVPL: income = holding gain + dividends received.
Year-end value = 12% × 610 = $73.2m → holding gain = 73.2 − 66 = $7.2m
Dividends = 12% × 25 = $3.0m
Pre-tax income = 7.2 + 3.0 = $10.2m (Pell's net income is not recognised under FVPL).

questions.q: The goodwill included in Investment 2 is closest to:
options: €90 million
€60 million
questions.why:
Goodwill = purchase price − % × book value of net assets − % × (FV − BV) of identifiable assets
= 360 − 0.30 × 900 − 0.30 × 100 = 360 − 270 − 30 = €60m.

questions.q: The carrying value of Investment 2 at 31 December is closest to:
options: €396 million
€381 million
€378 million
questions.why:
Investment account = purchase price + % × net income − % × dividends − amortisation of excess purchase price
= 360 + 0.30 × 120 − 0.30 × 50 − (0.30 × 100)/10
= 360 + 36 − 15 − 3 = €378m.

questions.q: Montclair's equity income from Rosen (contribution to net earnings), before any adjustment for the inventory sale, is closest to:
options: €33 million
€18 million
€36 million
questions.why:
Contribution to earnings = % × net income − amortisation of the excess = 36 − 3 = €33m.
Dividends reduce the investment account but are not part of earnings.

questions.q: Regarding Rosen's sale of inventory to Montclair, Montclair should:
options: eliminate 100% of the profit, because the companies are under common control
defer its share of the unrealised profit on the inventory still held until it is sold to third parties
recognise its full share of the profit immediately, because the sale is upstream
questions.why: Under the equity method, the investor's share of unrealised profits on intercompany (upstream or downstream) sales is deferred until the goods are sold to outside parties.

vignettes.body:
Brenner builds a two-year binomial tree to compute the CVA of a 3% annual-coupon corporate bond. At the end of year 2 the tree has three nodes with bond values (before the coupon) of 101.40, 103.10 and 104.60, reached with probabilities of 25%, 50% and 25%. The coupon of 3 is paid at every node at the end of year 2.

Brenner's manager remarks that when the expected return of a bond is adjusted for possible rating changes over the year, the adjustment is usually negative.

questions.q: The expected exposure at the end of year 2 is closest to:
questions.why:
Expected exposure = Σ (node value × node probability) + coupon
= 0.25 × 101.40 + 0.50 × 103.10 + 0.25 × 104.60 + 3 = 103.05 + 3 = 106.05
Use the node probabilities, not a simple average.

questions.q: The manager's remark is best explained by the fact that:
options: modified duration rises after a downgrade, which always lowers the coupon
upgrades are more likely than downgrades, but have smaller price effects
rating changes are skewed toward downgrades, and spreads widen far more on downgrades than they narrow on upgrades
questions.why: Credit migration typically reduces expected returns because (1) the transition distribution is skewed toward downgrades and (2) the spread increase for a downgrade is much larger than the spread decrease for an upgrade.

vignettes.body:
Victoria Novak, CFA, was waiting in line at a coffee shop when she overheard a conversation between two people talking about an individual financial adviser. According to the two, this adviser had received numerous complaints over the past month, including some suspected illegal activity regarding a complex financial transaction. One particular comment caught her attention, “We would not have this case on our hands right now if we had included an industry standard in our new regulations requiring all licensees, who we regard as our clients, to abide by the CFA Code of Ethics and Standards of Professional Conduct.”

Novak approaches the two and says, “I’m sorry, but I couldn’t help but overhear your conversation. I’m Victoria Novak, a CFA charterholder. Are you charterholders, too?”

In response, Abraham Kovi introduces himself and his colleague, Stanley Marin, and says, “We’re both CFA Level 2 Program candidates and work at the Capital Market Regulatory Authority (Regulators).”

Novak responds, “I’m really passionate about ethics and would love to talk more.”

After the three find a table, Novak asks about their desire to implement the CFA Code and Standards as an industry standard.

Marin responds, “We regularly check the CFA Institute website to see if anyone in our jurisdiction has been sanctioned for improper behaviors. Those individuals are subject to greater scrutiny because of their past misbehaviors.”

Kovi adds, “For instance, we recently discovered from the CFA Institute website that Mario Jovic, CFA, the owner of a small licensed financial advisory firm in our jurisdiction was subject to a public sanction. Consequently, we have started our own investigation and found several clients had registered complaints with the firm.”

Kovi continues, “We have also received several complaints against another adviser who is running his own firm and is a charterholder. The complaints are related to how the investment management fees were calculated on active management accounts as per their client agreements. The adviser had placed client funds at a commercial bank in fixed-term deposits at above-market rates. Subsequently, the deposits were frozen by the Central Bank as part of a bank restructuring program and reset at lower-than-market rates. Part of the restructuring restricted the withdrawal of any deposits for three years to give the bank time to recover without a threat of a run on the bank. The adviser continues to charge management fees on these deposits based on their anticipated maturity values, despite not being able to manage them as per client mandates. He includes the assets in performance presentations, noting in a footnote they are not available for withdrawal.”

Novak asks the two, “If you had the Code and Standards in place industry-wide right now, what sanctions would you consider against this adviser?”

Marin responds, “Three sanctions come to my mind.”

Sanction 1: Require the adviser to pay into an Investor Protection Fund whereby clients can make claims to help recover their losses and to deter future abuses and violations.

Sanction 2: Require the adviser to hire an independent compliance consultant to undertake an assessment and recommend and implement processes and procedures to prevent and detect violations.

Sanction 3: Require the adviser to design a formal training program for existing staff and any new hires to help them understand their responsibilities as required by the Code and Standards

questions.q: Is the comment regarding the requirement for all licensees that Novak overheard while waiting in line at the coffee shop most likely correct?
options: Yes, with regards to Standard IV(C), Responsibilities of Supervisors.
No.
Yes, with regards to Standard I(A), Knowledge of Law.
questions.why: The comment “We would not have this case on our hands now if we had included an industry standard in our new regulations requiring all licensees to abide by the CFA Code of Ethics and Standards of Professional Conduct,” is not correct with regards to Standard I(A), Knowledge of Law, or Standard IV(C), Responsibilities of Supervisors.

questions.q: After Novak and the two regulators found a table, who most likely violated CFA Standards of Professional Conduct?
options: Marin
Novak
Kovi
questions.why: Kovi violated Standard III(E), Preservation of Confidentiality, by citing the name of the individual currently under the regulator’s investigation. Mentioning Jovic’s previous CFA sanction, however, does not violate the standard in that this is public information. Standard III(E) requires CFA Institute members and CFA candidates to keep information about current, former, and prospective clients confidential.

questions.q: To avoid violating CFA Standards of Professional Conduct, which of the following actions is most appropriate for the adviser to address client complaints regarding bank deposits?
options: Reimburse past fees charged on deposits and stop future management fees
Review the client agreement with his largest clients
Remove the deposits from future performance presentations
questions.why: To avoid violating CFA Standards of Professional Conduct, reimbursing past fees charged on deposits and stopping future fees would be the adviser’s most appropriate action. As a CFA® charterholder, the adviser has the responsibility to put the interests of his clients before his own or his firm’s as per Standard III(A), Loyalty, Prudence, and Care.

questions.q: Which proposed sanction against the adviser most likely complies with CFA Standards of Professional Conduct?
options: Sanction 3
Sanction 1
Sanction 2
questions.why: Sanction 2, Require the adviser to hire an Independent Compliance Consultant to undertake an assessment, and recommend processes and procedures to prevent and detect violations, most likely complies with CFA Standards of Professional Conduct.

vignettes.body:
Mattias Holm, a derivatives analyst at Selwyn Capital, values an American-style call option on Selwyn Group shares with a two-period binomial model. The shares pay no dividends. The option matures at the end of the second period. Exhibit 1 shows the inputs.

Exhibit 1: Binomial Inputs
# Item | Value
Current share price | $50
Exercise price of the call option | $48
Risk-free rate per period | 3%
Up factor (u) | 1.20
Down factor (d) | 0.90

questions.q: The value of the American call option on Selwyn Group is closest to:
questions.why:
Risk-neutral probability of an up move q = (1 + r − d) ÷ (u − d) = (1.03 − 0.90) ÷ (1.20 − 0.90) = 0.4333.
Prices at the end of period 2: 72.00, 54.00 and 40.50. Call values there: 24.00, 6.00 and 0.
Up node (S = 60): continuation value = (0.4333 × 24.00 + 0.5667 × 6.00) ÷ 1.03 = 13.40; exercise value = 60 − 48 = 12.00. The larger value is 13.40 (do not exercise).
Down node (S = 45): continuation value = (0.4333 × 6.00 + 0.5667 × 0) ÷ 1.03 = 2.52; exercise value = 0, so the node value is 2.52.
Today: (0.4333 × 13.40 + 0.5667 × 2.52) ÷ 1.03 = $7.03; exercising now is worth only 50 − 48 = 2.00.
Early exercise is never optimal for a call on a non-dividend-paying stock, so the American call equals the European call.
$6.44 wrongly assumes exercise at the up node (12.00). $8.48 uses a probability of 0.5 instead of 0.4333.

vignettes.body:
Elena Varga, a derivatives analyst at Norden Bank, values an American-style put option on Calder Industries shares with a two-period binomial model. Calder pays no dividends. The put matures at the end of the second period. Exhibit 1 shows the inputs.

Exhibit 1: Binomial Inputs
# Item | Value
Current share price | $60
Exercise price of the put option | $65
Risk-free rate per period | 3%
Up factor (u) | 1.20
Down factor (d) | 0.85

questions.q: The value of the American put option on Calder Industries is closest to:
questions.why:
Risk-neutral probability of an up move q = (1 + r − d) ÷ (u − d) = (1.03 − 0.85) ÷ (1.20 − 0.85) = 0.5143.
Prices at the end of period 2: 86.40, 61.20 and 43.35. Put values there: 0, 3.80 and 21.65.
Up node (S = 72): continuation value = (0.4857 × 3.80) ÷ 1.03 = 1.79; exercise value = 0. The node value is 1.79.
Down node (S = 51): continuation value = (0.5143 × 3.80 + 0.4857 × 21.65) ÷ 1.03 = 12.11; exercise value = 65 − 51 = 14.00. The larger value is 14.00: early exercise.
Today: (0.5143 × 1.79 + 0.4857 × 14.00) ÷ 1.03 = $7.50; exercising now is worth only 65 − 60 = 5.00.
$6.60 is the European put value (no early exercise at the down node). $7.89 reverses the probabilities (uses 0.4857 for the up move).

vignettes.body:
Rosa Almeida, a real estate analyst at Kestrel Bank, sets the maximum loan on an office building. Almeida's bank requires a minimum debt service coverage ratio (DSCR) of 1.30 and a maximum loan-to-value (LTV) ratio of 70%. The loan would be interest only, with an annual interest rate of 6.5%. Exhibit 1 shows the property data.

Exhibit 1: Property Data
# Item | Value
Net operating income (NOI) | $1,500,000
Appraised value | $28,000,000

questions.q: The maximum loan allowed by the DSCR requirement is closest to:
options: $19.60 million.
$23.08 million.
$17.75 million.
questions.why:
DSCR = NOI ÷ debt service, so the maximum debt service = NOI ÷ minimum DSCR = 1,500,000 ÷ 1.30 = $1,153,846.
For an interest-only loan, loan amount = debt service ÷ interest rate = 1,153,846 ÷ 0.065 = $17.75 million.
$19.60 million is the LTV-based loan (70% × 28,000,000), which ignores the DSCR. $23.08 million = NOI ÷ interest rate leaves out the DSCR requirement. The maximum loan is the lower of the DSCR-based and LTV-based amounts, here the DSCR-based $17.75 million.

questions.q: If the bank instead made the maximum loan allowed by the LTV limit, the DSCR would be closest to:
questions.why:
Maximum LTV loan = 70% × 28,000,000 = $19,600,000. Interest-only debt service = 19,600,000 × 6.5% = $1,274,000.
DSCR = NOI ÷ debt service = 1,500,000 ÷ 1,274,000 = 1.18, which is below the required 1.30. The LTV loan is therefore too large: the DSCR constraint binds.
0.85 turns the ratio upside down (debt service ÷ NOI). 1.30 is the lender's minimum, not the result.

vignettes.body: Karel Novak, an analyst at Brenner Research, reviews a production line that Aldor Packaging holds for use. The production line has a carrying amount of $240 million. Aldor expects the line to generate undiscounted future cash flows of $225 million, which have a present value (value in use) of $210 million. The fair value of the line is $190 million, and the costs to sell it would be $5 million. Novak first computes the impairment loss under US GAAP and then, for comparison, under IFRS.

questions.q: The impairment loss under US GAAP is closest to:
options: $15 million.
$50 million.
$30 million.
questions.why:
US GAAP step 1 (recoverability): carrying amount $240 million > undiscounted future cash flows $225 million, so the asset is impaired.
Step 2: impairment loss = carrying amount − fair value = 240 − 190 = $50 million.
$15 million = 240 − 225 uses the undiscounted cash flows as the measure; they are only the test, not the measure. $30 million is the IFRS answer.

questions.q: The impairment loss under IFRS is closest to:
options: $55 million.
$50 million.
$30 million.
questions.why:
IFRS: recoverable amount = higher of fair value less costs to sell (190 − 5 = 185) and value in use (210) = $210 million.
Impairment loss = carrying amount − recoverable amount = 240 − 210 = $30 million (the carrying amount exceeds the recoverable amount).
$55 million uses fair value less costs to sell (240 − 185) instead of the higher value in use. $50 million is the US GAAP answer.

title: Practice set 6
desc: Mixed topics from the key notes, with 4 Ethics questions (52 questions, 2 h 36 min)

vignettes.body:
Liang Wu, a portfolio manager at Corwen Asset Management, enters a one-year equity swap with quarterly settlement on a notional of $40 million. Corwen receives the total return on the Meridian 500 index and pays a fixed rate. No fixed rate is quoted, so Wu must set it at initiation from the present value factors in Exhibit 1 (90-day periods, 360-day year).

Exhibit 1: Present Value Factors at Initiation
# Days | Present value factor
90 | 0.9950
180 | 0.9896
270 | 0.9838
360 | 0.9775

During the first quarter the Meridian 500 total return is −1.6%.

Separately, suppose that sixty days after initiation (before the first settlement) the index has risen from 1,000 to 1,025. Exhibit 2 shows present value factors at that date.

Exhibit 2: Present Value Factors 60 Days After Initiation
# Days | Present value factor
30 | 0.9985
120 | 0.9930
210 | 0.9870
300 | 0.9805

questions.q: The annualised fixed rate on the equity swap is closest to:
questions.why:
Periodic fixed rate = (1 − Z4) / ΣZ = (1 − 0.9775) / 3.9459 = 0.5702% per quarter
Annualised = × 4 = 2.281%
0.57% is the quarterly rate.

questions.q: For the first quarter, Corwen's net settlement is closest to:
options: Corwen pays $868,085
Corwen receives $411,915
Corwen pays $411,915
questions.why:
Corwen pays fixed: 0.5702% × 40,000,000 = $228,085
Corwen receives the equity return, which is negative: −1.6% × 40,000,000 = −$640,000, so Corwen also pays $640,000.
Net = 228,085 + 640,000 = Corwen pays $868,085

questions.q: Sixty days after initiation, the value of the swap to Corwen (receive equity, pay fixed) is closest to:
questions.why:
Fixed leg per $1 = coupon × ΣZ + last Z = 0.005702 × 3.9590 + 0.9805 = 1.003075
Equity leg per $1 = Index now / Index at start = 1,025 / 1,000 = 1.025
Value (receive equity) = (1.025 − 1.003075) × 40,000,000 = $877,012

vignettes.body:
Marta Quiroga, an analyst at Solaris Bank, writes a note for clients on yields and spreads.

Statement 1: "A bond's yield to maturity is the return an investor earns only if the bond is held to maturity, there is no default, and all coupons are reinvested at the yield to maturity."
Statement 2: "In countries where government bonds trade with low liquidity, the swap curve is often a better benchmark than the government curve."
Statement 3: "The TED spread and the MRR–OIS spread both measure liquidity and credit risk in the banking system."

Quiroga also describes a measure of the spread that, when added to each spot rate on the benchmark curve, makes the present value of a bond's cash flows equal to its market price.

questions.q: If the coupons of a bond held to maturity are reinvested at a rate below its yield to maturity, the realised return will be:
options: above the yield to maturity
below the yield to maturity
equal to the yield to maturity
questions.why: One YTM assumption is that coupons are reinvested at the YTM. A lower reinvestment rate gives a realised return below the YTM.

questions.q: Which of Quiroga's statements are correct?
options: Statements 1, 2 and 3
Statement 3 only
Statements 1 and 2 only
questions.why: All three are correct. TED = three-month MRR − T-bill yield; MRR–OIS = MRR − overnight indexed swap rate; both reflect bank credit and liquidity risk. Where government bonds are illiquid, swap curves are a superior benchmark.

questions.q: The spread measure Quiroga describes is the:
options: I-spread
Z-spread
swap spread
questions.why:
Z-spread: constant spread added to each benchmark spot rate so that PV of cash flows = market price.
I-spread = bond yield − swap rate of the same maturity.
Swap spread = swap rate − government bond yield.

vignettes.body:
Two years ago, Vasquez Industrial, a eurozone company, entered a four-year currency swap with a US bank. At initiation, Vasquez exchanged €30 million for US dollars at the then spot rate of USD1.10/EUR. Vasquez pays a fixed USD rate of 4.0% (semi-annual) and receives floating EUR MRR (semi-annual) on the euro notional. Notional amounts are exchanged again at maturity.

Today, four USD payments remain, at 6, 12, 18 and 24 months. The next EUR floating payment is due in 135 days and was set at 3.10% (annualised) for the current 180-day period. Spot is USD1.15/EUR.

Exhibit 1: Present Value Factors
# Payment | USD factor | EUR factor
135 days | – | 0.9885
6 months | 0.9810 | –
12 months | 0.9620 | –
18 months | 0.9425 | –
24 months | 0.9230 | –

questions.q: The present value of the remaining USD fixed payments, including the notional, is closest to:
The value of the swap to Vasquez, in euros, is closest to:
questions.why:
Step 3: EUR floating leg = (30,000,000 + 3.10%/2 × 30,000,000) × 0.9885 = €30,114,652 (a floating leg is worth par plus the known coupon at the next reset)
Step 4: convert USD leg at TODAY's spot: 32,972,610 / 1.15 = €28,671,835
Value (receive EUR, pay USD) = 30,114,652 − 28,671,835 = €1,442,818
€139,552 wrongly uses the old spot rate 1.10.

vignettes.body:
Oskar Brandt reviews governance and ESG for Fennica Group.

Fact 1: Fennica and Saarinen Oy each own 10% of the other's shares.
Fact 2: Fennica's parent controls it through a chain of majority holdings.
Fact 3: Fennica's CEO sits on Saarinen's board, and Saarinen's CEO sits on Fennica's board.
Fact 4: Fennica's controlling family owns 25% of the shares but holds 60% of the votes through dual-class shares.
Fact 5: Brandt uses ESG ratings from a data vendor and Fennica's own sustainability report.
Fact 6: Fennica's green bond trades at a lower spread than a conventional Fennica bond with the same rating and maturity.

questions.q: Facts 1, 2 and 3 describe, respectively:
options: a horizontal (cross-holding) structure, a vertical structure and interlocking directorships
a vertical structure, a horizontal structure and a voting cap
interlocking directorships, a pyramid and a cross-holding
questions.why: Cross-holdings between companies → horizontal structure. One company controlling another down a chain → vertical (pyramid) structure. Executives on each other's boards → interlocking directorships (a governance issue).

questions.q: Fact 4 most likely creates which governance problem, and what is one remedy?
options: A principal–agent conflict between managers and shareholders; a voting cap
A principal–agent conflict; more independent directors only
A principal–principal conflict between controlling and minority shareholders; a voting cap
questions.why: Dispersed ownership and voting → principal–agent problem. Concentrated voting power (votes > ownership) → principal–principal problem. A voting cap limits how much any holder can vote.

questions.q: Regarding Fact 5, which statement is most accurate?
options: Company-reported data are audited and standardised across firms; vendor data are based only on public filings
Vendor data are objective and fully comparable across vendors; company-reported data are mandatory
Vendor data involve subjective analysis of sources and rankings; company-reported data can be inconsistent and voluntary
questions.why: ESG data vendors: subjective methods and rankings. Company-reported data (10-K, annual and sustainability reports, proprietary methods): inconsistent and voluntary.

questions.q: The tighter spread on the green bond in Fact 6 is best explained by:
options: shorter duration
lower credit risk, because green projects never default
strong investor demand, which raises the price and lowers the yield
questions.why: Same issuer, rating and maturity → the difference comes from demand: more buyers → higher price → lower yield → tighter spread.

vignettes.body:
