Kapoor decomposes Orion's active risk. Orion's active risk (tracking error) is 4.0%, so active risk squared is 16.0 (%²). Exhibit 1 shows the active factor risk attributed to each factor and the active specific risk.

Exhibit 1: Active Risk Decomposition (%²)
# Source | Contribution
Market | 3.2
Size | 5.6
Value | 2.4
Active specific risk | 4.8
Total | 16.0

questions.q: The size factor's share of active risk squared is closest to:
questions.why: Contribution to active risk squared = factor's active risk (%²) / active risk squared = 5.6 / 16.0 = 35%.

questions.q: Active factor risk as a share of active risk squared is closest to:
questions.why: Active factor risk = 3.2 + 5.6 + 2.4 = 11.2 → 11.2/16.0 = 70%. Active specific risk = 4.8/16 = 30%.

vignettes.body:
Claire Dubois models quarterly time series at Nordhavn Bank.

Model 1 is an AR(1) model of a quarterly inflation measure (in %): x(t) = 0.96 + 0.60 x(t−1). The latest value of x is 3.10.

Model 2 is an AR(1) model of quarterly retail sales growth. The autocorrelations of its residuals are insignificant at lags 1 to 3, but the residual autocorrelation at lag 4 has a p-value of 0.012.

Model 3 is a log-linear trend model of annual revenue (in millions): ln(revenue) = 4.20 + 0.035t. The next period is t = 41.

Dubois also wants to regress one series on another. Both series have a unit root, and an Engle–Granger test shows they are cointegrated.

questions.q: Based on Model 1, the inflation measure next quarter is most likely to:
options: stay the same, because the slope coefficient is less than 1
rise, because 3.10 is below the mean-reverting level of 0.60
fall, because 3.10 is above the mean-reverting level of 2.40
questions.why:
Mean-reverting level = b0 / (1 − b1) = 0.96 / 0.40 = 2.40
Current value 3.1 > 2.40 → the series is expected to fall toward the mean.
Check: forecast = 0.96 + 0.6 × 3.1 = 2.82 < 3.1.

questions.q: Based on Model 2, Dubois should conclude that the model:
options: is correctly specified, because the first three lags are insignificant
shows seasonality, and a lag-4 term should be added
has a unit root, so the series should be first-differenced
questions.why:
Quarterly data → check the 4th lag (monthly data → the 12th lag).
p-value 0.012 < 0.05 → significant seasonal autocorrelation → add x(t−4).

questions.q: Based on Model 3, forecast revenue for t = 41 is closest to:
options: 5.63 million
69.0 million
280.1 million
questions.why:
ln(revenue) = 4.20 + 0.035 × 41 = 5.635
Revenue = e^5.635 = 280.1
If ln(1 + x) = a, then 1 + x = e^a: undo the log with e.

questions.q: Regarding the regression of one unit-root series on the other, the results are:
options: invalid, because both series have a unit root
valid, because the two series are cointegrated
valid only if each series is first-differenced into its own AR(1) model
questions.why: Neither has a unit root → valid. Only one has a unit root → invalid. Both have unit roots and are cointegrated → valid. Both have unit roots and are not cointegrated → invalid.

questions.q: A time series is covariance stationary if:
options: its slope coefficient in an AR(1) model is greater than 1
its values never move away from their mean
its mean, variance and covariance with its own lags are constant and finite
questions.why: Covariance stationarity: constant and finite expected value, constant and finite variance, and constant and finite covariance with leading or lagged values.

vignettes.body:
Ingrid Solheim, risk manager at Fjordline Asset Management, estimates parametric VaR for a $50 million equity portfolio. The portfolio's expected annual return is 9% and its annual standard deviation is 18%. She assumes 250 trading days a year and uses the one-tailed z-values in Exhibit 1.

Exhibit 1: One-Tailed z-Values
# Probability in the tail | z
10% | 1.28
5% | 1.65
2.5% | 1.96
1% | 2.33

Solheim also notes that the portfolio's returns have high kurtosis.

questions.q: The 5% annual VaR of the portfolio is closest to:
options: $19.35 million
$14.85 million
$10.35 million
questions.why:
Annual VaR = (z × σ_annual − μ_annual) × portfolio value = (1.65 × 0.18 − 0.09) × 50m = 0.207 × 50m = $10.35m
The expected return is subtracted, not added.

questions.q: The 1% daily VaR of the portfolio is closest to:
options: $1.308 million
$0.066 million
$1.042 million
questions.why:
Daily VaR = (z × σ_annual/√250 − μ_annual/250) × value = (2.33 × 0.18/15.811 − 0.09/250) × 50m = $1.308m
Volatility scales with √250; the mean scales with 250.

questions.q: Because of the high kurtosis, a VaR based on the normal distribution most likely:
options: is unaffected, because VaR uses only the mean and standard deviation
overstates the risk of extreme losses
understates the risk of extreme losses
questions.why: High kurtosis = fat tails → extreme downside losses are more likely than the normal distribution implies, so normal VaR understates tail risk. Low kurtosis → lower extreme downside risk.

vignettes.body:
Mara Kovacs, an analyst at Danubia Capital, estimates the cost of capital for several projects.

Project 1: A private domestic company. Kovacs uses an expanded CAPM with size and company-specific premiums.
Project 2: A subsidiary in an emerging market. She adds a country risk premium using an extended CAPM with global and country factors.
Project 3: She needs a pre-tax cost of debt for a company with no traded bonds, rated BBB, and with debt maturing in 7 years. Comparable BBB bonds yield 4.2% at 5 years and 5.1% at 10 years.
Project 4: A multinational. Kovacs uses an international CAPM: risk-free rate 2.5%, global market premium 5.0%, global beta 1.1, foreign currency risk premium 1.5% and currency beta 0.4.

questions.q: For Project 3, the interpolated pre-tax cost of debt is closest to:
For Project 4, the cost of equity is closest to:
Which matching of models to projects is most appropriate?
options: International CAPM for Project 1; expanded CAPM for Project 4
Expanded CAPM for Project 1; extended CAPM with a country risk premium for Project 2
Extended CAPM for Project 1; expanded CAPM for Project 2
questions.why: Expanded CAPM (size and company-specific premiums) → domestic private companies. Country risk premium / extended CAPM (global and country) → foreign operations in riskier countries.

vignettes.body:
Sven Aalto reviews the defined benefit pension plan of Kiruna Tech. Exhibit 1 shows plan data for the year (in $ millions).

Exhibit 1: Pension Plan Data
# Item | Amount
Beginning PBO | 500.0
Beginning plan assets | 440.0
Current service cost | 30.0
Past service cost (plan amendment this year) | 10.0
Discount rate | 4.5%
Expected return on plan assets | 6.0%
Actual return on plan assets | 20.0
Actuarial loss | 8.0
Employer contributions | 35.0
Benefits paid | 25.0

Aalto asks which assumption change would most reduce Kiruna's pension cost under US GAAP.

questions.q: The interest cost under US GAAP and the net interest expense under IFRS are closest to:
options: $2.7 million and $19.8 million
$22.5 million and $2.7 million
$22.5 million and $22.5 million
questions.why:
US GAAP interest cost = beginning PBO × r = 500 × 4.5% = 22.5
IFRS net interest = beginning funded status × r = (440 − 500) × 4.5% = −2.7 → net interest expense of 2.7

questions.q: Pension cost reported in profit or loss under IFRS is closest to:
options: $42.7 million
$32.7 million
$26.1 million
questions.why:
IFRS P&L: service cost (current + past) + net interest = 30 + 10 + 2.7 = 42.7.
(US GAAP P&L: current service cost + interest cost − expected return = 30 + 22.5 − 26.4 = 26.1, with past service cost amortised from OCI.)

questions.q: Kiruna's net pension liability at year-end is closest to:
options: $65.5 million
$75.5 million
$60.0 million
questions.why:
Ending PBO = 500 + 30 + 10 + 22.5 + 8 − 25 = 545.5
Ending plan assets = 440 + 35 + 20 − 25 = 470
Net pension liability = 545.5 − 470 = 75.5

questions.q: Which change in assumptions would most likely reduce Kiruna's pension cost under US GAAP?
options: A decrease in the expected return on plan assets
A decrease in the discount rate
A decrease in the estimated rate of future salary increases
questions.why:
Lower salary growth → lower PBO and service cost → lower pension cost.
A lower discount rate usually raises PBO and service cost; a lower expected return raises US GAAP pension cost.

vignettes.body:
Rhea Castell, an alternatives analyst at Lucerne Advisors, reviews three strategies.

Strategy 1: A fund that is always net short, with little or no long exposure.
Strategy 2: A fund that has a short bias but holds some long positions, usually 30–60% net short.
Strategy 3: A fund that buys life insurance policies from policyholders (life settlements).

questions.q: Strategies 1 and 2 are best described as, respectively:
options: short-biased and dedicated short bias
equity market neutral and short-biased
dedicated short bias and short-biased
questions.why: Dedicated short: mostly 60–120% short, little long exposure. Short-biased: net short but with some long positions (roughly 30–60% net short).

questions.q: Strategy 3 is most attractive when the policy has:
options: a low surrender value, low ongoing premiums and an insured person likely to die sooner than the insurer expects
a high surrender value, low ongoing premiums and an insured person likely to live longer than expected
a high surrender value, high ongoing premiums and an insured person likely to live longer than expected
questions.why: The fund pays the premiums and receives the death benefit. It looks for low surrender value (cheap to buy), low premiums and earlier-than-expected death.

vignettes.body:
Osei analyses a convertible bond issued by Brightwater Energy. The conversion price is above Brightwater's current share price. The bond's terms include a threshold dividend: if Brightwater pays dividends above the threshold, the conversion ratio is adjusted.

Osei also notes that over the past month Brightwater's share price fell 12%, while the convertible's price fell only 4%.

questions.q: Because the conversion price is above the current share price, the convertible's risk and return are most likely driven by:
options: interest rates and credit spreads, like a straight bond
the share price, like the common stock
neither, because the bond is a hybrid
questions.why:
Conversion price > share price (option out of the money) → behaves like a bond: interest rate and credit spread risk.
Conversion price < share price → behaves like the stock.
Roughly equal → hybrid.

questions.q: If Brightwater pays a dividend above the threshold, the conversion ratio most likely:
options: increases, so the conversion price falls and the conversion value rises
stays the same, but the straight value of the bond rises to compensate holders
decreases, so the conversion price rises and the conversion value falls
questions.why:
Dividends above the threshold → conversion ratio rises to compensate holders.
Conversion price = par / conversion ratio → falls.
Conversion value = share price × conversion ratio → rises.

questions.q: The convertible fell less than the share price mainly because:
options: the call option on the shares gained value as the share price fell
its conversion ratio rose when the share price fell
its straight value sets a floor under its price
questions.why: Convertible = straight bond + call option on the stock. As the share price falls, the bond's straight value (the floor) limits the decline, so the convertible falls by a smaller percentage than the stock.

vignettes.body:
Hanna Moberg manages equity hedges for Silverlake Pension Fund. On 1 March she enters a long six-month forward contract on 100,000 shares of Torvik AB. Torvik's share price is SEK62.00, and Torvik will pay a dividend of SEK1.20 per share in three months. The risk-free rate is 3.0% a year (annual compounding).

On 1 June, just after the dividend is paid, Torvik's share price is SEK58.50. The risk-free rate is unchanged.

Moberg's assistant notes that Torvik is considering selling one of its divisions and paying the cash out to shareholders as a one-off liquidating dividend.

questions.q: The forward price agreed on 1 March is closest to:
questions.why:
F0 = S0 × (1 + r)^T − FV of dividends
= 62.00 × 1.03^0.5 − 1.20 × 1.03^0.25
= 62.9231 − 1.2089 = 61.71
The dividend is compounded to expiration (3 months left after it is paid).

questions.q: On 1 June, the value of the long forward position per share is closest to:
questions.why:
F0 does not change: 61.7142.
The dividend has already been paid, so nothing is subtracted now.
Ft = 58.50 × 1.03^0.25 = 58.9339
Value (long) = (Ft − F0) / 1.03^0.25 = (58.9339 − 61.7142) / 1.007417 = -2.76
-3.21 is just S − F0; -3.96 subtracts the dividend again even though it was paid.

questions.q: The dividend the assistant describes is best described as a:
options: scrip dividend: a dividend paid in new shares instead of cash
liquidating dividend: a payout funded by selling assets, which returns capital to shareholders
special dividend: extra cash paid on top of the regular dividend from earnings
questions.why:
Liquidating dividend = sell part of the business and pay the proceeds out (return of capital).
Scrip dividend = stock dividend.
Special dividend = extra cash above the regular dividend.

vignettes.body:
Irene Castell, a credit analyst at Duvall Bank, reviews two CDS positions.

Position 1: A five-year CDS on Kessler Chemicals has a standard coupon of 1.00%. The current CDS spread is 3.20% and the CDS duration is 4.6.

Position 2: Duvall owns €10 million par of Rocher SA bonds and bought €10 million of CDS protection on Rocher. Rocher has just defaulted. Duvall's bonds now trade at 40% of par, and the cheapest-to-deliver Rocher bond trades at 32% of par. The CDS is cash settled.

questions.q: The CDS price per 100 of par for Position 1 is closest to:
questions.why:
Upfront premium ≈ (CDS spread − coupon) × duration = (3.20% − 1.00%) × 4.6 = 10.12% of notional (paid by the protection buyer).
CDS price per 100 par = 100 − upfront premium = 100 − 10.12 = 89.88

questions.q: For Position 2, the total value of Duvall's bonds plus the CDS payoff is closest to:
options: €10.0 million
€9.2 million
€10.8 million
questions.why:
Bonds: €10m × 40% = €4.0m
CDS payoff (cash settled on the cheapest-to-deliver): €10m × (1 − 32%) = €6.8m
Total = €10.8m. The payoff is based on the cheapest-to-deliver bond, not on the bond Duvall holds.

vignettes.body:
Ethics: Standards of Professional Conduct
Four independent questions. Each one can be answered on its own.

questions.q: A member under investigation by CFA Institute's Professional Conduct Program (PCP) faces possible sanctions. Must the member tell clients about the possible sanctions?
options: Yes, immediately, under VI(A)
No: the sanctions are not yet official
Yes, but only the key clients
questions.why: Possible sanctions are not officialised until the process ends, so there is nothing to disclose yet.

questions.q: Carter works for Invest Today, a local asset management firm. A broker that provides Carter with proprietary research through client brokerage arrangements is offering a new trading service. The broker is offering low-fee, execution-only trades to complement its traditional full-service execution-and-research trades. To entice Carter and other asset managers to send additional business its way, the broker will apply the commissions paid on the new service toward satisfying the brokerage commitment of the prior full-service arrangements. Carter has always been satisfied with the execution provided on the full-service trades, and the fees of the new low-fee trades are comparable to those of other brokers currently used for the accounts that prohibit soft dollar arrangements. Which of the following is most appropriate for Carter?
options: Carter can trade for his accounts that prohibit soft dollar arrangements under the new low-fee trading scheme.
Carter cannot use the new trading scheme because the commissions are prohibited by the soft dollar restrictions of the accounts.
Carter should trade only through the new low-fee scheme and should increase his trading volume to meet his required commission commitment.
questions.why: The question relates to Standard III(A) Loyalty, Prudence, and Care. Carter believes the broker offers effective execution at a fee that is comparable with those of other brokers, so he is free to use the broker for all accounts. Answer B is incorrect because the accounts that prohibit soft dollar arrangements do not want to fund the purchase of research by Carter.

questions.q: A manager, in a hurry, routes trades through brokers not yet on the firm's approved list. The main concern is Standard:
options: II(B) Market Manipulation
V(A) Diligence and Reasonable Basis
VII(A) Conduct as Participants in CFA Programs
questions.why: Skipping the firm's broker due-diligence process and risking poor execution shows a lack of diligence in taking investment action (and raises best-execution concerns under III(A)).

questions.q: When Abdullah Younis, CFA, was hired as a portfolio manager at an asset management firm two years ago and was told he could allocate his work hours as he saw fit. At that time, Younis served on the board of three nonpublic golf equipment companies and managed a pooled investment fund for several members of his immediate family. Younis was not compensated for his board service or for managing the pooled fund. Younis’ investment returns attract interest from friends and co-workers who persuade him to include their assets in his investment pool. Younis recently retired from all board responsibilities and now spends more than 80% of his time managing the investment pool for which he charges non-family members a management fee. Younis has never told his employer about any of these activities. To comply with the CFA Institute Standards of Professional Conduct with regards to his business activities over the past two years, Younis would least likely be required to disclose which of the following to his employer?
options: Family investment pool management
Non-family member management fees
Board activities
questions.why: Correct because golf equipment is a business independent of the financial services industry such that any board obligations would not likely be considered a conflict of interest requiring disclosure according to Standard IV(B), Additional Compensation Arrangements.

vignettes.body:
Marin turns to exchange rates and capital flows.

Fact 1: The Canadian dollar has depreciated against the US dollar.
Fact 2: Over the past decade, inflation in Country X averaged 6% and in Country Y 2%. Over the past quarter, the X/Y exchange rate barely moved.
Fact 3: New Zealand's one-year rate is 5.5% and the euro area's is 3.0%. Spot is 0.5500 EUR/NZD.
Fact 4: A fund borrows in yen at 0.2% and invests in euro deposits at 3.0%.
Fact 5: Country Z has a large current account deficit, falling foreign reserves, a sharply appreciated real exchange rate, rapid credit growth and rising M2 relative to reserves.

questions.q: Based on Fact 1, the USD/CAD quote (USD per CAD) has most likely:
options: fallen
not changed
risen
questions.why: USD/CAD = USD per 1 CAD. If CAD depreciates, one CAD buys fewer USD → USD/CAD falls.

questions.q: Fact 2 is most consistent with:
options: relative PPP failing in the long run but holding in the short run
absolute PPP holding in the short run but not in the long run
relative PPP holding in the long run but not in the short run
questions.why: Relative PPP: currency of the higher-inflation country depreciates by the inflation difference. It works poorly in the short run but reasonably over long periods.

questions.q: Under uncovered interest rate parity, the expected EUR/NZD spot rate in one year is closest to:
questions.why: Expected spot (EUR per NZD) = 0.5500 × (1 + i_EUR)/(1 + i_NZD) = 0.5500 × 1.030/1.055 = 0.5370. The high-yield currency (NZD) is expected to depreciate by the rate difference.

questions.q: The strategy in Fact 4 is best described as a:
options: carry trade, which profits if the yen does not appreciate by more than the rate difference
covered interest arbitrage, which locks in a riskless profit from the rate difference
carry trade, which profits only if the yen appreciates against the euro
questions.why: Carry trade: borrow the low-yield currency (JPY), invest in the high-yield currency (EUR). It earns the rate difference unless the funding currency appreciates enough, i.e. it bets that UIRP fails.

questions.q: Fact 5 most likely signals:
options: a high risk of a currency crisis
a current account surplus
a low risk of crisis, because credit growth supports the economy
questions.why: Warning signs of currency crises: large current account deficit, falling reserves, overvalued (appreciated) real exchange rate, rapid credit growth, rising M2 relative to reserves, and capital inflows that reverse.

vignettes.body: Marta Osei, an analyst at Corvin Partners, values a small private manufacturer by comparing it with listed companies. Before she applies public company multiples to the private company's earnings, she normalizes them.

questions.q: In private company valuation, normalizing earnings most likely means:
options: adjusting for the cyclicality of the company's revenues and costs.
adjusting revenues and costs so that the private company's results can be compared with those of public companies.
adjusting the earnings for the lack of marketability of the shares.
questions.why: Normalizing removes distortions in revenues and costs (non-market owner pay, personal expenses, non-recurring items) so that the private company's results are comparable with public companies. Cyclicality is a separate issue and the lack of marketability is handled by a discount (DLOM), not by changing earnings.

vignettes.body: Tolland Joinery is a private furniture maker. Its reported EBITDA is EUR 5.20 million. Its founder and CEO, Anselm Tolland, is paid EUR 250,000 a year, while CEOs of similar companies earn EUR 520,000 on average.

questions.q: Tolland's normalized EBITDA is closest to:
options: EUR 5.47 million.
EUR 5.20 million.
EUR 4.93 million.
questions.why: The CEO is paid EUR 0.27 million LESS than the market rate, so reported costs are too low. Normalized EBITDA = 5.20 − (0.52 − 0.25) = EUR 4.93 million. Overpaid owners work the other way (costs are added back). 5.47 adds the difference instead of subtracting it.

vignettes.body:
Hana Brandt is valuing a family-owned bakery. Her client points out the following about the business.

Item 1: The bakery's employees are paid about the same as employees of other bakeries in the area.
Item 2: The owner's spouse works full time in the bakery and takes no salary.
Item 3: The shop is rented from the owner's brother at a rent well below market rates.

questions.q: Which item would least likely require an adjustment to normalize the bakery's earnings?
options: Item 1
Item 2
Item 3
questions.why: Employees paid at market level need no adjustment. The unpaid spouse (Item 2) makes the costs too low, and the below-market related-party rent (Item 3) does too: both must be adjusted to market levels.

vignettes.body:
Ravi Menon is valuing Karstad Foods, a family-owned company that is for sale. Menon reviews its statements and finds the following.

Family members' compensation, included in SG&A, is $600,000 a year higher than is typical for companies of its size.
An annual management retreat costs $40,000 (included in SG&A) and is considered unnecessary.
The company owns a boat with annual operating expenses of $12,000 and annual depreciation of $25,000. A business purpose would justify costs of only $3,000 a year.
The owners own a 300,000 square foot warehouse which they rent to Karstad at $9 a square foot a year. Market rents for similar space are $7 a square foot. The rent is included in SG&A.

Exhibit 1: Karstad Foods, As Reported
# Item | Amount
EBIT | $4,200,000
Pro forma taxes (30%) | $1,260,000
Operating income after taxes | $2,940,000

questions.q: Karstad's normalized operating income after taxes is closest to:
questions.why:
Adjust EBIT first, then tax it. Add back the excess compensation 600,000, the retreat 40,000, the excess boat operating cost 12,000 − 3,000 = 9,000, the excess rent 300,000 × (9 − 7) = 600,000 and the boat depreciation 25,000 (the boat is removed).
Normalized EBIT = 4,200,000 + 600,000 + 40,000 + 9,000 + 600,000 + 25,000 = 5,474,000.
Tax at 30% = 1,642,200; operating income after taxes = $3,831,800.
$3,814,300 leaves out the boat depreciation; $3,825,500 leaves out the 9,000 boat cost.

title: Practice set 7
desc: Relationships from the main tables, theory questions and earlier mistakes (52 questions, 2 h 36 min)

vignettes.body:
Bettina Kral, a fixed-income analyst at Danube Capital, presents two short-rate models, which she writes with r as the short rate and dz as the random term:

Model 1: dr = a(b − r)dt + σ√r dz
Model 2: dr = θ dt + σ dz

She also values an option-free bond on a binomial tree calibrated to the current benchmark curve, studies a callable bond, and reads a quoted spread between the money market rate and the T-bill rate for the same maturity.

questions.q: Which statement about the two models is correct?
options: Model 1 has volatility that rises with the level of rates and cannot produce negative rates; Model 2 has constant volatility and no mean reversion.
Both models have constant volatility and mean reversion.
Model 1 has constant volatility and can produce negative rates; Model 2 has volatility that rises with the level of rates.
questions.why: Model 1 is Cox–Ingersoll–Ross: volatility σ√r rises with the rate, rates cannot be negative. Model 2 is Ho–Lee: constant volatility, no mean reversion (θ is time-dependent).

questions.q: If interest rates fall sharply, compared with the straight bond, the callable bond's effective duration will most likely:
options: fall, and its convexity can turn negative.
rise, and its convexity stays positive.
stay the same as the straight bond's duration.
questions.why: Callable bond when rates fall: the call is likely to be exercised, so duration is lower than the straight bond's and convexity falls (can turn negative). When rates rise, it behaves like the straight bond.

questions.q: The spread between the money market rate and the T-bill rate for the same maturity is the:
options: TED spread, which shows liquidity and credit risk of the banking sector.
Z-spread, which shows the constant spread added to each spot rate.
I-spread, which shows how much a credit-risky bond yield exceeds the swap rate.
questions.why: TED spread = MRR − T-bill rate (same maturity): liquidity and credit risk of the banking sector, an economy-wide measure rather than one government bond.

questions.q: If Kral raises the volatility assumption of the calibrated tree, the value of the option-free bond will:
options: fall.
stay the same.
rise.
questions.why: A calibrated tree reprices the benchmark bonds, so an option-free bond has the same value whatever volatility is assumed. Volatility matters only for bonds with embedded options.

vignettes.body:
Anja Lindqvist, an analyst at Fjell Research, answers three questions.

Ostmark Glass pays dividends that are far below its FCFE, and its dividends have little relation to its ability to pay. Lindqvist must choose a valuation model.

A colleague says that Corbin Foods must have both a higher-than-average growth rate and a higher-than-average risk to justify its high P/E.

Lindqvist also screens Company R for earnings quality. She separates its accruals into normal accruals, explained by a regression on business activity, and the residual.

questions.q: Lindqvist should most likely value Ostmark Glass with:
options: a dividend discount model, because Ostmark pays dividends.
a residual income model, because FCFE is positive.
an FCFE model, because dividends differ greatly from the capacity to pay them.
questions.why: Use FCFE instead of a DDM when dividends differ significantly from FCFE (the capacity to pay), when there are no dividends, or from a control perspective. A residual income model is chosen when free cash flow is negative or hard to forecast.

questions.q: The colleague's statement about Corbin Foods is:
options: incorrect with respect to risk, because higher risk lowers the justified P/E.
correct, because a high P/E needs both higher growth and higher risk.
incorrect with respect to growth, because higher growth lowers the justified P/E.
questions.why: Higher expected growth justifies a higher P/E; higher risk (a higher required return) justifies a lower P/E.

questions.q: The residual of Lindqvist's accruals regression represents:
options: cash earnings.
discretionary accruals, which may signal earnings manipulation.
non-discretionary accruals, which arise from normal operations.
questions.why: The part explained by the regression is normal (non-discretionary) accruals. The residual comes from unusual choices: discretionary accruals, a warning sign of manipulation.

vignettes.body:
Yuna Park, an analyst at Seabright Funds, tests three regression models that explain monthly fund returns. Exhibit 1 summarises what she sees in each model.

Exhibit 1: Diagnostics for Three Models
# Model | What Park observes
Model A | R² is large and the F-statistic is significant, but no slope t-statistic is significant and the standard errors are inflated
Model B | The variance of the residuals rises with the size of the fund's assets
Model C | The Durbin–Watson statistic is 1.12; the lower limit is 1.35 and the upper limit is 1.59

Park wants to name each problem and decide on a test and a fix.

questions.q: Model A most likely suffers from:
options: heteroskedasticity.
serial correlation.
multicollinearity.
questions.why: Signals of multicollinearity: R² large, F-statistic significant, t-statistics low or insignificant, standard errors inflated. All four are in Model A.

questions.q: For the problem in Model A, the main danger in the t-tests is:
options: Type I errors, because the standard errors are too low; the F-test is unreliable.
Type I errors, because the standard errors are too low; the F-test is too high.
Type II errors (failing to reject a false null), because the standard errors are too high; the F-test is not affected.
questions.why: Multicollinearity: standard errors High, t-test Low (Type II error), F-test not affected.

questions.q: Model B is best handled by:
options: testing with Breusch–Pagan and using robust (White) standard errors.
testing with the VIF and dropping a variable.
testing with Breusch–Godfrey and using Newey–West standard errors.
questions.why: Heteroskedasticity (variance of the residuals changes with a variable): test = Breusch–Pagan, fix = robust (White) standard errors, error type = Type I. The VIF is for multicollinearity; Breusch–Godfrey and Newey–West are for serial correlation.

questions.q: Model C's Durbin–Watson statistic most likely indicates:
options: positive serial correlation, with standard errors too low and t-tests and the F-test too high.
an inconclusive result, because the statistic lies between the limits.
negative serial correlation, with standard errors too high and t-tests too low.
questions.why: 1.12 is below the lower limit of 1.35, so reject: positive serial correlation. Serial correlation: standard errors Low, t-test High, F-test High (Type I errors).

vignettes.body:
Elias Brandt, an economist at Northwind Capital, summarises three views presented at a seminar on long-run growth.

View 1: Population rises when income is high and pushes income per person back down to subsistence.
View 2: Capital has diminishing returns, technology comes from outside the model and income per person reaches a steady state.
View 3: Investment in human capital and research has no diminishing returns, so income per person keeps growing.

Brandt also studies Tarland, where strong growth raises the threat of inflation. The central bank says it will use its monetary tools to prevent the inflation.

questions.q: The three views correspond to which growth theories?
options: View 1 classical, View 2 neoclassical, View 3 endogenous.
View 1 neoclassical, View 2 endogenous, View 3 classical.
View 1 endogenous, View 2 classical, View 3 neoclassical.
questions.why: Classical: population growth pushes income per capita back to subsistence. Neoclassical: diminishing returns to capital, exogenous technology, steady state. Endogenous: no diminishing returns (human capital, R&D), income per capita grows permanently.

questions.q: According to the theory in View 2, a permanent increase in the saving rate most likely:
options: raises the long-run growth rate of income per person permanently.
has no effect, because technology comes from outside the model.
raises the level of income per person in the steady state but not its long-run growth rate.
questions.why: Neoclassical: capital has diminishing returns, so more saving gives only a temporary boost to growth; income per capita reaches a new, higher steady-state level, while long-run growth is set by technology.

questions.q: A policy that subsidises research and education is most consistent with:
options: the theory in View 1, because it raises income per person permanently.
the theory in View 3, because it can raise long-run growth permanently.
the theory in View 2, because technology is determined inside the model.
questions.why: Endogenous growth: investment in human capital and R&D is not subject to diminishing returns, so such policies can permanently raise the growth rate. Classical and neoclassical theories do not give that result.

questions.q: To prevent the inflation, Tarland's central bank will most likely:
options: sell securities to the private sector.
buy securities from the private sector.
lower its policy rate.
questions.why: To fight inflation, reduce the money supply: sell securities (money out), raise the policy rate, raise reserve requirements. Buying securities or lowering the rate adds money and fuels inflation.

vignettes.body:
Naoko Ebisu, an analyst at Quill Analytics, prepares text from 20,000 broker reports for a sentiment model. Her raw text contains HTML tags, punctuation, numbers and extra white space.

Ebisu also compares two candidate regression models of fund flows in Exhibit 1.

Exhibit 1: Candidate Models
# Model | AIC | BIC
Model 1 | 412 | 431
Model 2 | 405 | 438

Finally, she tests a price series for a unit root, and the Dickey–Fuller test does not reject its null hypothesis.

questions.q: Removing HTML tags, punctuation, numbers and extra white space from the raw text is part of:
options: text wrangling (preprocessing).
text exploration.
text cleansing.
questions.why: Cleansing removes noise from the raw text: HTML tags, punctuation, numbers, white space. Wrangling works on tokens (lowercasing, stop words, stemming, lemmatisation). Exploration (bag of words, DF, MI) comes after.

questions.q: Which statement about choosing between the two models is correct?
options: Model 2 is better for forecasting (lower AIC) and Model 1 is better for goodness of fit (lower BIC).
Model 1 is better for forecasting (lower AIC) and Model 2 is better for goodness of fit (lower BIC).
Model 2 is better for both purposes because its AIC is lower.
questions.why: AIC: better forecast; BIC: better goodness of fit. Lower is better for both. Model 2 has the lower AIC (405 vs 412); Model 1 has the lower BIC (431 vs 438).

questions.q: Because the Dickey–Fuller test does not reject its null hypothesis, the price series:
options: is covariance stationary and can be modelled directly with an AR(1) model.
has no unit root, so adding a second lag will remove the trend.
has a unit root, is not covariance stationary and should be first-differenced before an autoregressive model is used.
questions.why: The Dickey–Fuller null hypothesis is that the series has a unit root. Failing to reject means a unit root: not covariance stationary, so transform it (usually first differences).

vignettes.body:
Dev Menon, a portfolio manager at Meridian Wealth, evaluates the Titan Equity Fund with a three-factor model. Exhibit 1 shows the fund's factor sensitivities.

Exhibit 1: Titan Equity Fund Factor Sensitivities
# Factor | Fund sensitivity
Market | 1.15
Size | 0.40
Value | −0.10

Menon's assistant, Lena Voss, uses a macroeconomic factor model whose factors are surprises with an expected value of zero. For Portfolio 1 the intercept is 2.58% and last year's return was 6.00%.

Voss compares fundamental and macroeconomic factor models, and Menon asks about an index fund that meets its investment objective exactly.

questions.q: Based on Exhibit 1, the fund's style is best described as:
options: aggressive (beta above 1), large-cap and value.
aggressive (beta above 1), small-cap and growth.
defensive (beta below 1), large-cap and value.
questions.why: Market 1.15 > 1: aggressive. Size positive: small-cap orientation. Value negative: growth orientation.

questions.q: In Voss's macroeconomic factor model, the expected return of Portfolio 1 is:
options: 2.58%, the intercept.
3.42%, the part of last year's return explained by the surprises.
6.00%, last year's return.
questions.why: In a macroeconomic factor model the factors are surprises with an expected value of zero, so the expected return is the intercept. Last year's 6.00% is an actual return that includes the factor surprises.

questions.q: In which type of model are the factor sensitivities estimated last?
options: the fundamental factor model (in the macroeconomic model they are determined first).
the macroeconomic factor model (in the fundamental model they are determined first).
both, because sensitivities are always estimated by regression.
questions.why: Fundamental model: sensitivities (company attributes) are determined first, then factor returns are estimated. Macroeconomic model: the surprises are given and the sensitivities are estimated last by regression.

questions.q: The information ratio of an index fund that meets its objective exactly is most likely:
options: positive but indeterminate.
zero.
equal to its Sharpe ratio.
questions.why: An index fund that tracks its benchmark exactly has zero active return, so the information ratio (active return ÷ active risk) is zero.

vignettes.body:
Sol Park, a credit analyst at Hanover Credit Partners, reviews a risky corporate bond and the CDS market.

Park compares two credit models. Model X relies on the company's balance sheet and option pricing. Model Y relies on macroeconomic and company-specific data to estimate a default intensity with a regression.

Exhibit 1: Five-Year Market Data for the Company
# Item | Spread over the benchmark
Bond | 240 bps
CDS | 210 bps

Park expects the economy to improve and considers trades on a high-yield index and an investment-grade index. A client sold protection on the company last year, when its CDS spread was 150 bps, and asks about the position today.

questions.q: A weakness of Model Y compared with Model X is that Model Y:
options: does not explain why default happens and treats default as a random surprise.
assumes the company's assets are traded in the market.
is burdensome because of complex balance sheets.
questions.why: Reduced-form model (Y): disadvantages: does not explain why default happens; default is treated as a random event. Strengths: does not assume assets trade, default intensity changes with fundamentals. The structural model (X) has the weaknesses in the other two options.

questions.q: Given the spreads in Exhibit 1, the arbitrage trade is most likely to:
options: buy the bond and sell protection through the CDS.
buy the bond and buy protection through the CDS.
sell the bond and sell protection through the CDS.
questions.why: Bond spread (240) > CDS spread (210): buy the bond and buy the CDS (protection). If the bond spread were below the CDS spread: sell both.

questions.q: Expecting the economy to improve, Park should most likely:
options: buy protection on the high-yield index and sell protection on the investment-grade index.
sell protection on the high-yield index and buy protection on the investment-grade index.
sell protection on both indexes.
questions.why: Economy improves: high yield → sell protection; investment grade → buy protection.

questions.q: Compared with the original spread, the client's position today most likely shows:
options: a loss, because the spread has widened.
a gain, because the spread is above the coupon.
a gain, because the spread has widened.
questions.why: Protection seller: spread narrows → gain; spread widens → loss. Today's spread (210 bps) is above the original 150 bps, so the seller has a loss. Gain or loss compares the current spread with the ORIGINAL spread.

vignettes.body:
Mateo Ruiz, an analyst at Granite Research, studies Corvane Systems, which grants stock options and restricted stock units (RSUs) and sponsors a defined benefit pension plan. Corvane reports under US GAAP; its closest peer reports under IFRS.

Corvane's advisor says that expected share price volatility at the grant date has risen. Ruiz also compares how the two frameworks treat the expected return on plan assets. Finally, employees recently exercised options when the share price was well above the grant-date fair value.

questions.q: Higher expected volatility at the grant date will most likely:
options: lower the fair value and expense of the options and raise net income.
raise the fair value and expense of the options and lower net income, with no effect on the RSUs.
raise the fair value of the options and of the RSUs, and lower net income.
questions.why: Higher volatility: stock option fair value ↑, operating expense ↑, net income ↓. RSU fair value, expense and net income are the same.

questions.q: Which statement about the expected return on plan assets is correct?
options: Under US GAAP it is deducted in the pension cost; under IFRS it is not deducted separately.
It is deducted under both frameworks.
Under IFRS it is deducted in the pension cost; under US GAAP it is not deducted separately.
questions.why: Pension cost: US GAAP deducts the expected return on plan assets; IFRS does not deduct it separately (interest cost on the funded status instead).

questions.q: The recent option exercises at a share price well above the grant-date fair value are most likely to:
options: raise the effective tax rate under US GAAP and lower it under IFRS.
lower the effective tax rate under both frameworks.
lower Corvane's effective tax rate under US GAAP, but not under IFRS.
questions.why: Windfall (settlement-date price higher than grant-date value): larger tax deduction, tax lower than expected. US GAAP: effective tax rate ↓. IFRS: the windfall goes straight to equity, so the rate is not affected.

vignettes.body:
After spending years employed as a research analyst covering Asian exchanges at an investment management firm based in Singapore and then undertaking further training, Vishram Mehta, CFA, recently launched a new career as an independent asset consultant. His first client is Montfill Tech (“Montfill”), a small software development company with offices in Singapore and India. Montfill is struggling to retain top developers for more than two years. Consequently, the company feels it is not able to fully capitalize on the investments it has made in employee training and development. Montfill is considering introducing a retirement benefit plan to supplement the statutory government-sponsored individual employee defined contribution (DC) plans. It feels the extra benefit designed with no risk to the employee will help with retention. Mehta’s assignment is to design a defined benefit (DB) package that includes an Investment Policy Statement and asset allocation.

To begin the assignment, Mehta researches the rules and regulations concerning pension plans in Singapore and India. Mehta initially thinks the pension plan regulations are tougher in India than in Singapore. Given the extensive regulations, however, he realizes he needs some help and thus considers speaking with an expert in global pension plan regulations. Subsequently, during a short conversation with a manager working in the Human Resources (HR) department of a multinational, Mehta asks the manager to outline the prominent features of their pension plan. Mehta contemplates what his next step should be based on the information he has received so far.

To start determining an asset allocation for Montfill’s DB plan, Mehta reviews the answers he captured during his initial conversations with management to help him assess Montfill’s investment profile, including return objectives, risk tolerances, previous investment history, and current and projected financial status. He has yet to receive the detailed answers to the questionnaire he sent to Montfill’s HR department about employee demographics. While he is awaiting the questionnaire responses, he drafts an asset allocation based on his understanding of the client’s needs.

Before Mehta begins to draft the Investment Policy Statement, he recalls the earlier conversation he had with the HR manager. The HR manager advised him to have a consultation with Risner Employee Benefits Law, a global legal firm with a stellar reputation in over 150 countries. The HR manager also mentioned Mehta might want to offer his services as a pension trustee or consultant to the client given all his years of experience in Asia. Mehta remembers his remarks: “Those are great ideas, particularly as I have direct work experience in all the countries where my client operates. I think I might also recommend that Risner draft the needed legal documents if I find their services are appropriate after my conversation and due diligence. But I’ll work out a referral fee arrangement first and include those details in my recommendation to the client.”

Mehta wants to include the following items in the Investment Policy Statement:

As previously disclosed in the contract between us:

Item 1: In lieu of evaluating new providers of third-party economic research needed to help determine asset class return forecasts, I hired those used by my former employer. The fees I pay them are part of normal operating expenses so are not directly expensed back to the client.

Item 2: As an independent asset consultant, there may be times when I am working on similar projects concurrently. These assignments may be for clients within the same industry (i.e., competitors). Systems and processes are in place to protect the privacy and data of all clients.

Item 3: Each assignment is undertaken with the best interests of the client in mind to meet their overall objectives as defined in our contract. It is up to each client to seek outside legal counsel and implement only the recommendations they deem fit.

questions.q: What should Mehta’s next step most likely be to avoid violating the CFA Institute Standards of Professional Conduct?
options: Consult with a legal specialist.
Limit his research to India.
Replicate the multinational firm’s pension plan.
questions.why: To avoid violating Standard I(A): Knowledge of the Law, Mehta should consult with legal specialists who understand the pension regulations in both Singapore and India. He has recognized he needs help after his initial desktop research. If he limited his desktop research to India, he would likely be violating Standard I(A): Knowledge of the Law in that he would not take into consideration Singaporean regulations.

questions.q: Will Mehta’s draft asset allocation recommendation most likely conform to Standard III(C): Suitability?
options: No, with regard to Montfill’s profile
Yes
No, with regard to the HR department request
questions.why: Mehta’s draft asset allocation will most likely violate Standard III(C) given he has not received responses to the questionnaire addressing employee demographics. To understand liquidity needs of the funds, it is critical to understand the age profile of the client’s labor force, any planned early retirements due to known medical conditions, etc.

questions.q: If Mehta proposes Risner’s and his services to his client (Montfill), which component of the CFA Institute Standards of Professional Conduct will least likely be violated?
options: Misconduct
Referral fees
Misrepresentation
questions.why: Mehta would least likely violate Standard VI(C): Referral Fees as he noted he will include any referral fee arrangements in the proposal to Montfill. Standard VI(C): Referral Fees requires Members and Candidates to disclose to their employer, clients, and prospective clients, as appropriate, any compensation, consideration, or benefit received from or paid to others for the recommendation of products or services.

questions.q: Which of the items Mehta wants to include in the Investment Policy Statement most likely reflects a violation of the CFA Institute Standards of Professional Conduct?
options: Item 2
Item 3
Item 1
questions.why: Item 1 most likely reflects a violation of the CFA Institute Standards of Professional Conduct. Mehta is using economic data from third-party providers to help determine expected asset class returns to formulate his asset class recommendations to clients.

vignettes.body:
Tomas Berg, a derivatives analyst at Oslo Capital, answers four questions.

Lakeshore Utilities has issued fixed-rate bonds. Its CFO says: "I want our debt to behave like floating-rate debt so that the market value of our liabilities is less sensitive to changes in interest rates."

A three-month forward contract on a stock is quoted in the market at 52.40, while the carry model gives a fair forward price of 51.10.

A client sells a call option on an index.

A commodity has a convenience yield that is higher than its storage cost.

questions.q: To meet the CFO's objective, Lakeshore should enter into a swap in which it:
options: pays fixed and receives an equity return.
pays fixed and receives floating.
pays floating and receives fixed.
questions.why: Lakeshore already pays fixed on its bonds. Receiving fixed and paying floating cancels the fixed payments and leaves floating-rate debt, whose value is much less sensitive to rates.

questions.q: The forward contract is most likely:
options: cheap, so the arbitrage is to buy the forward, short the stock and lend.
expensive, so the arbitrage is to sell the forward, borrow and buy the stock (cash-and-carry).
fairly priced, so there is no arbitrage.
questions.why: Quoted price (Q = 52.40) above the model price (F = 51.10): the forward is expensive → Sell forward, Borrow, Buy the asset (cash-and-carry). Q below F: Buy forward, Short, Lend.

questions.q: The signs of the Greeks of the call option the client sold are most likely:
options: positive gamma and positive vega, with negative theta.
negative gamma and negative vega, with positive theta.
negative gamma and positive vega, with positive theta.
questions.why: Long call: delta +, gamma +, vega +, theta −, rho +. Short call: all signs reversed: delta −, gamma −, vega −, theta +, rho −.

questions.q: The commodity's futures curve is most likely in:
options: contango, with inventories rising.
backwardation, with inventories falling.
backwardation, with inventories rising.
questions.why: Convenience yield > storage cost: backwardation and inventory falls. Convenience yield < storage cost: contango and inventory rises.

vignettes.body:
Nadia Corsi, an analyst at Lakeview Partners, analyses Brightmill Foods, which owns 50% of a joint venture and two foreign subsidiaries. The joint venture is reported under the equity method; Corsi wants to see the effect of proportionate consolidation.

Subsidiary A is in Mexico and uses the Mexican peso as its functional currency. Brightmill's presentation currency is the US dollar, and Subsidiary A has a net asset exposure. The peso is depreciating.

Subsidiary B is in Poland and uses the US dollar as its functional currency, with a net monetary liability exposure in zloty. The zloty is appreciating.

questions.q: Compared with the equity method, proportionate consolidation of the joint venture will most likely:
options: increase total assets only, leaving revenue unchanged.
increase revenue, total assets and net income.
increase revenue and total assets, with the same net income and equity.
questions.why: Equity method: revenue unchanged, assets unchanged. Proportionate: revenue and assets increase. Net income and equity increase by the same amount under both methods.

questions.q: Because the peso is depreciating, Subsidiary A's translation adjustment (CTA) in equity most likely:
options: increases.
is not affected, because translation gains and losses go to net income.
decreases.
questions.why: Local functional currency → current rate method. With a net asset exposure, a depreciating foreign currency makes CTA decrease (and an appreciating one makes it increase).

questions.q: For Subsidiary B, the zloty's appreciation most likely causes:
options: a decrease in CTA.
a gain in other comprehensive income.
a remeasurement loss that reduces net income.
questions.why: Presentation currency as functional currency → temporal method, where the remeasurement gain or loss goes to net income (the plug). With a net monetary liability, an appreciating foreign currency produces a loss.

questions.q: Because the peso is depreciating, the higher gross margin for the Mexican subsidiary is reported under:
options: either method, because the margins are equal.
the current rate method.
the temporal method.
questions.why: Foreign currency appreciating → temporal gives the higher margin. Foreign currency depreciating → current rate gives the higher margin.

vignettes.body:
Gabriela Silva, a portfolio manager at Tamsin Fixed Income, compares a callable bond, a putable bond and a convertible bond. The callable and putable bonds have the same issuer, maturity and coupon as a straight bond. She prices them on a binomial tree and computes their option-adjusted spreads (OAS) with the same volatility assumption.

Silva expects interest rate volatility to rise. The convertible bond's conversion price is well above the current share price of the issuer.

questions.q: If interest rate volatility rises, the value of the callable bond will most likely:
options: rise and the value of the putable bond will fall.
fall and the value of the putable bond will fall.
fall and the value of the putable bond will rise.
questions.why: Callable bond = straight bond − call; putable bond = straight bond + put. Higher volatility raises the value of the option: callable ↓, putable ↑.

questions.q: If Silva raises the volatility assumption in the tree, the OAS of the callable bond will most likely:
options: fall and the OAS of the putable bond will rise.
rise and the OAS of the putable bond will fall.
fall and the OAS of the putable bond will fall.
questions.why: Higher volatility raises the value of the call, so the callable bond's model value falls below its market price; to match the market price the OAS must fall. For the putable bond the put is worth more, the model value rises and the OAS must rise. Volatility ↑: OAS of the callable ↓, OAS of the putable ↑.

questions.q: The risk and return of the convertible bond most likely resemble those of:
options: a hybrid of a bond and a stock.
a stock, driven by the share price.
a bond, driven by interest rates and the credit spread.
questions.why: Conversion price above the share price: the bond-like case: interest rate and credit spread risk. Conversion price below the share price: stock-like. Equal: hybrid.

vignettes.body:
Ingrid Solberg, an economist at Fjord Capital, reviews the emerging country of Maravia, whose government opened its capital market.

Exhibit 1: Maravia Indicators over the Past Two Years
# Indicator | Change
Capital inflows | Surged
Official reserves | Fell
Real exchange rate | Overvalued
Inflation | Rose
Banking stress | Rose
M2 to reserves | Increased quickly

Solberg also considers a carry trade. A euro-based investor borrows euros, converts them into yen at today's rate S0 (yen per euro), invests in yen and converts back at maturity at S1 (yen per euro).

Maravia has low capital mobility and is thinking of tightening both monetary and fiscal policy. A developed country with high capital mobility is expanding monetary policy while restricting fiscal policy.

questions.q: The indicators in Exhibit 1 are most consistent with:
options: a currency that is about to appreciate because of tight policy.
an economy with improving fundamentals and a stable currency.
a rising risk of a currency crisis.
questions.why: Currency crisis signals (CRRIB M2): Capital inflows up, Reserves down, Real exchange rate overvalued, Inflation up, Banking stress up, M2/reserves increasing quickly. All six are in Exhibit 1.

questions.q: In euro terms, the return of the carry trade is most likely reduced by:
options: the yen depreciating against the euro (S1 rises).
a fall in the euro borrowing rate.
the yen appreciating against the euro (S1 falls).
questions.why: EUR terms: return = S0 × (1 + R_JPY) × 1/S1 − 1 − R_EUR. A higher S1 (more yen per euro, so a weaker yen) lowers the return. A lower euro rate raises the return and a yen appreciation raises it.

questions.q: Using the Mundell–Fleming relationships, Maravia's planned policy mix most likely leads its currency to:
options: have an ambiguous effect.
appreciate.
depreciate.
questions.why: Restrictive monetary / restrictive fiscal with low capital mobility (emerging): Appreciation. (With high mobility the mix is ambiguous.)

questions.q: For the developed country, the policy mix most likely leads its currency to:
options: appreciate.
depreciate.
have an ambiguous effect.
questions.why: Expansionary monetary / restrictive fiscal with high capital mobility (developed): Depreciation. (With low mobility it is ambiguous.)

vignettes.body: Lena Hartmann, an analyst at Corvin Research, studies the defined benefit pension plan of Valtor Industries, which reports under US GAAP. At the beginning of the year the projected benefit obligation (PBO) was $620 million and the fair value of plan assets was $560 million. The accumulated unrecognized net actuarial loss at the beginning of the year was $95 million, and the average remaining service life of the active employees is 12 years. Valtor amortizes actuarial gains and losses with the corridor approach. Hartmann also notes that a peer company reports under IFRS.

questions.q: The amortization of the actuarial loss included in Valtor's pension cost for the year is closest to:
options: $3.25 million.
$2.75 million.
$7.92 million.
questions.why:
Corridor = 10% × the greater of beginning PBO and beginning plan assets = 10% × 620 = $62 million.
The accumulated loss of $95 million exceeds the corridor by 95 − 62 = $33 million; only this excess is amortized.
Amortization = 33 ÷ 12 = $2.75 million.
$7.92 million = 95 ÷ 12 ignores the corridor. $3.25 million uses plan assets for the corridor (10% × 560 = 56) although the PBO is the greater amount.

questions.q: Which statement about the corridor approach and the peer company's IFRS reporting is most accurate?
options: The corridor approach is required under IFRS and optional under US GAAP.
Under IFRS, actuarial gains and losses are recognized in profit or loss immediately.
The corridor approach is a US GAAP method; under IFRS the remeasurements go to OCI and are not amortized into profit or loss.
questions.why:
The corridor approach (amortizing only the part of the accumulated actuarial gains and losses outside the corridor) is a US GAAP method.
Under IFRS, remeasurements of the net defined benefit liability (including actuarial gains and losses) are recognized in OCI and are not amortized into profit or loss later.
The other two statements reverse or misstate the treatment.

vignettes.body:
Priya Rao, a real estate analyst at Norden Capital, compares two office markets with the observations in Exhibit 1.

Exhibit 1: Office Market Observations
# Observation | Market A | Market B
Vacancy rate | Rising | Near its cyclical high
Rent growth | Slowing but still positive | Negative
New construction | Projects started earlier are still being completed | Halted
Lenders | Still willing to finance projects | Tightening credit
Property prices | Flat | Falling

questions.q: Based on Exhibit 1, Market A is most likely in the:
options: expansion phase.
hyper-supply (oversupply) phase.
recession phase.
questions.why:
Cycle order: recovery → expansion → hyper-supply → recession.
Market A: construction started earlier is still delivering new space while vacancy rises and rent growth slows: supply is running ahead of demand, which is the hyper-supply (oversupply) phase.
Expansion would show falling vacancy and rising rents. Recession shows negative rent growth, halted construction and falling prices.

questions.q: Based on Exhibit 1, Market B is most likely in the:
options: hyper-supply (oversupply) phase.
recovery phase.
recession phase.
questions.why:
Market B: vacancy near its cyclical high, negative rent growth, halted construction, tightening credit and falling property prices are the signs of a recession.
Hyper-supply still has construction being completed and flat to slowing rents. Recovery follows the recession, with little new construction but stabilizing vacancy and rents, not falling prices.

title: Practice set 8
desc: Wrong questions of Mocks 5-9 as short key-point vignettes, no calculations (46 questions, 1 h 30 min)

vignettes.body: Ines Moreau values a stock with a multistage residual income model. She assumes residual income stays at its last forecast level forever. Her supervisor suggests that residual income fades quickly because the firm has extreme accounting returns.

questions.q: Compared with Moreau's assumption, a persistence factor close to zero gives an estimate of the stock's value that is:
options: the same, because the persistence factor only affects book value.
lower, because residual income vanishes soon after the forecast horizon.
higher, because residual income grows faster.
questions.why: Constant residual income forever means a persistence factor of 1. A factor near zero means residual income fades at once, so the terminal value and the stock value are lower.

vignettes.body: Ana Costa studies a BBB bond. Expected return over the next year must include credit migration. A second bond is valued on a binomial tree: the value without default (VND) is reduced by the credit valuation adjustment (CVA) to get the fair value, whose yield exceeds the benchmark yield. The recovery rate of the bond is one-quarter of the exposure.

questions.q: Including credit migration, the expected one-year return of the BBB bond is:
options: equal to its yield to maturity if spreads stay stable.
higher than its yield to maturity, because upgrades and downgrades cancel out.
lower than its yield to maturity, because downgrades cost more than upgrades gain.
questions.why: Expected return ≈ YTM − Σ probability × modified duration × (change in spread). Spreads widen more on a downgrade than they narrow on an upgrade, and downgrades are the larger part of the migration risk, so the net effect lowers the expected return.

questions.q: The credit spread of the second bond is the:
options: CVA divided by the VND.
yield on the bond valued at VND minus the benchmark yield.
yield on the bond valued at VND − CVA minus the benchmark yield.
questions.why: The credit spread is the yield of the credit-risky bond minus the benchmark yield. The risky bond's value is VND − CVA (the fair value, lower than VND), and the yield at that lower price exceeds the benchmark yield. Discounting at VND gives only the benchmark yield (a spread of zero).

questions.q: With a recovery rate of one-quarter of the exposure, the loss given default used in the CVA is:
options: 75% of the exposure.
50% of the exposure.
25% of the exposure.
questions.why: LGD = 1 − recovery rate. Using the recovery rate (or 50%) as the loss understates the CVA and the spread.

vignettes.body: Marta Ricci compares Investment 1, a real estate operating company (REOC), with Investment 2, a real estate investment trust (REIT), for a taxable client.

questions.q: Compared with the REOC, the REIT most likely:
options: requires less expertise in real estate investing.
avoids double taxation of the income received by investors.
is better able to hold properties under development.
questions.why: REITs are tax-advantaged pass-through structures: no corporate income tax, only the investor pays tax on dividends. REOCs are ordinary taxable companies and have more operating flexibility (development, no payout requirement).

vignettes.body: An ESG data firm gives one point for each favorable governance feature. A two-tiered board is favorable. In a one-tiered board, which is considered unfavorable, independent directors must make up at least 60% to be favorable. CEO duality absent, average board tenure below ten years, and each independent committee (audit, compensation, director selection) are one point each.

questions.q: Under this scoring system, a board structure earns the independence point when:
options: the board has fewer than ten directors with an average tenure above ten years.
the board is one-tiered with a simple majority of independent directors, the general rule.
the board is two-tiered, or it is one-tiered with at least 60% independent directors.
questions.why: Two-tiered is favorable by structure; a one-tiered board needs the higher 60% threshold because that structure is considered unfavorable.

vignettes.body: Joanna Whitfield says the advantages of VaR are that it estimates the downside exposure in a worst-case scenario, avoids subjectivity and can be used for performance evaluation. She estimates VaR with the parametric method, which assumes a normal distribution.

questions.q: Of Whitfield's three claims, the correct one is that VaR:
options: estimates the downside exposure in a worst-case scenario.
avoids subjectivity.
can be used for performance evaluation (risk-adjusted returns).
questions.why: Performance evaluation is correct: VaR can be used to compare risk-adjusted returns across managers or units. The other two claims are wrong: VaR needs subjective inputs (confidence level, horizon, method), and it is the minimum loss at a given confidence level, not a worst case; losses can exceed it.

questions.q: A limitation of the parametric VaR method is that it:
options: assumes normally distributed returns, a poor fit for fat tails and options.
uses actual past returns, so it cannot capture risks that are new.
requires a very large number of random scenarios generated by a model.
questions.why: Historical simulation uses past returns; Monte Carlo generates random scenarios. Parametric assumes a normal distribution.

vignettes.body: Peter Marlow explains forward pricing. A bond futures contract is compared with the underlying bond. The cost of holding the bond until the futures expiry must be considered, and the futures-side price must include the accrued interest at expiry.

questions.q: To find the no-arbitrage price of the bond futures, the bond price plus accrued interest today is:
options: left unchanged, because the bond pays coupons.
carried forward to the expiry date at the risk-free rate.
discounted back from the expiry date at the risk-free rate.
questions.why: No-arbitrage futures price = (bond price + accrued interest) × (1 + r)^T (less the future value of coupons). Only the final profit is discounted to today.

vignettes.body: Daniel Kwon reviews a storage REIT and an office REIT. Entry into self-storage is easy, while office buildings can become obsolete. Retail REITs depend on their tenants' sales per square foot.

questions.q: The risk factor most likely to hurt an investment in the storage REIT is:
options: obsolescence of existing space.
the tenants' sales per square foot.
new competing facilities.
questions.why: Match the risk to the sub-sector: storage = overbuilding and new competing facilities (easy entry); office = obsolescence and remote work; retail = tenants' sales per square foot.

vignettes.body: Helen Marsh explains a sale-leaseback plan of Mercury Corp.: the company sells its real estate, rents it back and uses the cash to retire debt. It expects an investment-grade rating after the transactions.

questions.q: Which statement about Mercury's motivations is INCORRECT?
options: The transactions allow the company to sell a business that is not its core business.
The expected credit rating upgrade will increase the cost of capital.
The transactions unlock the value of the company's real estate assets.
questions.why: Less debt and a better rating lower, not raise, the cost of capital. Sale-leasebacks unlock real estate value and real estate is not a grocer's core business.

vignettes.body: Leon Fischer believes that the spot curve one year from today will reflect the current forward curve. He also expects a flight to quality and a bullish flattening of the yield curve.

questions.q: Fischer's view that the future spot curve equals the current forward curve is most consistent with:
options: the pure expectations theory.
the liquidity preference theory.
the segmented markets theory.
questions.why: Pure expectations: forward rates are unbiased predictors of future spot rates, no premium. Liquidity preference adds a premium; segmented markets price each maturity separately.

vignettes.body: Leo Park tests a regression with 20 observations and 3 independent variables. He compares the t-statistics of two slope coefficients with the critical t-value at the 5% level.

questions.q: A slope coefficient is statistically significant when:
options: its t-statistic is positive.
its t-statistic exceeds 1.96, whatever the sample size.
the absolute value of its t-statistic exceeds the critical t-value.
questions.why: Reject H0 (coefficient = 0) when |t| > critical t, with df = n − k − 1 = 20 − 3 − 1 = 16. The sign does not matter and the critical value for a small sample is larger than 1.96.

vignettes.body: Tierra Dorada reports a defined benefit plan. From 20X2 to 20X3 it lowered its estimated future salary increases, its expected long-term return on plan assets and its discount rate, and it raised its inflation estimate.

questions.q: Which change most favorably affects 20X3 pension cost and earnings?
options: the lower expected long-term return on plan assets.
the lower discount rate.
the lower estimated future salary increases.
questions.why: Lower salary growth reduces the service cost. A lower expected return on assets raises the periodic cost; a lower discount rate raises the obligation and usually the interest cost.

questions.q: Which pair of 20X3 assumptions is most likely internally inconsistent?
options: a higher inflation estimate with lower estimated salary increases.
a lower discount rate with a lower expected return on plan assets.
a lower discount rate with lower estimated salary increases.
questions.why: Salary increases normally move with inflation (positive relation). The discount rate and the expected return on assets both depend on market rates and move in the same direction.

vignettes.body: A foundation needs US dollars for its supply contracts. It enters a fixed-for-fixed currency swap in which it pays won and receives dollars. Present value factors are given for both currencies.

questions.q: The fixed rate the foundation RECEIVES on the swap is calculated with:
options: the won present value factors, because it pays won.
the average of the dollar and won factors.
the US dollar present value factors.
questions.why: Each leg is priced with its own currency's factors. The foundation receives dollars, so the rate it receives comes from the dollar factors; the won rate is the one it pays.

vignettes.body: Karl Voss integrates ESG factors into the credit analysis of KT Hotels. The board has only 1 independent member out of 15, only 2 women among its members, and only 20% of its members have hotel industry experience.

questions.q: After integrating the ESG factors, the credit spread on KT Hotels' bonds is most likely to:
options: increase.
remain unchanged.
decrease.
questions.why: Weak governance (few independent directors, little diversity, little industry experience) and social risk raise the credit risk, so investors ask for a higher spread.

vignettes.body: Anna Wexford reviews the earnings quality of DB. The balance-sheet accruals relative to operating assets are small and trending downward over the last years.

questions.q: Which accruals trend would most strongly raise a concern that management manipulates reported performance?
options: accruals that trend upward relative to operating assets.
a small absolute level of accruals.
accruals that trend downward relative to operating assets.
questions.why: Upward-trending accruals give management room to manipulate earnings; downward-trending accruals leave less room, which supports DB's performance.

vignettes.body: Three analysts comment on implied volatility. Maddox says the volatility surface shows implied volatility across exercise prices and maturities. Jeffries says the skew keeps the same shape whatever the demand for hedging is. Birch says implied volatility is computed from historical volatility.

questions.q: Whose comment is most likely correct?
options: Maddox's.
Jeffries's.
Birch's.
questions.why: The surface plots implied volatility against both strike and maturity. The skew steepens when hedging demand rises. Implied volatility is backed out of market option prices and reflects expected future volatility, not historical volatility.

vignettes.body: Nils Sorensen explains how an investor uses ETFs to obtain exposure to parts of the benchmark that the portfolio does not hold, so that the whole portfolio matches the benchmark.

questions.q: Sorensen's explanation of benchmark exposure describes:
options: liquidity management.
completion strategies.
portfolio rebalancing.
questions.why: Completion: ETFs fill the gaps so that overall exposures match the benchmark. Rebalancing restores target weights after market moves; liquidity management uses ETFs to stay invested while holding cash needs.

vignettes.body: Rosa Varela values Aldeia S.A. on 1 January. She has the price, the earnings per share of the last four quarters, the analysts' EPS forecast for the next four quarters, and the average EPS of the last full business cycle.

questions.q: Aldeia's trailing P/E, ignoring any business-cycle influence, is the price divided by:
options: the EPS of the last four quarters.
the analysts' EPS forecast for the next four quarters.
the average EPS of the last full business cycle.
questions.why: Trailing P/E = price ÷ EPS of the most recent four quarters. Forward (leading) P/E uses expected EPS; the cycle average gives a normalized P/E.

vignettes.body: Henrik Dahl needs the bid EUR/AUD cross rate. The interbank market quotes EUR/USD and AUD/USD with bid and offer prices.

questions.q: The bid EUR/AUD cross rate is obtained by:
options: multiplying the offer EUR/USD by the inverse of the bid AUD/USD.
multiplying the bid EUR/USD by the inverse of the offer AUD/USD.
multiplying the bid EUR/USD by the bid AUD/USD.
questions.why: Selling EUR for AUD means: sell EUR for USD (bid EUR/USD), then sell USD to buy AUD, which uses the AUD/USD OFFER (1/offer). Multiplying the two bids is the common mistake.

vignettes.body: Chloe Brandt ranks three bonds. In a recession that is turning into a recovery, credit spreads narrow. One of her colleagues states that the expected loss of a bond equals the probability of default times its recovery rate.

questions.q: When credit spreads narrow in an economic recovery, the improvement is likely to be greatest for:
options: the bonds with the highest credit rating and the narrowest spread.
the bonds with the lowest credit rating and the widest spread.
all bonds equally, whatever their rating.
questions.why: Weaker credits have more spread to give back; in a recession the good credits outperform and spreads between low and high quality widen.

questions.q: The expected loss of a bond is the probability of default times:
options: one plus the recovery rate of the bond.
the loss given default (1 minus the recovery rate).
the recovery rate of the bond.
questions.why: Expected loss = PD × LGD = PD × (1 − recovery rate). Multiplying by the recovery rate is the colleague's mistake.

vignettes.body: Lisa Park explains inflation-linked bonds. The break-even inflation rate is the difference between the yields of nominal and inflation-linked bonds of the same maturity. Investors are uncertain about future inflation.

questions.q: An increase in the uncertainty about future inflation is associated with:
options: no change, because the break-even rate reflects only expected inflation.
a lower break-even inflation rate.
a higher break-even inflation rate.
questions.why: Break-even inflation = expected inflation + a premium for inflation uncertainty (inflation risk premium); more uncertainty raises it.

vignettes.body: Greta Lund compares price multiples. She states that higher expected growth and higher risk both raise a high P/E. She also averages P/Es of an index with market-cap weights, using the weighted harmonic mean.

questions.q: According to the constant growth model, a justified P/E is:
options: lower for higher expected growth and lower for higher risk (a lower required return).
higher for higher expected growth and lower for higher risk (a higher required return).
higher for higher expected growth and also higher for higher risk (a higher required return).
questions.why: P/E = payout ÷ (r − g): growth g up raises it, risk (r) up lowers it.

questions.q: Compared with the weighted arithmetic mean, the weighted harmonic mean of the P/Es is:
options: higher, because it gives more weight to the high P/Es.
lower, because it gives more weight to the low P/Es.
the same, because both use the same weights.
questions.why: The harmonic mean averages the E/P (inverse) values, so it reduces the effect of large outliers and is below the arithmetic mean.

vignettes.body: Lucas Mendes manages a government bond portfolio split into a short bucket and a long bucket. The mandate keeps each bucket between 40% and 60% of the portfolio. He expects yields to rise by 50 bp at all points along the yield curve.

questions.q: To minimize his risk, Mendes should most likely:
options: move money out of the long bucket into short maturities, but only until the long bucket reaches its 40% minimum.
move all of the long bucket into three-year bonds to avoid every rate risk, even below the 40% minimum.
lengthen the duration of both buckets, because higher yields raise the income on longer bonds.
questions.why: Yields rising means prices fall, so shorten duration. The 40%–60% limit per bucket still has to be respected, so the shift stops at the limit.

vignettes.body: Alex Thorne adjusts the financial statements of Coleridge Ltd. Its pension discount rate is 0.5% higher than its industry competitors' discount rates, and a higher discount rate lowers the estimated pension obligation. Thorne lowers the discount rate to the peers' level.

questions.q: Compared with its peers, Coleridge's higher pension discount rate is:
options: neutral, because the plan is underfunded in any case, so the assumption does not matter.
aggressive, because it lowers the reported pension obligation and expense.
conservative, because it raises the reported pension expense and obligation.
