questions.why: PBO is the present value of future benefits, so a higher discount rate means a smaller PBO and a smaller deficit. Higher than peers = aggressive.

questions.q: After Thorne lowers the discount rate to the peers' level, which ratio DECREASES?
options: book value per share.
the financial leverage ratio.
the debt-to-equity ratio.
questions.why: The obligation rises, the deficit grows, shareholders' equity falls (through accumulated other comprehensive income). Equity falls, so BVPS falls while debt-to-equity and leverage rise.

vignettes.body: Daniel Ashworth chooses a valuation metric for Harlan Company: its debt-to-equity ratio is much higher than its competitors', and it spent heavily on advertising to build a brand that is not on the balance sheet.

questions.q: The most appropriate metric for Harlan is:
options: dividend yield.
price to book.
enterprise value to sales.
questions.why: Very different leverage → use an enterprise value multiple. An internally generated brand is missing from book value, so price to book is poor. Dividend yield ignores growth.

vignettes.body: Ben Lam uses factor models. In a macroeconomic factor model the factors are surprises in economic variables and have an expected value of zero. In fundamental models the sensitivities come from company attributes. Lam claims that multifactor models are useful for active management but not for passive management.

questions.q: In a macroeconomic factor model with surprise factors, a stock's expected return equals:
options: the intercept of the model.
the intercept plus the average of the factor sensitivities.
the actual return of the last year.
questions.why: Every surprise has an expected value of zero, so E(R) = a (the intercept). Actual return minus the intercept is the effect of the surprises.

questions.q: Which statement about estimating factor sensitivities is correct?
options: In fundamental models the sensitivities come first from company attributes; in macroeconomic models they are estimated last.
In both models the sensitivities are estimated last by regression of the returns on the factors.
In macroeconomic models the sensitivities come first from company attributes; in fundamental models they are estimated last.
questions.why: Fundamental: attributes give the sensitivities, factor returns are estimated. Macroeconomic: surprises are the factors, the sensitivities come from the regression.

questions.q: Lam's claim about multifactor models is:
options: correct: passive managers replicate an index and do not need factor exposures.
incorrect: they are useful for both active and passive management.
incorrect: they are useful only for passive management, where tracking error is controlled.
questions.why: Active: factor tilts and active risk analysis. Passive: replicating an index's factor exposures and controlling tracking error.

vignettes.body: Priya Nair studies how a country with few natural resources can raise its potential growth. Channel 1 is investment in human capital, Channel 2 is adopting leading technology, Channel 3 is keeping the currency low to support export demand.

questions.q: The channel least likely to raise the growth rate of aggregate SUPPLY is:
options: Channel 1: human capital.
Channel 3: keeping the currency low.
Channel 2: leading technology.
questions.why: Human capital and technology raise potential output directly. A low exchange rate is a demand-side policy for exports; it affects supply only indirectly.

vignettes.body: Thabo Ndlovu analyses a firm with book value per share of R20 and intrinsic value per share of R22 from a residual income model. He also computes market value added using the market value and book value of its capital.

questions.q: The intrinsic value of R22 against a book value of R20 means that the present value of future residual income is:
options: negative.
zero.
positive.
questions.why: Intrinsic value = book value per share + PV of future residual income. 22 > 20, so the PV of residual income is positive.

questions.q: Market value added is the difference between:
options: the intrinsic value and the market price of the shares, as an estimate of mispricing.
the market value of equity only and the book value of equity, leaving debt out of both.
the market value of the firm (equity plus debt) and the book value of its total capital.
questions.why: MVA = market value of the company (equity + debt) − accounting book value of total capital (equity + debt). Leaving debt out is the common trap.

vignettes.body: The central bank of Golden Island says it will use monetary tools to stop the inflation that comes from faster growth.

questions.q: To fight the inflation, the central bank will most likely:
options: lower the interest rate on loans to banks.
sell securities to the private sector.
buy securities from the private sector.
questions.why: Fighting inflation means tightening: reduce the money supply by selling securities, raising the policy rate or raising reserve requirements. Buying securities or cutting rates adds money.

vignettes.body: Aiko Ishikawa reviews KH, a property and casualty insurer, and Basel III for banks. The P&C market has been in a hard phase for a few years. KH's loss ratio is below 100%, but its combined ratio is above 100%.

questions.q: Which statement about Basel III is most accurate?
options: It raised the equity capital required against risk-weighted assets.
It aims mainly at improving the earnings quality of banks' reported profits.
It prefers interbank deposits to consumer deposits as a source of stable funding.
questions.why: Basel III: more and better capital against risk-weighted assets, plus liquidity and stable funding requirements where consumer deposits are considered MORE stable than interbank funding.

questions.q: After a long hard phase in the P&C market, a cyclical shift most likely brings:
options: new competitors entering and weaker underwriting standards.
tighter underwriting standards and fewer competitors.
capital adequacy that becomes easier to achieve as premiums rise.
questions.why: Hard market: high premiums and profits attract competitors; premiums fall and standards weaken (soft market); capital is depleted.

questions.q: A combined ratio above 100% means that the insurer's underwriting is:
options: profitable, because the loss ratio is below 100%.
unprofitable: claims and expenses exceed the premiums.
break-even, because the combined ratio uses premiums written.
questions.why: Combined ratio = loss ratio + expense ratio. Above 100% = underwriting loss; below 100% = underwriting profit. Judging on the loss ratio alone ignores the expense ratio.

vignettes.body: Sam Hollis describes calibrating a binomial interest rate tree: it uses a volatility assumption, a log-normal interest rate model and the observed market prices of benchmark bonds.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT an input to the calibration of the tree?
options: the value of the bond being evaluated.
the assumption of log-normality.
the volatility assumption.
questions.why: The tree is calibrated to benchmark bonds so that it reproduces their market prices. The bond being valued is priced afterwards on the calibrated tree.

vignettes.body: Walter Dunn explains the standard error of estimate (SEE) of a regression. He says the SEE is the standard deviation of the differences between the estimated values for the independent variables and the actual observations for the independent variable. A strong relationship gives a small SEE, and violations of the model assumptions affect it.

questions.q: The SEE is the standard deviation of the differences between:
options: the mean and the actual values of the independent variable.
the estimated and the actual values of the independent variables.
the estimated and the actual values of the DEPENDENT variable.
questions.why: SEE = standard deviation of the regression residuals (actual minus predicted dependent variable). A small SEE means a close fit.

vignettes.body: Fjord Mining has surplus cash. It compares paying its usual dividend plus a one-time special dividend with raising its regular dividend permanently. It is also thinking about repurchasing shares with the surplus cash.

questions.q: A special dividend differs from a higher regular dividend because it:
options: is a stock dividend that leaves total cash paid unchanged.
is paid every quarter at a permanently higher level once earnings improve.
is a one-time payment and does not commit the company to a higher dividend in the future.
questions.why: A special (extra) dividend is paid once, usually after unusually good earnings, so the regular dividend is not raised. A stock dividend pays no cash.

questions.q: If Fjord repurchases shares with surplus cash, which item most likely DECREASES?
options: the debt-to-assets ratio.
the debt-to-equity ratio.
total book value.
questions.why: Cash is paid out, so assets and shareholders' equity fall; debt is unchanged, so the leverage ratios (debt-to-assets, debt-to-equity) rise.

vignettes.body: Anke Thiessen reviews three ways in which current account and capital flows can move exchange rates: the flow supply/demand channel, the portfolio balance channel and the debt sustainability channel.

questions.q: The mechanism that best explains the LONG-run equilibrium value of an exchange rate is the:
options: flow supply/demand channel: the current flow of currency supply and demand sets the long-run equilibrium value.
debt sustainability channel: a deficit financed by growing external debt forces the currency to adjust.
portfolio balance channel: shifts in global asset preferences move the exchange rate until the current account balances.
questions.why: Flow supply/demand is a short-term effect; the portfolio balance channel works through medium-term wealth shifts; the debt sustainability channel drives the long-run equilibrium because external debt cannot grow without limit.

title: Mock 7
desc: 8 new vignettes + 3 re-done (names and numbers changed); scored separately

vignettes.body:
Marisa Cheng, CFA, is a portfolio manager with a large full-service investment advisory firm. She has been invited to speak on a podcast with a target audience of recent university graduates entering the investment industry. Cheng decided to focus her talk on her favorite topic: “How to Advance Your Career.” During the podcast, she mentions that most portfolio managers start in the Research Department. She then shares her philosophy that when entering the industry as an entry-level research analyst, you should create a research report at least once a week to prove yourself. This is particularly easy if you are an equity analyst, as the research analysis process should be the same regardless of the security being analyzed.

Cheng then offers advice to the audience about the benefits of changing employers, which she believes allows a person to move into higher positions with greater responsibilities. She explains “Based on my experience, younger employees get overlooked when employers are filling middle to senior management positions. By moving to a different firm every three to five years, you can typically join at a more senior level with higher pay. However, when you move to a new firm, you need to be cautious so your employer and client relationships are not harmed.”

Cheng recommends the following actions:

Action 1: Utilize your own viewpoints based on your skills and experiences.
Action 2: Share policies and processes utilized in past positions.
Action 3: Notify clients of your new role before changing employers.
The podcast interviewer asks, “I know this is a bit off today’s topic, but I was wondering, as a CFA® charterholder, how do you ensure you are serving your clients’ interests as required by the CFA Code of Ethics and Standards of Professional Conduct? For instance, what would you do if you learned in a meeting with your client that due to a change in their circumstances, the investment product they have invested in no longer meets their investment goals and constraints outlined in their investment policy statement?”

Cheng responds, “Let’s consider three options.”

Option 1: I could advise them to add some of our other investment products to their existing investment portfolio, so their new overall investment return objectives and risk profile could be met given their new circumstances.
Option 2: I could immediately reassure them their existing product is still suitable even under their changing circumstances.
Option 3: I could advise them to shop around to determine whether other investment management firms had a more appropriate product to meet their investment goals and give them a list of questions to ask so they could compare services.
After thanking the interviewer for the opportunity to speak, Cheng makes the following final statement:

“I would like to encourage all the listeners who are interested in advancing their careers in the investment industry to become CFA charterholders. The three sequential exams are very tough, as you can be tested on a wide array of curriculum topics, including financial analysis, economics, and derivatives. Becoming a charterholder also demonstrates you are more professional than those without the CFA® charter. By upholding the CFA Code of Ethics and Standards of Professional Conduct, you send a message to the industry that you really care about the interests of your clients and the integrity of the capital markets.”

questions.q: Is Cheng’s philosophy regarding an entry-level research analyst role most likely consistent with guidance for Standard V(A) Diligence and Reasonable Basis?
options: Yes, with regard to the equity analysis process.
No.
Yes, with regard to weekly research reports.
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Cheng’s philosophy regarding an entry-level research analyst’s role is inconsistent with the guidance for Standard V(A) Diligence and Reasonable Basis. Standard V(A) requires members and candidates to exercise diligence, independence, and thoroughness in analyzing investment, making investment recommendations, and taking investment action. It also requires members and candidates to have a reasonable and adequate basis, supported by appropriate research and investigations for any investment analysis, recommendation, or action. Members and candidates must put forth the necessary effort to support the recommendations they are making. At times, one week may not be enough time to undertake a thorough analysis of an investment, make a recommendation, and determine the suitability of the investment for the clients. When determining the suitability of an investment for the client, the necessary level of research and analysis will differ with the security under review, even if all are equity securities. Each security can vary in its complexity, particularly if the underlying assets are vastly different, are in different geographic locations, and have different business models. In providing an investment service, members and candidates typically use a variety of resources, including company reports, third-party research, and results from quantitative models.
B. Correct. Cheng’s philosophy regarding an entry-level research analyst’s role – that is, you should create a research report at least once a week and it is particularly easy if you are an equity analyst as the research process is the same regardless of the security – is inconsistent with the guidance for Standard V(A) Diligence and Reasonable Basis. Standard V(A) requires members and candidates to exercise diligence, independence, and thoroughness in analyzing investment, making investment recommendations, and taking investment action. It also requires members and candidates to have a reasonable and adequate basis, supported by appropriate research and investigations for any investment analysis, recommendation, or action. Members and candidates must put forth the necessary effort to support the recommendations they are making. At times, one week may not be enough time to undertake a thorough analysis of an investment, make a recommendation, and determine the suitability of the investment for the clients. When determining the suitability of an investment for the client, the necessary level of research and analysis will differ with the security under review, even if all are equity securities. Each security can vary in its complexity, particularly if the underlying assets are vastly different, are in different geographic locations, and have different business models. In providing an investment service, members and candidates typically use a variety of resources, including company reports, third-party research, and results from quantitative models.
C. Incorrect. Cheng’s philosophy regarding an entry-level research analyst’s role is inconsistent with the guidance for Standard V(A) Diligence and Reasonable Basis. Standard V(A) requires members and candidates to exercise diligence, independence, and thoroughness in analyzing investment, making investment recommendations, and taking investment action. It also requires members and candidates to have a reasonable and adequate basis, supported by appropriate research and investigations for any investment analysis, recommendation, or action. Members and candidates must put forth the necessary effort to support the recommendations they are making. At times, one week may not be enough time to undertake a thorough analysis of an investment, make a recommendation, and determine the suitability of the investment for the clients. When determining the suitability of an investment for the client, the necessary level of research and analysis will differ with the security under review, even if all are equity securities. Each security can vary in its complexity, particularly if the underlying assets are vastly different, are in different geographic locations, and have different business models. In providing an investment service, members and candidates typically use a variety of resources, including company reports, third-party research, and results from quantitative models.

questions.q: Given Cheng’s advice regarding changing jobs, which recommended action should an employee most likely take to avoid violating the CFA Standards of Professional Conduct?
options: Action 1
Action 2
Action 3
questions.why:
A. Correct. A member or candidate is allowed to utilize their viewpoints based on their skills and the experiences gained from their former employment without violating Standard IV(A) Loyalty. By doing so, they would not potentially harm their former employer. Standard IV(A) Loyalty requires members and candidates to act for the benefit of their employer and not deprive their employer the advantage of their skills and abilities, divulge confidential information, or otherwise cause harm to their employer. By informing their old employer’s clients of their new role before changing employers and sharing policies and processes used at the old employers, they likely would harm their old employer and thus violate Standard IV(A).
B. Incorrect. Action 1, Share policies and processes utilized in past positions, would violate Standard IV(A) Loyalty. Standard IV(A) requires members and candidates to act for the benefit of their employer and not deprive their employer of the advantage of their skills and abilities, divulge confidential information, or otherwise cause harm to their employer.
C. Incorrect. Action 3, Notify clients of your new role before changing employers, would violate Standard IV(A) Loyalty. Standard IV(A) requires members and candidates to act for the benefit of their employer and not deprive their employer of the advantage of their skills and abilities, divulge confidential information, or otherwise cause harm to their employer.

questions.q: To avoid violating CFA Standards of Professional Conduct, which of Cheng’s options in response to the interviewer’s question is least appropriate?
options: Option 1
Option 2
Option 3
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Option 1, I could advise them to add some of our other investment products to their existing investment portfolio, so their new overall investment return objectives and risk profile could be met given their new circumstances, could be considered appropriate action if adding some of the firm’s other investment products to the client’s portfolio would result in a better match of the client’s investment objectives and risk profile as required under Standard III(C) Suitability.
B. Correct. Option 2, I could immediately reassure them their existing product is still suitable even under their changing circumstances, would not be appropriate. Before giving any investment advice, Cheng should better understand the changing circumstances of the client and determine whether the existing product is still suitable rather than immediately state that it is. By failing to understand their changing circumstances and to reassess their current portfolio, Cheng would be in violation of Standard III(C) Suitability. This standard requires members and candidates to determine whether an investment is suitable for the client’s financial situation and consistent with the client’s written objectives, mandates, and constraints before making an investment recommendation or taking investment action. The steps outlined in Options 2 and 3 would comply with Standard III(C) Suitability – that is, both consider the change in the client’s circumstances.
C. Incorrect. Option 3, I could advise them to shop around to determine whether other investment management firms had a more appropriate product to meet their investment goals and give them a list of questions to ask so they could compare services, would not violate CFA Standards of Professional Conduct. By doing so, Cheng would be helping the client to determine which investment product is best for them in accordance with Standard III(C) Suitability. Cheng also would be putting the interests of the client before hers or her firms as required by Standard III(A) Loyalty, Prudence, and Care.

questions.q: Which component of Cheng’s final statement most likely causes her to violate CFA Standards of Professional Conduct?
options: Comment on testing and curriculum
A CFA charterholder’s level of professionalism
The message to the industry
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Cheng does not violate Standard VII(A) Responsibilities as a CFA Institute member or CFA candidate when making the statement that the test is hard and you can be tested on a wide array of curriculum topics (she is not stating what was tested on a specific exam) or examples of the core curriculum covered in the CFA Program. She stated, “While the three sequential exams are very tough, the core curriculum covers a wide array of topics, including financial analysis, economics, and derivatives.” This is not confidential program or exam information in that it is publicly available on the Internet as a part of the CFA Program descriptions. Standard VII(A) Responsibilities as a CFA Institute member or CFA candidate requires members and candidates to not engage in any conduct that compromises the reputation or integrity of CFA Institute or the CFA designation or the integrity, validity, or security of CFA Institute programs. Cheng did not violate the standard when she stated, “By upholding the CFA Code of Ethics and Standards of Professional Conduct you send a message to the industry that you really care about the interests of your clients and the integrity of the capital markets,” as she did not misrepresent or exaggerate the meaning of the CFA charter.
B. Correct. Cheng’s comment, “Becoming a charterholder also demonstrates you are more professional than those without the CFA charter, violates Standard VII(B) Reference to CFA Institute, the CFA® designation, and the CFA® Program. By making such a claim, she is exaggerating the meaning of the charter. Standard VII(B) requires members and candidates when referring to CFA Institute, CFA Institute memberships, the CFA designation, or candidacy in the CFA Program to not misrepresent or exaggerate the meaning or implications of membership in CFA Institute, holding the CFA designation, or candidacy in the CFA Program. Cheng does not violate Standard VII(A) Responsibilities as a CFA Institute member or CFA candidate when making the statement about what could be tested (she is not stating what was tested on a specific exam), giving curriculum specifics or examples of the core curriculum covered in the CFA Program. This information is publicly available on the CFA Institute website. Cheng does not misrepresent or exaggerate the meaning of the CFA charter when stating, “By upholding the CFA Code of Ethics and Standards of Professional Conduct you send a message to the industry that you really care about the interests of your clients and the integrity of the capital markets.” Therefore, she does not violate Standard VIII(B).
C. Incorrect. Cheng does not misrepresent or exaggerate the meaning of the CFA charter when stating, “By upholding the CFA Code of Ethics and Standards of Professional Conduct you send a message to the industry that you really care about the interests of your clients and the integrity of the capital markets.” Therefore, she did not violate Standard VII(B) Reference to CFA Institute, the CFA designation, and the CFA® Program. Standard VII(B), which requires members and candidates when referring to CFA Institute, CFA Institute memberships, the CFA designation, or candidacy in the CFA Program to not misrepresent or exaggerate the meaning or implications of membership in CFA Institute, holding the CFA designation, or candidacy in the CFA Program.

vignettes.body:
Tim Wang is a financial adviser specializing in commercial real estate investing. He is meeting with Mark Caudill, a new client who is looking to diversify his investment portfolio by adding real estate investments. Caudill has heard about various investment vehicles related to real estate from his friends and is seeking a more in-depth understanding of these investments from Wang.

Wang begins the meeting by advising Caudill of four options that are available when investing in real estate, including the following:

Option 1. Publicly traded real estate investment trusts

Option 2. Publicly traded real estate operating companies

Option 3. Direct ownership in real estate

Option 4. Publicly traded residential mortgage-backed securities

Wang next asks Caudill about his investment preferences. Caudill responds by telling Wang that he prefers to invest in equity securities that are highly liquid, provide high income, and are not subject to double taxation.

Caudill asks Wang how the economic performance of REITs and REOCs is evaluated and how their shares are valued. Wang advises Caudill there are multiple measures of economic performance for REITs and REOCs, including the following:

Measure 1. Adjusted funds from operations

Measure 2. Net operating income

Measure 3. Funds from operations

In response, Caudill asks Wang,

“Which of the three measures is the best measure of a REIT’s current economic return to shareholders?”

To help Caudill’s understanding of valuation, Wang presents Caudill with data on Baldwin, a health care REIT that primarily invests in independent and assisted senior housing communities in large cities across the United States. options: exposure to double taxation of dividends.
lower liquidity and larger investment requirements.
less control over property-level investment decisions.
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Direct ownership pays no corporate-level tax on the property income, so there is no double taxation (that is a REOC issue; REITs avoid it).
B. Correct. Direct ownership is illiquid and needs a large amount of capital per property, while publicly traded REITs and REOCs can be bought in small amounts and sold quickly.
C. Incorrect. Direct ownership gives MORE control over property-level decisions than holding REIT or REOC shares; that is its main advantage.

options: Measure 1.
Measure 2.
Measure 3.
questions.why: A is correct. Measure 1, adjusted funds from operations, is a refinement of FFO that is designed to be a more accurate measure of current economic income. In essence, FFO is adjusted to remove any non-cash rent and to include a provision for maintenance-type capital expenditures and leasing costs. Maintenance expenses are required for a business to continue as a going concern.

vignettes.body:
Ingrid Halvorsen is the CFO of Kestrel Yachts (KY), a Swedish manufacturer of sailing yachts. Halvorsen is reviewing KY's dividend policy before recommending a course of action to the Board of Directors on the current year dividend payment.

KY's business is influenced by many factors, including commodity prices, interest rates and general economic conditions.

Exhibit 1
# | Current Year | Prior Year | Two Years Ago
Pre-tax income (SEK millions) | 585 | 415 | 385
After-tax net income (SEK millions) | 410 | 290 | 270
Dividends paid (SEK millions) | --- | 110 | 100
Number of shares outstanding (millions) | 5 | 5 | 5
KY's shares currently trade at SEK 380.

Exhibit 1 shows that KY had a very strong year, generating an additional SEK 120 million of net income over the previous year. Halvorsen considers four options, in addition to the regular dividend, to return part of this additional capital to shareholders in the current year:

Option 1: Issue a stock dividend of 15%.
Option 2: Increase the annual per share dividend by 15% over the prior year.
Option 3: Maintain the current annual dividend and pay a special dividend of SEK 9 per share.
Option 4: Repurchase SEK 150 million of shares at a SEK 30 premium to the current share price.

questions.q: For KY, Option 1 would most likely:
options: affect its capital structure.
increase the value of each shareholder's ownership position in the company.
reduce the volatility of its share price.
questions.why:
A stock dividend has no economic effect on the company, so it does not change the capital structure (a cash dividend would).
The increase in shares held is offset by a lower price per share, so each shareholder's ownership value is unchanged.
Correct: the stock dividend increases the float, which improves liquidity and dampens share price volatility.

questions.q: Compared to Option 2, Option 3 results in a total current year dividend payment per share that is:
options: lower by SEK 5.70.
higher by SEK 5.70.
higher by SEK 9.00.
questions.why:
Prior DPS = 110 ÷ 5 = SEK 22.00.
Option 2 = 22.00 × 1.15 = SEK 25.30.
Option 3 = 22.00 + 9.00 = SEK 31.00.
Option 3 − Option 2 = 31.00 − 25.30 = +SEK 5.70 (higher).
'Lower by 5.70' reverses the options; 'higher by 9.00' looks only at the special dividend.

questions.q: Based on Exhibit 1, the safety of KY's dividend in the prior year compared with two years ago:
options: decreased.
remained the same.
increased.
questions.why:
Dividend coverage = after-tax net income ÷ dividends paid.
Two years ago: 270 ÷ 100 = 2.700.
Prior year: 290 ÷ 110 = 2.636.
Coverage fell, so the dividend became less safe: decreased.

questions.q: If Option 4 is implemented using surplus cash, which of the following is most likely to decrease? KY's:
options: debt-to-assets ratio.
total book value.
debt-to-equity ratio.
questions.why:
A repurchase with surplus cash lowers both assets (cash) and shareholders' equity, so total book value falls.
Debt is unchanged while assets and equity fall, so debt-to-assets and debt-to-equity both rise.
Whether book value per share rises or falls depends on the price paid versus BVPS.

vignettes.body:
Golden Island is a flourishing country because of tourism. The island is governed by a Governor General, a parliamentary body of elected legislators, and a couple of agencies to regulate the island’s economic and social environment. Recently, prospectors in the mountain range bordering the southern coast of the island discovered large deposits of gold, silver, and platinum. The government is concerned that development of these deposits will harm the tourist trade. Elena Trippi has been asked to participate in a series of fact-finding sessions conducted jointly by the island’s ministries of finance and tourism. This blue-ribbon fact-finding committee has been meeting weekly for the past two months.
Trippi began a recent meeting of the committee by presenting a summary of Golden Island’s current financial and economic conditions. Comparing Golden Island with other developing nations, she presents these conditions in Exhibit 1.
Exhibit 1 Current Financial and Economic Conditions
Relative to other developing nations, Golden Island
1. has a relatively low level of capital per worker.
2. does not have competitive financial markets. The island’s single commercial bank also acts as the central bank of Golden Island.
3. has a relatively low rate of savings and investment.
4. has a low level of literacy (about half the population is illiterate).
5. has well-established property rights.
6. tightly regulates capital flows into and out of the economy.
Trippi states that these conditions do not necessarily cause great harm to the tourist industry. But the mining and processing of gold, silver, and platinum will require re-examination of economic policies and circumstances. In particular, Trippi is concerned about the issue of tariffs because Golden Island has relatively high tariffs on capital goods.
Trippi states:
"Golden Island will benefit from continuing to protect domestic capital goods by maintaining its relatively high tariff on non-domestic capital goods. High tariffs have little impact on foreign direct investment (FDI), and they generate revenue for the government."
Rishi Chatterjee is Golden Island’s Interim Deputy Minister for Tourism. He states that he is not very knowledgeable about the gold business but believes that developing the island’s gold deposits will affect the relative value of its currency, the sona (Sn). The current exchange rate of the sona against the US dollar is Sn8.50/USD. Chatterjee states that increased FDI will cause the sona to strengthen against world currencies. Tourism will be harmed because goods and services priced in sonas will appear more expensive to the non-domestic visitors who make up the bulk of the tourist trade.
Trippi shows the committee Exhibit 2, which contains data from the currency exchange markets relative to the sona. On the basis of this data, Trippi states that markets currently anticipate that the sona will weaken, not strengthen, against both the dollar and the British pound.
Exhibit 2 Exchange Rates, Interest Rates, and Inflation Rates
#   | Current Spot Rates | One-Year Interest Rate (%) | One-Year Inflation Rate (%)
Golden Island | Sn8.50/USD | 6.5 | 3
United Kingdom | GBP0.62/USD | 4.05 | 1.6
United States | --- | 3.5 | 1.3
Golden Island’s Minister of Finance and president of the Central Bank, Rajiv Sengupta, addresses the issues of potential inflation as the island transitions to greater growth. He assures the committee that Golden Island’s central bank stands ready to use monetary tools to prevent such inflation

questions.q: How many of the current financial and economic conditions listed in Exhibit 1 at least partially explain why Golden Island faces limited economic growth?
options: Exactly three of the six are limitations on growth.
All six are limitations on growth.
Exactly five of the six are limitations on growth.
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. All of the factors except 'well-established property rights' represent limitations to growth hence, exactly 5 factors are limitations.
B. Incorrect. All of the factors except 'well-established property rights' represent limitations to growth hence, exactly 5 factors are limitations.
C. Correct. All of the factors except 'well-established property rights' represent limitations to growth. Hence, exactly five factors are limitations.

questions.q: Trippi’s statement regarding tariffs is best described as:
options: incorrect, because high tariffs support increases in FDI.
incorrect, because eliminating high tariffs on manufactured goods will increase Golden Island’s physical capital and contribute to higher productivity.
correct.
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Developing countries could benefit from policies that encourage investment from abroad, such as eliminating high tariffs on foreign imports (especially capital goods). Such free trade policies serve to increase a nation’s capital stock and increase productivity.
B. Correct. Developing countries could benefit from policies that encourage investment from abroad, such as eliminating high tariffs on foreign imports (especially capital goods). Such free trade policies serve to increase a nation’s capital stock and increase productivity.
C. Incorrect. Developing countries could benefit from policies that encourage investment from abroad, such as eliminating high tariffs on foreign imports (especially capital goods). Such free trade policies serve to increase a nation’s capital stock and increase productivity.

questions.q: Based on Exhibit 2, the one-year forward exchange rate of the Sn/GBP is closest to:
options: Sn8.75/GBP.
Sn13.45/GBP.
Sn14.03/GBP.
questions.why:
A. Incorrect because it uses the Sn/USD spot rate and the sona over US interest rates: 1.065/1.035 × 8.50 = 8.7464.
B. Incorrect because it uses the incorrect ratio of rates. It uses the Sn/USD spot rate and the sona over US interest rates: 1.0405/1.065 × 13.70968 = 13.4522.
C. Correct. First, find the current Sn/GBP exchange rate. Then, find the one-year forward Sn/GBP rate. Sn/GBP = Sn/USD × USD/GBP = 8.50 × 1.6129 = Sn 13.70968/GBP. Note that 1.6129 is the inverse of 0.62, which is the GBP/USD exchange rate given in Exhibit 2. The forward rate equals the spot rate multiplied by the ratio of one plus the sona one-year rate divided by one plus the pound one-year rate. In this case, the forward rate = 13.70968 × 1.065/1.0405 = 14.03249. An alternative approach is to convert USD1 into SN and GBP and determine what an investment in each of those currencies would be worth in one year at the Golden Island and UK interest rates, respectively. The one-year forward rate will then be the number of Sn required to purchase GBP 1 at that time. MAX17024-IS-Fb

questions.q: Which of the following will Sengupta most likely use to address the monetary issues relating to greater growth of the island’s economy? The central bank will:
options: reduce the interest rate on loans to the private sector.
buy domestic securities from the private sector.
sell domestic securities to the private sector.
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. To reduce the money supply, the central bank would raise rates on loans to the private sector.
B. Incorrect. The central bank will sell domestic securities to the private sector.
C. Correct. The threat is inflation. To counter such a threat, the central bank will want to reduce the money supply. The central bank will sell domestic securities to the private sector.

vignettes.body:
Seo-jun Pak is the CEO of the Nakdong Foundation (“the Foundation”), an organization located in Busan, South Korea, whose mission is to support rural healthcare initiatives. The Foundation has a KRW220 billion portfolio consisting entirely of actively managed South Korean equities. The portfolio manager, Ha-eun Kang, has an excellent 14-year track record of beating the KOSPI 200, an index of the 200 largest firms traded on the Korea Exchange. She is permitted to use derivatives to control risks within the portfolio and to synthetically alter positions without trading the underlying securities, many of which are somewhat illiquid.

Kang is meeting with Pak to review a forward position in the portfolio and to discuss two other positions she is considering establishing. Kang explains that six months ago she was concerned the Korean stock market was going to experience a substantial downward price movement in the near term, so she entered into a one-year forward contract to sell KRW180 million times the KOSPI 200, which was at 270.00, at a forward price of 265.07.

Pak asks, “Why did you agree to sell the index at a forward price that is less than the price it was trading at that time? Stocks are generally expected to rise in value over time.” Kang responds, “Forward agreements are priced using an arbitrage model that considers the current price of the asset, the level of interest rates, any carry benefits received from owning the asset, and any carry costs associated with owning the asset. Carry benefits can include dividends or coupon payments, while carry costs can include storage, insurance, waste, or interest paid to borrow funds to purchase the asset. The forward price is the future value of the current price plus the future value of the carry costs less the future value of the carry benefits.”

Pak notes the KOSPI 200 has risen to 278.50 over the last six months and asks, “How much have we lost on the KRW180 million forward position to date?” Kang responds, “I’ll calculate the loss taking into account the current six-month interest rate of 0.68% and the continuously compounded dividend yield on the KOSPI 200, which is 2.20%.”

Kang tells Pak she is considering entering into a currency swap because the Foundation has a number of long-term contracts to purchase supplies and equipment for rural clinics and these contracts are priced in US dollars. She explains, “A fixed-for-fixed currency swap would help reduce the risk from fluctuating USD/KRW exchange rates by providing fixed US dollar payments in exchange for fixed Korean won payments. I’m looking at a five-year swap with annual payments. I’ve done some analysis of this swap based on current Korean and US interest rates and present value factors, which I’m providing to you in Exhibit 1.”

Exhibit 1 Korean and US Interest Rates and PV Factors
# T | Korean Treasury Yield | Present Value KRW1 | US Treasury Yield | Present Value USD1
1 | 1.82 | 0.9821 | 1.17 | 0.9884
2 | 2.05 | 0.9602 | 1.23 | 0.9758
3 | 2.18 | 0.9374 | 1.29 | 0.9623
4 | 2.26 | 0.9145 | 1.37 | 0.9470
5 | 2.30 | 0.8925 | 1.55 | 0.9260
Kang also brings up a concern about the portfolio’s 100% allocation to Korean equities. She tells Pak, “The KOSPI 200 has been far more volatile over the past 15 years than other major market indexes. Although I have great confidence in my ability to continue to beat the index, it would be useful to diversify our holdings by using a swap to exchange some of the underlying index return for another return, such as the S&P 500. Assuming no dividends, as is the case for these two indexes, equity-for-equity swaps do not need to be priced. The carry arbitrage model shows that the two parties to the swap must agree to swap the index returns without any adjustment because the swap is equivalent to two equity-for-fixed swaps. The fixed interest payments will be the same and will cancel each other out. The fixed interest rates will also be the same as those for a fixed-for-floating interest rate swap of the same maturity entered into at the same time.”

questions.q: Is Kang most likely correct in her description of the pricing of forward contracts?
options: No, she is incorrect regarding inputs to the arbitrage model
No, she is incorrect regarding her examples of carry costs and carry benefits
Yes
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Kang is correct in describing the inputs that are used in the arbitrage model to calculate the forward price.
B. Correct. Kang is incorrect because she has included borrowing costs in the list of potential carry costs of owning the asset. Under the arbitrage model, the future value calculations (of the current price and the carry costs and carry benefits of ownership) use a discount rate that takes into account the cost of borrowing funds to purchase and hold the asset. Including these costs again in the carry costs would be double counting and therefore inaccurate. Kang is correct in her description of carry benefits.
C. Incorrect. Kang is incorrect in the list of potential carry costs because she has included borrowing costs.

questions.q: Given the information Kang provided in her response to Pak’s question about the equity forward position, the loss on the position is closest to:
options: KRW0.38 billion.
KRW1.65 billion.
KRW2.03 billion.
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. This is the loss measured as the present value of the difference between the current spot and the new forward price or V 0 = P V ( F 0.5 − S 0.5 ) = 276.39 − 278.50 e 0.0068 × 0.5 = − 2.10 , multiplied by KRW180 million equals a loss on the equity forward position of KRW0.38 billion.
B. Incorrect. This is the loss that would be measured if no adjustment was made for the half-year maturity of the new (reversing) forward contract or F 0.5 = S 0.5 e ( r c + C C − C B ) = 278.50 e ( 0.0068 + 0 − 0.022 ) = 274.30 and V 0 = P V ( F 0 − F 0.5 ) = 265.07 − 274.30 e 0.0068 = − 9.17 , multiplied by KRW180 million equals a loss on the equity forward position of KRW1.65 billion.
C. Correct. Given the current spot index value and six-month interest rate, the forward price for a contract initiated today and maturing in six months would be F 0.5 = S 0.5 e ( r c + C C − C B ) T = 278.50 e ( 0.0068 + 0 − 0.022 ) 0.5 = 276.39 . The value of the short (selling) forward position is the present value of the difference between the new forward price (agree to buy to “cancel” exiting contract) and the original forward price (agree to sell at that price) or V 0 = P V ( F 0 − F 0.5 ) = 265.07 − 276.39 e 0.0068 × 0.5 = − 11.28 . The decline in the forward price is multiplied by the contract size of KRW180 million to give a loss on the equity forward position of KRW2.03 billion.

questions.q: Based on the information in Exhibit 1, the interest rate that the Foundation would receive in the proposed currency swap is closest to:
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. This is the geometric average of the US interest rates.
B. Correct. The Foundation would receive the US fixed interest rate, which is calculated as [ 1 − P V n , U S ( 1 ) ] [ ∑ i = 1 n P V i , U S ( 1 ) ] = [ 1 − 0.9260 ] [ 0.9884 + 0.9758 + 0.9623 + 0.9470 + 0.9260 ] = 0.074 4.7995 = 0.0154 or 1.54%.
C. Incorrect. This is the Korean fixed rate, which the Foundation would pay, not receive.

questions.q: Is Kang most likely correct in her description of equity-for-equity swaps?
options: No, she is incorrect regarding the relationship between the pricing of equity swaps and interest rate swaps.
Yes.
No, she is incorrect regarding the need to price the swap.
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Kang is correct that the fixed rate for an equity-for-fixed swap would be the same as for a fixed-for-floating interest rate swap of the same maturity entered into at the same time.
B. Correct. Kang is correct in both descriptions. The carry arbitrage model shows equity-for-equity swaps do not need to be priced because they can be replicated by an equity-for-fixed swap and a fixed-for-equity swap. The fixed rates will be the same for both swaps and will cancel out. Further, the fixed rate will be the same as it would be for a fixed-for-floating interest rate swap with the same maturity entered into at the same time.
C. Incorrect. Kang is correct that equity-for-equity swaps do not need to be priced.

vignettes.body:
Henrik Vos is an analyst at Northgate Asset Management, which runs a range of investment funds. He analyses the recent performance of Aurelia Drinks AG (AD), a multinational producer of carbonated soft drinks that recently entered the energy drinks market. As a core holding, AD's strong position in Europe gives Northgate geographic diversification, because its funds are mostly invested in North America.

Vos reviews AD's balance sheets for the most recent and previous years and comments: "AD is continuing to follow a growth-by-acquisition strategy." He also adjusts AD's most recent income statement to find the company's net income under the direct control of management, using the information (in EUR millions) in Exhibit 1.

Exhibit 1
# | Most Recent Year
Income from operations | 1,920
Income from investments in associates | 236
Interest expense | (731)
Taxes | (271)
Net income | 1,154
Of which: |  
Net income attributable to non-controlling interests | 102
Net income attributable to shareholders | 1,052

Vos and his team assess the quality of AD's overall performance. The team's view is positive, but Vos disagrees for the following reasons:
Reason 1: Balance-sheet-based accruals are trending down relative to total assets.
Reason 2: Income from operations is consistently higher than cash generated from operations.
Reason 3: The cash-flow-based accruals ratio has fluctuated very little over the last five years.

Vos and his team note from AD's annual report that the company has four segments. They analyse the segments using the information (in EUR millions) in Exhibit 2.

Exhibit 2
# Segment | Sales (recent) | EBIT (recent) | Assets (recent) | Sales (previous)
Carbonated drinks – Europe | 3,010 | 1,021 | 13,120 | 2,905
Carbonated drinks – North America | 2,040 | 586 | 6,240 | 1,850
Carbonated drinks – Asia Pacific | 590 | 181 | 2,880 | 560
Energy drinks | 318 | 19 | 1,330 | 231
Total | 5,958 | 1,807 | 23,570 | 5,546

After the segment analysis, the team concludes:
Statement 1: The sales growth rate of carbonated drinks – North America is stronger than that of energy drinks.
Statement 2: The EBIT margin of carbonated drinks – Europe is higher than that of carbonated drinks – North America.
Statement 3: The asset turnover of carbonated drinks – Europe is better than that of AD overall.

questions.q: Which balance sheet line item is most appropriate to justify Vos's comment about AD's growth strategy?
options: Long-term debt
Property, plant and equipment
Goodwill
questions.why:
Goodwill arises only when a company acquires another business, so a rising goodwill balance is the hallmark of growth by acquisition.
Long-term debt and PP&E may also rise after acquisitions, but they can change for many other reasons (capital structure changes, organic capital spending).

questions.q: After Vos's adjustment, AD's net income (in EUR millions) under management's direct control is:
questions.why:
Management controls the subsidiaries in full (including the non-controlling interest share) but not the associates.
Start from total net income: 1,154.
Remove income from associates: 1,154 − 236 = 918.
816 = 1,052 − 236 wrongly also removes the non-controlling interest; 1,052 still includes the associates and excludes the NCI.

questions.q: Which reason best supports Vos's disagreement with his team about AD's overall performance?
options: Reason 1
Reason 2
Reason 3
questions.why:
Downward-trending balance-sheet accruals give less room for manipulation: not a concern.
Correct: operating income persistently above operating cash flow means earnings are not backed by cash, a warning sign of low earnings quality.
A steady, low-fluctuation accruals ratio is not a concern; an erratic or rising one would be.

questions.q: With respect to the segment analysis, which statement is correct?
options: Statement 1
Statement 2
Statement 3
questions.why:
Statement 1: growth North America = 2,040/1,850 − 1 = 10.3%; energy drinks = 318/231 − 1 = 37.7%. North America is weaker: false.
Statement 2: EBIT margin Europe = 1,021/3,010 = 33.9%; North America = 586/2,040 = 28.7%. Europe is higher: true.
Statement 3: asset turnover Europe = 3,010/13,120 = 0.229; AD overall = 5,958/23,570 = 0.253. Europe is lower: false.

vignettes.body:
Anna Lebedeva is a fixed-income portfolio manager. Paulina Kowalski, a junior analyst, and Lebedeva meet to review several positions in Lebedeva’s portfolio.

Lebedeva begins the meeting by discussing credit rating migration. Kowalski asks Lebedeva about the typical impact of credit rating migration on the expected return on a bond. Lebedeva asks Kowalski to estimate the expected return over the next year on a bond issued by Entre Corp. The BBB rated bond has a yield to maturity of 5.50% and a modified duration of 7.54. Kowalski calculates the expected return on the bond over the next year given the partial credit transition and credit spread data in Exhibit 1. She assumes that market spreads and yields will remain stable over the year.

Exhibit 1 One-Year Transition Matrix for BBB Rated Bonds and Credit Spreads
# Rating | AAA | AA | A | BBB | BB | B | CCC, CC, C
Probability (%) | 0.02 | 0.30 | 4.80 | 85.73 | 6.95 | 1.75 | 0.45
Credit spread | 0.60% | 0.90% | 1.10% | 1.50% | 3.40% | 6.50% | 9.50%

Lebedeva next asks Kowalski to analyze a three-year bond, issued by VraiRive S.A., using an arbitrage-free framework. The bond’s coupon rate is 5%, with interest paid annually and a par value of 100. In her analysis, she makes the following three assumptions:
The annual interest rate volatility is 10%.
The recovery rate is one-third of the exposure each period.
The annual probability of default each year is 2.00%.

Selected information on benchmark government bonds for the VraiRive bond is presented in Exhibit 2, and the relevant binomial interest rate tree is presented in Exhibit 3.

Exhibit 2 Par Curve Rates for Annual Payment Benchmark Government Bonds
# Maturity | Coupon Rate | Price | Discount Factor | Spot Rate | Forward Rate
1 | 3.00% | 100 | 0.970874 | 3.0000% | 3.0000%
2 | 4.20% | 100 | 0.920560 | 4.2255% | 5.4656%
3 | 5.00% | 100 | 0.862314 | 5.0618% | 6.7547%

Exhibit 3 One-Year Binomial Interest Rate Tree for 10% Volatility (risk-neutral probabilities in parentheses)
Date 0 rate: 3.00%. Date 1 rates (top to bottom): 6.0139%, 4.9238%. Date 2 rates (top to bottom): 8.1823%, 6.6991%, 5.4848%.

Kowalski estimates the value of the VraiRive bond assuming no default (VND) as well as the fair value of the bond. She then estimates the bond’s yield to maturity and the bond’s credit spread over the benchmark in Exhibit 2. Kowalski asks Lebedeva, “What might cause the bond’s credit spread to decrease?”

Lebedeva and Kowalski next discuss the drivers of the term structure of credit spreads. Kowalski tells Lebedeva the following:
Statement 1: The credit term structure for lower-rated securities is often steeper, and credit spreads widen with expectations of strong economic growth.
Statement 2: The credit term structure for the most highly rated securities tends to be either flat or slightly upward sloping.

Next, Kowalski analyzes the outstanding bonds of DLL Corporation, a high-quality issuer with a strong, competitive position. Her focus is to determine the rationale for a positive-sloped credit spread term structure.

Lebedeva ends the meeting by asking Kowalski to recommend a credit analysis approach for a securitized asset-backed security (ABS) held in the portfolio. This non-static asset pool is made up of many medium-term auto loans that are homogeneous, and each loan is small relative to the total value of the pool.

questions.q: The most appropriate response to Kowalski’s question regarding credit rating migration is that it has:
options: no impact.
a positive impact.
a negative impact.
questions.why: C is correct. Credit spread migration typically reduces the expected return: rating-change probabilities are skewed toward downgrade, and the spread increase on downgrades is much larger than the spread decrease on upgrades.

questions.q: Based on Exhibit 1, the one-year expected return on the Entre Corp. bond is closest to:
questions.why: A is correct. Expected return = YTM + expected % price change from migration. Each transition: −7.54 × (new spread − 1.50%) × probability. Sum = −1.76715%. Expected return = 5.50% − 1.77% = 3.73%.

questions.q: Based on Kowalski’s assumptions and Exhibit 2 and Exhibit 3, the credit spread on the VraiRive bond is closest to:
questions.why: C is correct. Step 1: VND from the tree (discount at tree forward rates, risk-neutral probs 0.5) = 100.0000. Step 2: CVA = sum of PV(expected exposure × LGD fraction × POD): exposures 103.0000, 103.3535, 105.0000; LGD = 2/3 of exposure; POD 2%, 1.96%, 1.9208%; discounted at benchmark spot discount factors 0.970874, 0.920560, 0.862314 → 1.3333 + 1.2432 + 1.1594 = 3.7360. Fair value = 100 − 3.7360 = 96.2640. Step 3: YTM from 96.2640 = 6.4082%; spread = 6.4082% − 5.0000% = 1.4082%.

questions.q: Suppose instead that the ABS were backed by a static book of many small, homogeneous credit card receivables. Kowalski should then most likely recommend a:
options: portfolio-based approach.
statistics-based approach.
loan-by-loan approach.
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. A portfolio-based approach suits medium-term, homogeneous and granular pools that change over time (such as the auto loans in the vignette).
B. Correct. A static book of short-term, homogeneous and granular receivables suits a statistics-based approach built on historical default and loss data.
C. Incorrect. A loan-by-loan approach suits pools of a small number of large, heterogeneous (non-granular) loans.

vignettes.body:
Housing industry analyst Elaine Smith has been assigned the task of forecasting housing foreclosures. Specifically, Smith is asked to forecast the percentage of outstanding mortgages that will be foreclosed upon in the coming quarter. Smith decides to employ multiple linear regression and time series analysis.
Besides constructing a forecast for the foreclosure percentage, Smith wants to address the following two questions:
Research Question 1: Is the foreclosure percentage significantly affected by short-term interest rates?
Research Question 2: Is the foreclosure percentage significantly affected by government intervention policies?
Smith contends that adjustable rate mortgages often are used by higher risk borrowers and that their homes are at higher risk of foreclosure. Therefore, Smith decides to use short-term interest rates as one of the independent variables to test Research Question 1.
To measure the effects of government intervention in Research Question 2, Smith uses a dummy variable that equals 1 whenever the Federal government intervened with a fiscal policy stimulus package that exceeded 2% of the annual Gross Domestic Product. Smith sets the dummy variable equal to 1 for four quarters starting with the quarter in which the policy is enacted and extending through the following 3 quarters. Otherwise, the dummy variable equals zero.
Smith uses quarterly data over the past 5 years to derive her regression. Smith's regression equation is provided in Exhibit 1:
Exhibit 1: Foreclosure Share Regression Equation
foreclosure share = b0 + b1(dINT) + b2(STIM) + b3(CRISIS) + e
where: Foreclosure share = the percentage of all outstanding mortgages foreclosed upon during the quarter; dINT = the quarterly change in the 1-year Treasury bill rate (e.g., dINT = 2 for a two percentage point increase in interest rates); STIM = 1 for quarters in which a Federal fiscal stimulus package was in place; CRISIS = 1 for quarters in which the median house price is one standard deviation below its 5-year moving average.
The results of Smith's regression are provided in Exhibit 2:
Exhibit 2: Foreclosure Share Regression Results
# Variable | Coefficient | t-statistic
Intercept | 3.00 | 2.40
dINT | 1.00 | 2.22
STIM | -2.50 | -2.10
CRISIS | 4.00 | 2.35
The ANOVA results from Smith's regression are provided in Exhibit 3:
Exhibit 3: Foreclosure Share Regression Equation ANOVA Table
# Source | Degrees of Freedom | Sum of Squares | Mean Sum of Squares
Regression | 3 | 15 | 5.0000
Error | 16 | 5 | 0.3125
Total | 19 | 20
Smith expresses the following concerns about the test statistics derived in her regression:
Concern 1: If my independent variables are correlated with each other, my F-statistic will be overestimated.
Concern 2: If my regression errors exhibit conditional heteroskedasticity, my t-statistics will be underestimated.
Before completing her analysis, Smith runs a regression of the changes in foreclosure share on its lagged value. The following regression results and autocorrelations were derived using quarterly data over the past 5 years (Exhibit 4 and Exhibit 5, respectively):
Exhibit 4: Lagged Regression Results
d foreclosure share_t = 0.05 + 0.25 (d foreclosure share_t-1)
Exhibit 5: Autocorrelation Analysis
# Lag | Autocorrelation | t-statistic
1 | 0.05 | 0.22
2 | -0.35 | -1.53
3 | 0.25 | 1.09
4 | 0.10 | 0.44
Exhibit 6 provides critical values for the Student's t-Distribution
Exhibit 6: Critical Values for Student's t-Distribution. Area in Both Tails Combined
Degrees of Freedom | 20% | 10% | 5% | 1%
16 | 1.337 | 1.746 | 2.120 | 2.921
17 | 1.333 | 1.740 | 2.110 | 2.898
18 | 1.330 | 1.734 | 2.101 | 2.878
19 | 1.328 | 1.729 | 2.093 | 2.861
20 | 1.325 | 1.725 | 2.086 | 2.845

questions.q: Based on her regression results in Exhibit 2, using a 5% level of significance, Smith should conclude that:
options: stimulus packages do not have significant effects on foreclosure percentages, but housing crises do have significant effects on foreclosure percentages.
both stimulus packages and housing crises have significant effects on foreclosure percentages.
stimulus packages have significant effects on foreclosure percentages, but housing crises do not have significant effects on foreclosure percentages.
questions.why: The t-statistic is -2.10 for STIM and 2.35 for CRISIS. The critical t at the 5% level (16 degrees of freedom) is 2.12. STIM is not significant (|-2.10| < 2.12); CRISIS is significant (2.35 > 2.12).

questions.q: The standard error of estimate for Smith's regression is closest to:
questions.why: SEE = sqrt(SSE/(n - k - 1)) = sqrt(5/16) = 0.56. The SEE equals the standard deviation of the regression residuals; a low SEE implies a high R-squared.

questions.q: The most recent change in foreclosure share was +1 percent. Smith decides to base her analysis on the data and methods provided in Exhibit 4 and Exhibit 5, and determines that the two-step ahead forecast for the change in foreclosure share (in percent) is 0.125, and that the mean reverting value for the change in foreclosure share (in percent) is 0.071. Is Smith correct?
options: Smith is correct on both the forecast and the mean reverting level.
Smith is correct on the two-step ahead forecast for change in foreclosure share only.
Smith is correct on the mean-reverting level for forecast of change in foreclosure share only.

questions.q: Assume for this question that Smith finds that the foreclosure share series does NOT have a unit root. Under these conditions, she can most reliably regress foreclosure share against the change in interest rates (dINT) if:
options: dINT has a unit root and is cointegrated with foreclosure share.
dINT has a unit root and is not cointegrated with foreclosure share.
dINT does not have a unit root.
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Cointegration needs both series to have a unit root; here the foreclosure share series does not, so one series has a unit root and the other does not, and the regression is not reliable.
B. Incorrect. One series with a unit root and one without gives unreliable results.
C. Correct. If neither series has a unit root, both are covariance stationary and linear regression can be used.

vignettes.body:
The Brookline Club is a small US investment club formed by a group of friends who recently graduated from university. At today's regular bimonthly meeting, two members present new companies for the club to analyse. The club uses a combination of comparables and forecasted fundamentals to make its investment decisions.

Nadia Ferro has done preliminary research on Ostler Ltd. (Ostler), a small Ohio-based manufacturer of products, supplies and food for pets. Ferro starts by showing the club a recent news release from Ostler's website (Exhibit 1).

Exhibit 1 Ostler Ltd. Press Release: Core EPS Announcement
We are pleased to report an increase in Core EPS from $1.09 to $1.44 for the year ended 31 December 2017. The company continues its growth-by-acquisition strategy, acquiring smaller specialty companies in the pet supplies industry. Acquisitions over the past two years have increased our asset base by 22%, and we expect similar opportunities for growth in the next few years.
# | 31 December 2017 | 31 December 2016
EPS | $1.12 | $0.95
Core EPS* | $1.44 | $1.09
* Core EPS is a non-GAAP measure that excludes acquisition charges of $0.20 and $0.14 in 2017 and 2016, respectively, and $0.12 in 2017 related to the settlement of a lawsuit.

Ferro notes that Ostler trades at $12.82. She reminds the club that the company was sued for making pet jackets with the logos of local professional sports teams without permission and settled quickly out of court. Ferro believes the company will not incur such legal costs again, but because its strategy is to grow by acquisition, acquisition costs will continue and are relevant to any analysis. She disagrees with excluding those costs from core EPS and calculates Ostler's trailing P/E on the basis of her beliefs.

Using NYSE data, Ferro finds the average P/E for the Consumer Goods Index (15.2) and for its Processed and Packaged Goods sector (31.4). She then screens that sector for other small processed and packaged goods producers to build her own index. Partial results are shown in Exhibit 2.

Exhibit 2 Partial Results of Market Screen: Ferro's Index
# Company | Market cap (US$ millions) | P/E
Hale Inc. | 6.40 | 13.4
Rivera Industries Inc. | 24.80 | 11.9
Booth Brothers Co. | 512.30 | 5.6
Corbin Foods Ltd. | 735.60 | 20.4
Linden Delights Inc. | 548.90 | 17.6

Ferro observes that Corbin Foods must have both a higher-than-average growth rate and higher-than-average risk to justify its high P/E, and suggests the club look at Corbin at its next meeting.

The members discuss the wide range of market capitalisations and P/Es in Ferro's index and whether the arithmetic mean is the best value to use. Ferro decides to calculate the weighted harmonic mean of the index and says:

"The harmonic mean can be used to mitigate the effects of both large and small outliers."

questions.q: Based on Exhibit 1 and Ferro's beliefs about recurring costs, her trailing P/E for Ostler is closest to:
questions.why:
Acquisition charges recur, so they stay in EPS; the lawsuit cost does not recur, so it is added back.
Recurring EPS 2017 = 1.12 + 0.12 = $1.24.
Trailing P/E = 12.82 ÷ 1.24 = 10.34.
8.90 uses the company's core EPS (1.44), which wrongly excludes acquisition charges; 11.45 uses GAAP EPS (1.12), which keeps the non-recurring lawsuit cost.

questions.q: Ferro's observation about Corbin Foods' high P/E is best described as:
options: correct.
incorrect with respect to the growth rate.
incorrect with respect to the risk.
questions.why:
Higher expected growth justifies a higher P/E: she is right on growth.
Higher risk raises the required return and justifies a LOWER P/E: she is wrong on risk.

questions.q: The weighted harmonic mean of the P/Es in Ferro's index (Exhibit 2) is closest to:
questions.why:
Weighted harmonic mean = total market cap ÷ Σ(market cap ÷ P/E).
Total cap = 6.40 + 24.80 + 512.30 + 735.60 + 548.90 = 1,828.0.
Σ(cap ÷ P/E) = 0.48 + 2.08 + 91.48 + 36.06 + 31.19 = 161.29.
1,828.0 ÷ 161.29 = 11.3.
13.8 is the simple arithmetic mean; 15.3 is the market-cap weighted arithmetic mean.

questions.q: Ferro's statement supporting the use of the harmonic mean is best described as:
options: correct.
incorrect with respect to large outliers.
incorrect with respect to small outliers.
questions.why:
The harmonic mean mitigates the effect of LARGE outliers.
It can aggravate the effect of SMALL outliers (although these are bounded by zero), so the statement is wrong about small outliers.

vignettes.body:
Hui Cheung, a portfolio manager, asks her assistant, Ronald Lam, to review the macroeconomic factor model currently in use and to consider a fundamental factor model as an alternative.

The current macroeconomic factor model has four factors:

Ri = ai + bi1FGDP + bi2FCAP + bi3FCON + bi4FUNEM + εi,
Where FGDP, FCAP, FCON, and FUNEM represent unanticipated changes in four factors: gross domestic product, manufacturing capacity utilization, consumer spending, and the rate of unemployment, respectively. Lam assumes the error term is equal to zero when using this model.

Lam estimates the current model using historical monthly returns for three portfolios for the most recent five years. The inputs used in and estimates derived from the macroeconomic factor model are presented in Exhibit 1. The US Treasury bond rate of 2.5% is used as a proxy for the risk-free rate of interest.

Exhibit 1
Inputs for and Estimates from the Current Macroeconomic Model
# Factor | Portfolio 1 | Portfolio 2 | Portfolio 3 | Benchmark | Factor surprise (%)
Intercept (%) | 2.58 | 3.20 | 4.33 | --- | ---
FGDP | 0.75 | 1.00 | 0.24 | 0.50 | 0.8
FCAP | −0.23 | 0.00 | −1.45 | −1.00 | 0.5
FCON | 1.23 | 0.00 | 0.50 | 1.10 | 2.5
FUNEM | −0.14 | 0.00 | −0.05 | −0.10 | 1.0
Annual returns, most recent year |  
Return (%) | 6.00 | 4.00 | 5.00 | 4.50 | ---
Lam uses the macroeconomic model to calculate the tracking error and the mean active return for each portfolio. He presents these statistics in Exhibit 2.

Exhibit 2
Macroeconomic Factor Model Tracking Error and Mean Active Return
# Portfolio | Tracking Error | Mean Active Return
Portfolio 1 | 1.50% | 1.50%
Portfolio 2 | 1.30% | −0.50%
Portfolio 3 | 1.00% | 0.50%
Lam considers a fundamental factor model with four factors:

Ri = aj + bj1FLIQ + bj2FLEV + bj3FEGR + bj4FVAR + εj,
where FLIQ, FLEV, FEGR, and FVAR represent liquidity, financial leverage, earnings growth, and the variability of revenues, respectively.

Lam and Cheung discuss similarities and differences between macroeconomic factor models and fundamental factor models, and Lam offers a comparison of those models to statistical factor models. Lam makes the following statements.

Statement 1:
The factor sensitivities are generally determined first in fundamental factor models, whereas the factor sensitivities are estimated last in macroeconomic factor models.

Statement 2:
The factors in fundamental factor models are based on attributes of stocks or companies, whereas the factors in macroeconomic factor models are based on surprises in economic variables.

Lam also tells Cheung:

An advantage of statistical factor models is that they make minimal assumptions, and therefore, statistical factor model estimation lends itself to easier interpretation than macroeconomic and fundamental factor models.

Lam tells Cheung that multifactor models can be useful in active portfolio management, but not in passive management. Cheung disagrees; she tells Lam that multifactor models can be useful in both active and passive management.

questions.q: Assuming that the information in Exhibit 1 reflects the analyst's view, the expected return for Portfolio 1 is closest to:
questions.why: A is correct. When using a macroeconomic factor model, the expected return is the intercept (when all model factors take on a value of zero). The intercept coefficient for Portfolio 1 in Exhibit 1 is 2.58.

questions.q: Based on Exhibit 2, which portfolio has the best information ratio?
options: Portfolio 1
Portfolio 2
Portfolio 3
questions.why:
A is correct. Portfolio 1 has the highest information ratio, 1.0, and thus has the best mean active return per unit of active risk:

IR = 
 = 
 = 1.00
This information ratio exceeds that of Portfolio 2 (−0.38) or Portfolio 3 (0.50).

questions.q: Which of Lam’s statements regarding macroeconomic factor models and fundamental factor models is correct?
options: Only Statement 1
Only Statement 2
Both Statements 1 and 2
questions.why: C is correct. In a macroeconomic factor model, the factors are surprises in macroeconomic variables that significantly explain returns. Factor sensitivities are generally specified first in fundamental factor models, whereas factor sensitivities are estimated last in macroeconomic factor models.

questions.q: Whose statement regarding the use of multifactor models in active and passive portfolio management is correct?
options: Both Lam and Cheung
Lam only
Cheung only
questions.why: C is correct. Analysts can use multifactor models in passively managed portfolios to replicate an index fund’s factor exposures.

vignettes.body:
Athena Advisors Inc. offers portfolio replication services to pension funds and insurance companies through the use of options. Clients are typically able to replicate market exposures with smaller than normal investments of funds. Athena manages exposures for its client Wertfin Insurance Company related to annuities indexed to the German Blue Chip Equity Index. Athena portfolio manager Hannes Messer is meeting with Wertfin's risk manager, Jens Szillat, who has asked to learn more about the principles behind the option strategies being employed.

Szillat tells Messer, "I am somewhat familiar with option valuation models; however, I would like to learn more about Athena's methodologies with respect to the index options you are managing for our portfolio."

Messer replies, "The binomial valuation model can be applied to the two-year European style index call options we purchased one year ago. The applicable underlying instrument is the German Blue Chip Equity price index, which excludes dividends. Exhibit 1 shows the option's characteristics at the time of purchase."

Exhibit 1
Binomial Model Variables
u | 1.15
d | 0.90
π | 0.52
Index price | EUR 720
Strike price | EUR 750
1-year interest rate | 3%
S– | 648

Messer explains, "Of course, the index has moved down 10% in the last 12 months."

Messer continues, "Twelve months ago, I noted that two-year American-style puts with a strike price of EUR750 cost EUR38.48. Using the information in Exhibit 1 and today's index value, the binomial valuation model calculates the current price of the put as EUR80.15. It is actually trading now above that price at EUR92."

Szillat responds, "I am curious whether you also use the Black–Scholes–Merton (BSM) model for valuation. I understand the BSM and binomial models both have the following three assumptions in common.

Assumption 1: The annualized returns on the underlying follow a normal distribution.
Assumption 2: Trading is possible at every instant.
Assumption 3: Volatility can be predicted with certainty.

Messer concludes, "We also use the BSM model to calculate the implied volatility. The implied volatilities of the index options expiring in one year are shown in Exhibit 2."

Exhibit 2
Implied Volatility Curve
# Strike Price | Implied Volatility
700 | 18.7
710 | 17.98
720 | 17.38
730 | 16.69
740 | 15.83
750 | 15.40
760 | 14.50
770 | 14.03
780 | 13.21
790 | 12.11
800 | 11.09

questions.q: Using the binomial valuation method and the data in Exhibit 1, the price Messer paid one year ago for the call option with a strike price of EUR750 is closest to:
questions.why:
B. Correct. S++ = 720 × 1.15² = 952.2, so c++ = 952.2 − 750 = 202.2; the other two terminal payoffs are zero. c+ = 0.52 × 202.2 ÷ 1.03 = 102.08 and c0 = 0.52 × 102.08 ÷ 1.03 = EUR51.54.
A. Incorrect. It reverses the probabilities of c+ and c−: 0.48 × 102.08 ÷ 1.03 = 47.57.
C. Incorrect. EUR102.08 is the value of c+ one year later, not the price at purchase.

questions.q: Does the put option with a strike price of EUR750 currently offer an arbitrage opportunity?
options: Yes
No, because the market has bid up the price of the put
No, because the put is deep in the money
questions.why:
A. Correct. The index has fallen 10% to 648, so exercising the American-style put now gives 750 − 648 = EUR102, more than its price of EUR92. Buying the put and exercising it while buying the index locks in a profit of 10.
B. Incorrect. The put's price of EUR92 is still below its exercise value of EUR102.
C. Incorrect. Being deep in the money does not remove the arbitrage; the test is whether the price is below the exercise value.

questions.q: Which of Szillat's assumptions is least consistent with the BSM model?
options: Assumption 1
Assumption 2
Assumption 3
questions.why:
A. Correct. The BSM model assumes that the continuously compounded (logarithmic) return, not the annualized return, is normally distributed.
B. Incorrect. Assumption 2 is part of the BSM model: trading is continuous.
C. Incorrect. Assumption 3 is part of the BSM model: volatility is assumed to be known.

questions.q: Exhibit 2 shows that the implied volatility of the EUR700 option (18.7) is higher than that of the EUR800 option (11.09), and falls steadily as the strike price rises. This pattern is best described as:
options: a volatility smile, in which implied volatility is higher at both low and high strike prices.
a volatility skew, in which implied volatility is higher for lower strike prices.
the term structure of volatility, in which implied volatility differs by time to expiration.
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. A smile is U-shaped: higher implied volatility at both ends of the strike range. Exhibit 2 falls steadily.
B. Correct. Implied volatility that varies with the strike price and falls steadily as the strike rises is a volatility skew; out-of-the-money puts (low strikes) are then more expensive than out-of-the-money calls.
C. Incorrect. The term structure of volatility is implied volatility across times to expiration; Exhibit 2 keeps the expiry at one year and changes the strike.

vignettes.body:
Mona Simmons is an analyst at Bluestone Fixed-Income Advisors, a fixed-income investment management firm located in Chicago, IL. Bluestone manages a variety of fixed-income strategies, primarily for institutional clients. Simmons provides economic research to portfolio managers by analyzing economic data and advising how these data may influence various segments of the fixed-income markets.

Simmons is working on an assessment of the current economic conditions and the resulting impact on future real risk-free interest rates for a number of countries. She plans to present her findings at the upcoming investment committee meeting. As part of her research, she has collected the data provided in Exhibit 1 through the end of the second quarter.

Exhibit 1 Actual & Estimated GDP Growth Data
# Economy | Actual Q1 Yr/Yr Growth | Actual Q2 Yr/Yr Growth | Estimated Q3 Yr/Yr Growth | Estimated 10-Year GDP Growth Rate | Estimated 10-Year Standard Deviation of GDP Growth
Germany | 2.9% | 2.7% | 2.8% | 2.9% | 1.9%
United Kingdom | 2.4% | 2.6% | 2.9% | 2.9% | 1.4%
United States | 2.5% | 2.8% | 2.7% | 2.7% | 1.6%
At the investment committee meeting, Simmons recommends purchasing United Kingdom inflation-linked government bonds. In her discussion, she makes the following statements about inflation-linked bonds:

Statement 1: “Increases in uncertainty about future inflation are associated with lower break-even inflation rates.”
Statement 2: “The break-even inflation rate incorporates the yield difference between longer dated and shorter dated inflation-linked bonds.”
Statement 3: “The difference between nominal and inflation-linked bond yields reflects the expectations of and uncertainty about the quantity of goods and services investors will be able to consume in the future.”
Lloyd Redfield, a portfolio manager on the foreign bond team, asks Simmons to review the current business cycle and yield curve in Australia. The Australian economy entered a recession approximately 6 months ago, and the Australian Central Bank has been reducing its policy rate. Simmons expects the Australian economy to gradually improve over the next 6–12 months.

Given the ongoing recession in Australia, Redfield is reviewing Australian corporate bonds with the same five-year maturity held in the foreign bond strategy. The three bonds being reviewed are listed in Exhibit 2. Redfield agrees with Simmons’ assessment of the Australian economy.
