Exhibit 2 Australia Corporate Bond Holdings
# Bond | Credit Rating | Sector | Probability of Default | Estimated Recovery Rate | Spread over Government Bonds
A | A | Consumer Staples | 0.5% | 40% | 200 bps
B | BBB– | Consumer Discretionary | 2.0% | 35% | 350 bps
C | BB | Industrial | 3.5% | 45% | 650 bps
Based on this information, Redfield makes the following comments to Simmons regarding the Australian bonds:
Comment 1: Relative to bond B and bond C, bond A has likely experienced the worst price return over the last 9 months.
Comment 2: Based on your economic forecasts, in 6–12 months overall credit spreads should narrow and the rate of improvement will likely be greatest for bond C.
Comment 3: You can calculate the expected loss by multiplying the probability of default by the recovery rate.

questions.q: Using only the data in Exhibit 1, which country will Simmons most likely expect to have the highest average real short-term risk-free interest rates over the forecasted horizon?
options: Germany
United Kingdom
United States
questions.why:
A. Correct. Germany has the highest combination of expected GDP growth and expected GDP volatility of the countries presented in Exhibit 1. Thus, all else held constant, it would have the highest expected real short-term risk-free rates.
B. Incorrect. While the United Kingdom has a relatively high expected GDP growth rate, it has the lowest expected volatility of GDP growth.
C. Incorrect. The United States has both a relatively low rate of expected GDP growth and expected GDP volatility.

questions.q: Which of Simmons’ statements concerning inflation-linked bonds is most likely correct?
options: Statement 1
Statement 2
Statement 3
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Statement 1 (Increases in uncertainty about future inflation are associated with lower break-even inflation rates.) is incorrect. Increases in uncertainty about future inflation would be associated with higher, not lower, break-even inflation rates.
B. Incorrect. Statement 2 (The break-even inflation rate incorporates the yield difference between longer dated inflation-linked bonds and shorter dated inflation-linked bonds.) is incorrect. The break-even inflation rate incorporates the yield difference between inflation-linked and non-inflation-linked government bonds of the same maturity, not the yield difference between longer dated inflation-linked bonds and shorter dated inflation-linked bonds.
C. Correct. Since Simmons makes her statements while looking at the yield difference between nominal and inflation-linked bonds, Statement 3 (The difference in yields reflects the uncertainty about the quantity of goods and services investors will be able to consume in the future.) is correct. The difference in yields incorporates uncertainty about future inflation and, therefore, the uncertainty about the quantity of goods and services investors will be able to consume in the future.

questions.q: Bond C's spread of 650 bps over government bonds in Exhibit 2 most likely compensates investors for:
options: a term premium for holding a longer-maturity bond than the benchmark government bond.
the expected credit loss only, because the spread equals default probability times loss.
the expected credit loss plus a premium for bearing credit and liquidity risk.
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. The three bonds have the same five-year maturity, and the spread is measured against a government bond of similar maturity, so it is not a term premium.
B. Incorrect. The spread is far larger than the expected loss alone.
C. Correct. A credit spread covers the expected loss (here 3.5% × (1 − 45%) = 1.925%, i.e. 192.5 bps) plus a risk premium for bearing credit and liquidity risk; 650 bps is much larger than the expected loss.

questions.q: Which of Redfield’s comments regarding the Australian corporate bonds in Exhibit 2 is most likely correct?
options: Comment 1
Comment 2
Comment 3
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Comment 1 is incorrect. The Australian economy entered recession approximately 6 months ago. As the business cycle turns down, those issuers with good credit ratings tend to outperform those with lower ratings as the spreads between low and higher quality issuers widen.
B. Correct. Comment 2 is correct. When credit spreads are generally narrowing, the rate of improvement will tend to be greater for those bonds issued by entities with a relatively weaker ability to pay. Bond C has the lowest credit rating, highest probability of default, and widest spread over government bonds and should experience the greatest rate of improvement as the Australian economy improves and spreads narrow.
C. Incorrect. Comment 3 is incorrect. Expected loss = Probability of default x (1 – Recovery rate). For example, bond B has an expected loss of 2% x (1 – 35%) = 1.3%.

vignettes.body:
Sofia Marangoni is a fixed-income portfolio manager. Tomasz Brandt, a junior analyst, and Marangoni meet to review several positions in Marangoni's portfolio.

Marangoni begins the meeting by discussing credit rating migration. Marangoni asks Brandt to estimate the expected return over the next year on a bond issued by Veldor Group. The BBB rated bond has a yield to maturity of 4.80% and a modified duration of 6.92. Brandt calculates the expected return on the bond over the next year given the partial credit transition and credit spread data in Exhibit 1. Brandt assumes that market spreads and yields will remain stable over the year.

Exhibit 1
One-Year Transition Matrix for BBB Rated Bonds and Credit Spreads
# Rating | AAA | AA | A | BBB | BB | B | CCC, CC, C
Probability (%) | 0.03 | 0.45 | 5.60 | 84.87 | 6.80 | 1.90 | 0.35
Credit spread | 0.50% | 0.80% | 1.00% | 1.35% | 3.10% | 6.00% | 9.00%

Marangoni next asks Brandt to analyze a three-year bond, issued by Norvalle S.A., using an arbitrage-free framework. The bond's coupon rate is 4%, with interest paid annually and a par value of 100. In the analysis, Brandt makes the following three assumptions:
The annual interest rate volatility is 15%.
The recovery rate is one-quarter of the exposure each period.
The annual probability of default each year is 1.50%.

Selected information on benchmark government bonds for the Norvalle bond is presented in Exhibit 2, and the relevant binomial interest rate tree is presented in Exhibit 3.

Exhibit 2
Par Curve Rates for Annual Payment Benchmark Government Bonds
# Maturity | Coupon rate | Price | Discount factor | Spot rate | Forward rate
1 | 2.50% | 100 | 0.975610 | 2.5000% | 2.5000%
2 | 3.30% | 100 | 0.936888 | 3.3133% | 4.1331%
3 | 4.00% | 100 | 0.887981 | 4.0396% | 5.5076%

Exhibit 3
One-Year Binomial Interest Rate Tree for 15% Volatility (risk-neutral probability of 50% on each branch)
# Date | 0 | 1 (top) | 1 (bottom) | 2 (top) | 2 (middle) | 2 (bottom)
Rate | 2.5000% | 4.7526% | 3.5208% | 7.2932% | 5.4029% | 4.0026%

Brandt estimates the value of the Norvalle bond assuming no default (VND) as well as the fair value of the bond. Brandt then estimates the bond's yield to maturity and the bond's credit spread over the benchmark in Exhibit 2. Brandt asks Marangoni, "What might cause the bond's credit spread to decrease?"

Marangoni and Brandt next discuss the drivers of the term structure of credit spreads. Brandt tells Marangoni the following:

Statement 1:
The credit term structure for lower-rated securities is often steeper, and credit spreads widen with expectations of strong economic growth.

Statement 2:
The credit term structure for the most highly rated securities tends to be either flat or slightly upward sloping.

questions.q: Based on Exhibit 1, the one-year expected return on the Veldor Group bond is closest to:
questions.why:
A. Correct. Expected return = YTM + expected percentage price change from migration. For each rating the price change = −modified duration × (new spread − 1.35%) × probability:
AAA: −6.92 × (0.50% − 1.35%) × 0.03% = +0.0018%
AA: −6.92 × (0.80% − 1.35%) × 0.45% = +0.0171%
A: −6.92 × (1.00% − 1.35%) × 5.60% = +0.1356%
BBB: no change = 0
BB: −6.92 × (3.10% − 1.35%) × 6.80% = −0.8235%
B: −6.92 × (6.00% − 1.35%) × 1.90% = −0.6114%
CCC, CC, C: −6.92 × (9.00% − 1.35%) × 0.35% = −0.1853%
Sum = −1.4656%. Expected return = 4.80% − 1.47% = 3.33%.
B. Incorrect. 4.80% is the yield to maturity only; it ignores the negative effect of migration.
C. Incorrect. 6.27% adds the absolute size of the migration effect (4.80% + 1.47%), treating it as a gain; downgrades have a larger price effect than upgrades, so migration lowers the expected return.

questions.q: Based on Brandt's assumptions and Exhibits 2 and 3, the credit spread on the Norvalle bond is closest to:
questions.why:
B. Correct. Step 1: VND from the tree (discount at the tree rates, probability 0.5 on each branch, coupon 4) = 100.0000.
Step 2: CVA = sum of DF × probability of default × LGD × expected exposure. Expected exposures 102.5000, 102.5665, 104.0000; LGD = 3/4 of exposure (recovery one-quarter); probabilities of default in each year 1.5000%, 1.4775%, 1.4553%; benchmark discount factors 0.975610, 0.936888, 0.887981. CVA = 1.1250 + 1.0648 + 1.0080 = 3.1978.
Step 3: Fair value = 100 − 3.1978 = 96.8022. The yield to maturity that prices the bond at 96.8022 is 5.1782%.
Step 4: Credit spread = 5.1782% − 4.0000% (3-year benchmark coupon) = 1.1782%.
A. Incorrect. 0.7796% results from using a loss given default of 50% of exposure instead of 75%.
C. Incorrect. 1.5828% results from assuming no recovery (loss given default of 100%).

questions.q: The most appropriate response to Brandt's question relating to the credit spread is:
options: an increase in the loss given default.
an increase in the probability of default.
a decrease in the risk-neutral probability of default.
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. A higher loss given default raises the CVA and widens the credit spread.
B. Incorrect. A higher probability of default raises the CVA, lowers the fair value and widens the credit spread.
C. Correct. A lower risk-neutral probability of default lowers the CVA, raises the fair value and lowers the yield and the credit spread.

questions.q: Which of Brandt's statements regarding the term structure of credit spreads is correct?
options: Only Statement 1
Only Statement 2
Both Statements 1 and 2
questions.why:
B. Correct. For the highest-rated issuers spreads are very low (with a floor at zero), so the credit term structure is flat or slightly upward sloping (Statement 2 is correct).
A. Incorrect. Lower-rated issuers are more sensitive to the credit cycle, but their credit spreads narrow (not widen) with expectations of strong economic growth, so Statement 1 is incorrect.
C. Incorrect. Statement 1 is incorrect.

vignettes.body:
Xyrees Taylor is an equity analyst evaluating the stock of Maclaurin Corporation. Taylor undertakes quantitative analysis to get a better understanding of how relevant valuation parameters have changed over time.

First, Taylor examines the quarterly sales (in $ millions) of the company for the past six years (24 observations) to forecast sales for the current quarter. Taylor uses Model A, a log-linear model (ln yt = b0 + b1t + εt) where yt represents quarterly sales for quarter t. The regression estimates for the intercept and the trend coefficient are 5.74820 and 0.03795, respectively.

Maclaurin's earnings are substantially export-driven. To understand the impact of foreign exchange rates on earnings, Taylor builds Model B, an autoregressive AR(1) model, for the exchange rate between Maclaurin's domestic currency and that of its primary export market. The regression estimates for the intercept and the coefficient of the first lag are 0.3000 and 0.9093, respectively.

Taylor builds another AR(1) model (Model C) for the exchange rate between Maclaurin's domestic currency and that of its secondary export market. Taylor suspects that the time series used for Model C may have a unit root and he runs a Dickey–Fuller test.

Before making his recommendation on the stock, Taylor also wants to model the movement of Maclaurin's share price (in natural logs). He uses an AR(1) model (Model D). After performing the relevant necessary transformations and reviewing the regression statistics, Taylor concludes that the intercept is 0.25 and the coefficient of the first lag is 1.

questions.q: Based on Model A, the predicted value of Maclaurin's sales for the current quarter is closest to:
options: $326 million.
$780 million.
$810 million.
questions.why:
C. Correct. Six years of quarterly data is 24 observations, so the current quarter is t = 25: exp(5.74820 + 0.03795 × 25) = exp(6.69695) = 809.93, about $810 million.
A. Incorrect. It uses t = 1 (the first out-of-sample quarter) instead of t = 25: exp(5.74820 + 0.03795) = 325.76.
B. Incorrect. It uses t = 24: exp(5.74820 + 0.03795 × 24) = 779.77.

questions.q: For Model B, the mean-reverting level is closest to:
questions.why:
C. Correct. For an AR(1) model the mean-reverting level is b0 ÷ (1 − b1) = 0.3000 ÷ (1 − 0.9093) = 3.31.
A. Incorrect. It swaps b0 and b1: b1 ÷ (1 − b0) = 0.9093 ÷ 0.7000 = 1.30.
B. Incorrect. It uses the ratio b1 ÷ b0 = 3.03, which is not a formula.

questions.q: Taylor suspects that the exchange rate series used for Model C may have a unit root. If his Dickey–Fuller test does not reject its null hypothesis, he should most likely:
options: first-difference the series before estimating an autoregressive model.
add a second lag to Model C, which removes the unit root.
estimate the AR(1) model on the original series, because a unit root makes the estimates more precise.
questions.why:
A. Correct. The null hypothesis of the Dickey–Fuller test is that the series has a unit root. If it is not rejected, the series is not covariance stationary, so it should be transformed, most commonly by first-differencing, before an AR model is estimated.
B. Incorrect. Adding lags does not remove a unit root.
C. Incorrect. Autoregressive estimates on a series with a unit root are unreliable because a random walk is not covariance stationary.

questions.q: Taylor's regression estimates for Model D indicate that the time series of Maclaurin's share price (in natural logs) is most likely:
options: a covariance stationary series.
a random walk with drift.
a simple random walk.
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. b1 = 1 means an undefined mean-reverting level, so the series is not covariance stationary.
B. Correct. A random walk with drift is the AR(1) special case with b1 = 1 and b0 ≠ 0. Here b1 = 1 and b0 = 0.25, so the series has a unit root and is not covariance stationary.
C. Incorrect. A simple random walk has b0 = 0. Here b0 = 0.25 ≠ 0, so it has drift.

vignettes.body:
D’Shaun Jackson, an individual do-it-yourself investor, is reviewing retail companies for potential addition to his portfolio. The first company he considers is Discount Days Ltd. (DDL) an up-and-coming regional competitor in the dollar store segment. Jackson’s analysis shows that the company is profitable and has strong positive operating cash flows. While the company is working to expand the number of stores in its network, investing cash flows are exceeding operating cash flows. To date, the company has not paid dividends, but Jackson believes it will likely start once it has finished its expansion plans. Jackson decides to use a dividend discount model to value the shares and estimates that DDL will start paying an annual dividend of $0.50 per share at the end of year 4 with a modest growth rate of 2% per year. He uses the capital asset pricing model to estimate a cost of equity of 7.25%.

Next, Jackson looks at a stock that has caught his eye due to its high current dividend and high growth rate. He summarizes the information he has gathered about the stock (Exhibit 1). He expects the growth rate to decline consistently over the next six years and decides to use the H-model to estimate a value for the stock.

Exhibit 1 Information About High Growth Stock
Current dividend | $2.00
Growth rate expected years 1–6 | 8%
Growth rate expected after year 6 | 4%
Required rate of return | 12%
Jackson has been researching how to value shares using a dividend growth model if the transition from one growth rate to a lower one is gradual. In that scenario, he understands he would use the H-model to evaluate the shares. If, however, the difference in growth rates is large, or the length of the high growth rate is extraordinarily long, then he would have to use a spreadsheet model instead.

questions.q: Which of the following factors would make the model Jackson selects to value DDL’s shares the most appropriate model to use?
options: The model considers Jackson’s opportunity cost of investing in the stock.
The company has intense capital demands for the next few years.
Jackson has a noncontrol perspective.
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. The residual income model considers the opportunity cost to an investor of investing in a stock, not a dividend discount model.
B. Incorrect. If a company has intense capital demands — as DDL does based on its investment cash flows exceeding its operating ones — it may have negative free cash flow and be unable to pay dividends. In this situation, a residual income model would be the most appropriate model to use. 
C. Correct. A dividend discount model (DDM) is most suitable when an investor takes a noncontrol perspective because he does not have the ability to meaningfully influence the timing or magnitude of a company’s cash flows and is therefore reliant on dividend policy. Because Jackson is looking for an investment for his personal portfolio, it is most likely that he has a noncontrol perspective.

questions.q: Based on Jackson’s estimates and his selected model for DDL, the current share price is closest to:
questions.why:
B. Correct. DDL pays no dividend in the first three years, so use a two-stage DDM: Gordon growth value at the end of year 3 = D4 ÷ (r − g) = 0.50 ÷ (0.0725 − 0.02) = $9.52. Discount it 3 years: 9.52 ÷ 1.0725³ = $7.72.
A. Incorrect. It discounts the $9.52 for four periods instead of three: 9.52 ÷ 1.0725⁴ = $7.20.
C. Incorrect. It discounts $9.52 for three years at r − g (5.25%): 9.52 ÷ 1.0525³ = $8.17.

questions.q: Using Exhibit 1 and Jackson’s selected model for the high growth stock, the value is closest to:
questions.why:
A. Correct. H-model: V0 = [D0 × (1 + gL) + D0 × H × (gS − gL)] ÷ (r − gL), with H = 6 ÷ 2 = 3.
First term: 2.00 × 1.04 ÷ (0.12 − 0.04) = $26.00.
Second term: 2.00 × 3 × (0.08 − 0.04) ÷ (0.12 − 0.04) = $3.00.
Value = 26.00 + 3.00 = $29.00.
B. Incorrect. It grows the first dividend at the higher rate (8%): 27.00 + 3.00 = $30.00.
C. Incorrect. It uses the full six years instead of the half-life H = 3: second term 6.00, total 26.00 + 6.00 = $32.00.

questions.q: Jackson’s understanding of when he would switch from an H-model to a spreadsheet model is best described as:
options: incorrect with respect to the difference in growth rates.
correct.
incorrect with respect to the length of the first growth period.
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Jackson’s understanding is correct with respect to the growth rates. The H-model is appropriate to use when the transition from a higher rate of growth to a lower one is linear over time. 
B. Correct. Jackson’s understanding is correct. The H-model is appropriate to use when the transition from a higher rate of growth to a lower one is linear over time but does not provide a very close approximation for a long extraordinary growth period or for a large difference in growth rates. 
C. Incorrect. Jackson’s understanding is correct with respect to the length of the first growth period. The H-model is appropriate to use when the transition from a higher rate of growth to a lower one is linear over time, but it does not provide a very close approximation for a long extraordinary growth period.

vignettes.body:
Marta Oyelaran, a portfolio manager, asks her assistant, Pieter Verhoeven, to review the macroeconomic factor model currently in use and to consider a fundamental factor model as an alternative.

The current macroeconomic factor model has four factors:

Ri = ai + bi1FGDP + bi2FCAP + bi3FCON + bi4FUNEM + εi,
Where FGDP, FCAP, FCON, and FUNEM represent unanticipated changes in four factors: gross domestic product, manufacturing capacity utilization, consumer spending, and the rate of unemployment, respectively. Verhoeven assumes the error term is equal to zero when using this model.

Verhoeven estimates the current model using historical monthly returns for three portfolios for the most recent five years. The inputs used in and estimates derived from the macroeconomic factor model are presented in Exhibit 1.

Exhibit 1
Inputs for and Estimates from the Current Macroeconomic Model
# Factor | Portfolio 1 | Factor surprise (%)
Intercept (%) | 2.14 | ---
FGDP | 0.62 | 0.6
FCAP | −0.31 | 0.4
FCON | 1.05 | 2.0
FUNEM | −0.18 | 0.8
Annual returns, most recent year |  | 
Return (%) | 5.20 | ---

Verhoeven uses the macroeconomic model to calculate the tracking error and the mean active return for each portfolio. He presents these statistics in Exhibit 2.

Exhibit 2
Macroeconomic Factor Model Tracking Error and Mean Active Return
# Portfolio | Tracking error | Mean active return
Portfolio 1 | 1.20% | 0.96%
Portfolio 2 | 1.60% | −0.40%
Portfolio 3 | 0.80% | 0.52%

Verhoeven considers a fundamental factor model with four factors:

Ri = aj + bj1FLIQ + bj2FLEV + bj3FEGR + bj4FVAR + εj,
where FLIQ, FLEV, FEGR, and FVAR represent liquidity, financial leverage, earnings growth, and the variability of revenues, respectively.

Verhoeven and Oyelaran discuss similarities and differences between macroeconomic factor models and fundamental factor models. Verhoeven makes the following statements.

Statement 1:
The factor sensitivities are generally determined first in fundamental factor models, whereas the factor sensitivities are estimated last in macroeconomic factor models.

Statement 2:
The factors in fundamental factor models are based on attributes of stocks or companies, whereas the factors in macroeconomic factor models are based on surprises in economic variables.

Verhoeven tells Oyelaran that multifactor models can be useful in active portfolio management, but not in passive management. Oyelaran disagrees; she tells Verhoeven that multifactor models can be useful in both active and passive management.

questions.q: Assuming that the information in Exhibit 1 reflects the analyst's view, the expected return for Portfolio 1 is closest to:
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. 4.34% is the return GIVEN the factor surprises: 2.14 + (0.62 × 0.6) + (−0.31 × 0.4) + (1.05 × 2.0) + (−0.18 × 0.8) = 2.14 + 2.204 = 4.34%. That is not the expected return.
B. Correct. In a macroeconomic factor model the expected return is the intercept, i.e. the return when every factor surprise is zero. The intercept for Portfolio 1 in Exhibit 1 is 2.14%.
C. Incorrect. 5.20% is the actual return of Portfolio 1 in the most recent year, not the model's expected return.

questions.q: Based on Exhibit 2, which portfolio has the best information ratio?
options: Portfolio 1
Portfolio 2
Portfolio 3
questions.why:
A. Correct. Information ratio = mean active return ÷ tracking error. Portfolio 1: 0.96 ÷ 1.20 = 0.80.
B. Incorrect. Portfolio 2: −0.40 ÷ 1.60 = −0.25.
C. Incorrect. Portfolio 3: 0.52 ÷ 0.80 = 0.65, below Portfolio 1.

questions.q: Which of Verhoeven's statements regarding macroeconomic factor models and fundamental factor models is correct?
options: Only Statement 1
Only Statement 2
Both Statements 1 and 2
questions.why:
C. Correct. In a macroeconomic factor model the factors are surprises in macroeconomic variables, whereas fundamental factors are attributes of stocks or companies (Statement 2 is correct). Factor sensitivities are generally specified first in fundamental factor models, while they are estimated last in macroeconomic factor models (Statement 1 is correct).
A. Incorrect. Statement 2 is also correct.
B. Incorrect. Statement 1 is also correct.

questions.q: Whose statement regarding the use of multifactor models in active and passive portfolio management is correct?
options: Oyelaran only
Verhoeven only
Both Verhoeven and Oyelaran
questions.why:
A. Correct. Multifactor models are useful in active management and also in passive management, for example to replicate an index fund's factor exposures. Only Oyelaran's statement is correct.
B. Incorrect. Verhoeven wrongly says the models are not useful in passive management.
C. Incorrect. Verhoeven's statement is not correct.

vignettes.body:
Abby Dormier is a sell-side analyst for a small Wall Street brokerage firm; she covers publicly and actively traded companies with listed equity shares. Dormier is responsible for issuing either a buy, hold, or sell rating for the shares of Company A and Company B. The appropriate valuation model for each company was chosen based on the following characteristics of each company:

Company A is an employment services firm with no debt and has fixed assets consisting primarily of computers, servers, and commercially available software. Many of the assets are intangible, including human capital. The company has a history of occasionally paying a special cash dividend.

Company B operates in three unrelated industries with differing rates of growth: tobacco (60% of earnings), shipbuilding (30% of earnings), and aerospace consulting (10% of earnings). The company pays a regular dividend that is solely derived from the earnings produced by the tobacco division.

Dormier considers the following development in making any necessary adjustments to the models before assigning ratings:

Company B has finalized the terms to acquire 70% of the outstanding shares of Company X, an actively traded tobacco company, in an all-stock deal.

Dormier assigns ratings to each of the companies and provides a rationale for each rating. The director of research asks Dormier: “How did you arrive at these recommendations? Describe how you used a top-down approach, which is the policy at our company.”

Dormier replies, “I arrived at my recommendations through my due diligence process. I have studied all of the public disclosure documents; I have participated in the company conference calls, being careful with my questions in such a public forum; and I have studied the dynamics of the underlying industries. The valuation models are robust and use an extensive set of company-specific quantitative and qualitative inputs.”

questions.q: Based on Company A’s characteristics, which of the following absolute valuation models is most appropriate for valuing that company?
options: Asset based
Free cash flow to the firm
Dividend discount
questions.why: B is correct. The free cash flow to the firm model is the most appropriate of the choices because it can be used whether the company has significant marketable assets or consistently pays a cash dividend. Much of Company A’s assets are intangible, and although the company has a history of paying a dividend, it has been only occasionally and in the form of a special dividend (i.e., not a consistent cash dividend).

questions.q: Based on Company B’s characteristics, which of the following valuation models is most appropriate for valuing that company?
options: Asset based
Dividend discount
Sum of the parts
questions.why: C is correct. This valuation model would be consistent with the characteristics of the company. Company B is a conglomerate operating in three unrelated industries with significantly different expected revenue growth rates. The sum-of-the-parts valuation model sums the estimated values of each of the company’s businesses as if each business were an independent going concern. Sum-of-the-parts analysis is most useful when valuing a company with segments in different industries that have different valuation characteristics.

questions.q: Which of the following is most likely to be appropriate to consider in Company B’s valuation of Company X?
options: Control premium
Blockage factor
Lack of marketability discount
questions.why: A is correct. A control premium may be reflected in the value of a stock investment that would give an investor a controlling position. Company B acquired 70% of the outstanding stock of Company X; more than 50% is considered a controlling ownership position.

questions.q: Based on Dormier’s response to the director of research, Dormier’s process could have been more consistent with the firm’s policy by:
options: evaluating the impact of general economic conditions on each company.
incorporating additional micro-level inputs into her valuation models.
asking more probing questions during publicly available company conference calls.
questions.why: A is correct. A top-down forecasting approach moves from macroeconomic forecasts to industry forecasts and then to individual company and asset forecasts. Analysts are expected to understand the general economic conditions before finalizing a research report and making a recommendation. According to Dormier’s response, she did not comment on the general economic conditions—although such considerations would be consistent with the firm’s policy of using a top-down approach.

vignettes.body:
Maxine Thorsell, a financial analyst, is examining the most recent annual financial report of Coleridge Ltd., a mature U.K.-based company that complies with IFRS. Thorsell wants to evaluate the quality of the company's financial reports for the purpose of making an investment recommendation to her firm. To begin her analysis, Thorsell observes the following:

Observation 1: The growth in revenues has exceeded the growth in receivables during the past 3-year period.
Observation 2: Increases in operating margin occurred during each of the past 3 years.
Observation 3: Average depreciation lives on assets were reduced by two years from that of preceding years.
Next, Thorsell notes that, consistent with past years, Coleridge has generated only accounting losses when it sells any one of its long-term assets. The losses are presented on the income statement after operating income, and when they occur they are significant in amount.

Thorsell next examines Coleridge's underfunded defined benefit pension plan and observes that the plan's discount rate assumption is 0.5% higher than its industry competitors' discount rates. For comparison purposes, Thorsell adjusts Coleridge's financial statements before computing the company's financial ratios.

questions.q: Which of the following Thorsell's observations most likely indicates a potential accounting warning sign?
options: Observation 1
Observation 2
Observation 3
questions.why:
A. Incorrect because according to the Accounting Warning Signs in the reading, it is an increasing trend of receivables growing faster than revenues that indicates a potential accounting warning sign. In the case of Coleridge, revenues are growing faster than receivables.
B. Correct because according to the Accounting Warning Signs in the reading, a trend of increasing operating margins indicates a potential accounting warning sign.
C. Incorrect because according to the Accounting Warning Signs in the reading, it is an increase in depreciation lives rather than a decrease in depreciation lives that indicates a potential accounting warning sign. In the case of Coleridge, average depreciation lives on assets were reduced.

questions.q: Compared with its industry competitors, Coleridge's pension discount rate assumption is most likely:
options: neutral, because the plan is underfunded in any case.
conservative, because it raises the reported pension expense.
aggressive, because it lowers the reported pension obligation.
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. The assumption changes the measured size of the deficit, so the plan being underfunded does not make it neutral.
B. Incorrect. A higher discount rate lowers, not raises, the reported obligation and expense.
C. Correct. A higher discount rate than peers lowers the present value of the pension obligation (and the reported expense), so the underfunding is understated: the assumption is aggressive.

questions.q: With respect to the sale of its long-term assets, Coleridge most likely displays:
options: both low earnings quality and low financial reporting quality.
low earnings quality only.
low financial reporting quality only.
questions.why:
A. Correct because a consistent pattern of recognizing accounting losses when any long-term assets are sold demonstrates that depreciation expense is being understated during the periods that the assets are in use. An understatement of depreciation expense will cause operating income to be higher than what it otherwise would be if there was no management bias in the depreciation expense estimate. Although the accounting losses are properly displayed on the income statement, there is an intentional lag in time (perhaps many years) as to when that ultimate cost is recognized. A biased accounting decision to understate depreciation expense does not faithfully represent the economic circumstances of the accounting periods in which it occurs because operating income and the carrying value of the long-term assets are both overstated. This is a clear indication of low financial reporting quality. Financial reports can range from those that contain relevant and faithfully representational information to those that contain information that is pure fabrication. Earnings quality will also be low because operating incomes are higher than what they should be each and every year because of the deliberate understatement of depreciation expense. Operating income infers sustainable income whereas net income does not (since net income also includes the non-recurring recognition of accounting gains and losses that are generated from the occasional disposal of long-term assets and settlement of long-term liabilities). Earnings (results) quality can range from high and sustainable to low and unsustainable.
B. Incorrect because this also displays low financial reporting quality.
C. Incorrect because this also displays low earnings quality.

questions.q: With respect to the defined benefit pension plan assumption, which of the following will decrease after Thorsell's adjustment?
options: Financial leverage ratio
Book value per share
Debt-to-equity ratio
questions.why:
A. Incorrect because the financial leverage ratio (average total assets ÷ average shareholders' equity) will increase since total assets will remain unchanged and total shareholders' equity will decrease after Thorsell makes the pension discount rate adjustment by reducing the discount rate by 0.5%. Total shareholders' equity (via accumulated other comprehensive income) will decrease.
B. Correct because the book value per share (common stockholders' equity ÷ total number of common shares outstanding) will decrease once Thorsell makes the pension discount rate adjustment. After reducing the discount rate by 0.5%, (a higher discount rate assumption results in a lower estimated pension obligation) the underfunded plan obligation will increase (that is, become even more underfunded) and total shareholders' equity (via accumulated other comprehensive income) will decrease. The number of common shares outstanding is not affected.
C. Incorrect because the debt-to-equity ratio (total debt ÷ total shareholders' equity) will increase since total debt will increase and total stockholders' equity will decrease after Thorsell makes the pension discount rate adjustment by reducing the discount rate by 0.5%.

vignettes.body:
Sugi Tyler is a chemical industry analyst for a global investment firm. Tyler is researching the impact of environment, social, and governance (ESG) issues as they relate to ChemiKa LLC (ChemiKa) and PlastiKa Corp (PlastiKa). She summarizes the companies' ownership and governance structures in Exhibit 1.

Exhibit 1
#   | ChemiKa | PlastiKa
Ownership | Concentrated | Dispersed
Voting power | Concentrated | Dispersed
Total number of directors | 19 | 8
Number of independent directors | 12 | 4
Two-tiered board | No | Yes
CEO duality | Yes | No
Average board tenure | 8 years | 14 years
Independent committees: |  
Audit | Yes | No
Compensation | Yes | Yes
Director selection | No | Yes
Tyler shares this data with her co-worker Kim Myer and asks Myer to determine the risk of ChemiKa’s governance structure. Myer states:"ChemiKa’s ownership and voting structure will likely diminish the ownership rights of minority shareholders which indicates principal-agent problem."

To evaluate the corporate governance policies and procedures of the two companies, Tyler considers the rankings provided by an independent ESG data analysis firm specializing in board and governance structure. The contributions of each board member are only considered after at least one year of service.

The ESG data analysis firm uses a scoring system awarding one point for favorable characteristics among the following:

CEO duality is absent.
Average board tenure is below ten years.
For board independence, a two-tiered board is considered favorable. A simple majority of independent directors is generally favorable. However, in a one-tiered board which is considered unfavorable, a 60% majority of independent directors is the favorable threshold.
Independent committees for audit, compensation and director selection are present (1 point for the presence of each independent committee).
In recent years, both companies have faced increasing concern about the environmental impact of their products. In response to actions by shareholders, regulators and other constituencies, industry producers have made substantial capital investments toward production of more biodegradable products. ChemiKa has built a large bio-plastics plant and financed the project with green bonds which go alongside of the company’s conventional “plain vanilla” corporate bonds. Tyler notices that ChemiKa’s green bonds trade with tighter spreads than its conventional bonds.

PlastiKa announces the addition of a chemical engineer as a new independent member of its board. Although not yet familiar with company's core operations, it is expected that he will lead the effort to meet increasing regulatory requirements and aid in new product research and development.

questions.q: Myer’s statement about ChemiKa's governance risk is:
options: incorrect with respect to principal-agent problem.
correct.
incorrect with respect to minority shareholders.
questions.why:
A. Correct because the conflict described for ChemiKa is a principal-principal problem, not a principal-agent problem. The combination of concentrated ownership and concentrated voting power often results in controlling shareholders maintaining a position of power over both managers and minority shareholders and this conflict is known as a principal–principal problem. Managers are considered weak whereas in a principal-agent conflict managers are strong.
B. Incorrect because the conflict described for ChemiKa is a principal-principal problem, not principal-agent problem. The combination of concentrated ownership and concentrated voting power often results in controlling shareholders maintaining a position of power over both managers and minority shareholders and this conflict is known as a principal–principal problem.
C. Incorrect because the statement is correct regarding minority shareholders. The conflict described for ChemiKa is a principal-principal problem. The combination of concentrated ownership and concentrated voting power often results in controlling shareholders maintaining a position of power over both managers and minority shareholders and this conflict is known as a principal–principal problem.

questions.q: Based on the ESG data analysis firm's scoring system and Exhibit 1, compared to PlastiKa, ChemiKa most likely ranks:
options: the same.
lower.
higher.
questions.why:
A. Correct. Scoring (1 point each): board independence: PlastiKa has a two-tiered board (1); ChemiKa's one-tiered board needs 60% independent directors and has 12 ÷ 19 = 63% (1); CEO duality absent: ChemiKa no (0), PlastiKa yes (1); average tenure below ten years: ChemiKa 8 years (1), PlastiKa 14 years (0); audit committee: ChemiKa yes (1), PlastiKa no (0); compensation committee: both yes (1 each); director selection committee: ChemiKa no (0), PlastiKa yes (1). Ownership, voting power and the number of directors are not scored. Each company totals 4 points, so they rank the same.
B. Incorrect. Both companies score 4 points.
C. Incorrect. Both companies score 4 points.

questions.q: The market pricing of ChemiKa's bonds that Tyler notices is most likely due to:
options: greater bondholder recourse with the green bonds.
market demand.
greenwashing.
questions.why:
A. Incorrect because green bonds normally have the same credit ratings and bondholder recourse as conventional bonds of the same issuer (all else being equal).
B. Correct because green bonds typically resemble an issuer’s conventional bonds, with the exception that the bond proceeds are earmarked for green projects. Green bonds normally have the same credit ratings and bondholder recourse as conventional bonds of the same issuer (all else being equal). Some green bonds, however, may command a premium, or tighter credit spread, versus comparable conventional bonds because of market demand.
C. Incorrect because greenwashing is the risk that the bond’s proceeds are not actually used for a beneficial environmental or climate-related project. If greenwashing were present, the proceeds from the new green bonds would have been used for additional non-green expenditures. ChemiKa's project to build a large bio-plastics plant is financed with green bonds. Also, greenwashing would diminish the company's credibility resulting in a lower value (higher credit spread) for all of its bonds.

questions.q: Which of the following board policies and practices will be most improved by PlastiKa's new board member?
options: Tenure
Governance
ESG risks
questions.why:
A. Incorrect because the new board member has not yet served for at least one year and will therefore have no immediate effect on tenure.
B. Incorrect because the new board member shows no evidence of broad experience or expertise in core company operations, management and governance. A board with concentrated skills and experience may lack sufficient expertise to govern, as may a board with diverse skills and expertise that are not directly related to the company’s core operations.
C. Correct because the new board member has expertise in chemical engineering to apply to environmental regulatory issues as well as product research and development. In certain sectors/industries that rely on natural resources or face potentially large ESG risks, board members typically have expertise in environmental, climate, or social issues.

vignettes.body:
Fiona O’Connor, CFA, who is based in Dublin, runs the asset management firm that manages the assets for the Step Up Social Impact Private Equity Fund (the Fund), which is registered in Ireland. The general partner of the Fund has asked O’Connor to meet with Elise Jensen, CFA, a pension asset consultant, to find out whether Jensen will pitch the Fund to her institutional clients looking for an environmental, social, and governance (ESG) approach. Jensen specializes in working with continental European–based pension funds, many of which are Swiss pension funds required by Swiss pension regulations to undertake an ESG assessment prior to making an investment. In addition, all her clients have a relatively low risk profile, because they are small funds. The few pension funds Jensen works with that do not require an ESG assessment still include the desire for this type of evaluation in their investment mandate.
During an introductory meeting that lasts about an hour, Jensen asks O’Connor to give an overview of the Fund. O’Connor makes the following three statements:
First, as you are aware, the Step Up Fund is a global social impact fund. Therefore, we have allocated 85% of our investment portfolio to education and health care. In addition, some of the companies we invest in offer scholarships or free services to those who cannot afford their services. As a result, our investment returns may not be as high as those of funds that have a strict “for-profit” investment strategy, but we still track our Fund against ESG indexes. We have also developed a set of “social impact” metrics that aim to show the Fund has a positive impact on people’s lives. Details of the investment strategy and how we select investments are clearly and extensively described in our fund prospectus. In addition, investors are notified prior to any changes being made in our investment process.
Second, let me explain how we select investments. I’ll give you the prospectus, too, for your further reference, because it contains all the details, and they’re quite extensive. We identify potential investments from around the globe through our own analysts’ research within the education and health care industries. We also use third-party agents to find potential investments. If we make an investment in the companies they present to us, we pay them a finder’s fee. One such agent we use is Make-a-Difference Consultants, an asset consulting firm that has adopted the CFA Institute Code and Standards.
Finally, I also want to disclose to you the compensation arrangements for the asset management firm’s six investment analysts, all of whom report to me directly. Two of the analysts work part-time, because they made earlier commitments with other asset management firms before I found them. But they do not work for other social impact funds, so I’m OK with this arrangement because we consider them independent contractors. We disclose this and other forms of management compensation to all clients and potential clients. All the analysts are paid monthly and participate in the firm’s year-end bonus program. The value of the bonus pool is determined by how well the company has performed.

questions.q: Based only on the information given, when providing investment advice to her clients, Jensen should most likely adhere to which of the following to avoid violating Standard I(A): Knowledge of the Law?
options: Irish legislation
CFA Institute Standards of Professional Conduct
Swiss regulations
questions.why:
A. Incorrect because Jensen would not likely be required to adhere to Irish legislation, because she is not directly associated with the Fund nor are her clients based in Ireland.
B. Incorrect because in this instance, the CFA Institute Code and Standards are less strict than Swiss regulations since they do not require members to undertake ESG assessments prior to taking investment action or making an investment recommendation.
C. Correct. Jensen should adhere to Swiss regulations. Standard I(A): Knowledge of the Law requires members and candidates to adhere to the stricter of any applicable legislation or regulations and the CFA Institute Standards of Professional Conduct. Therefore, when providing investment advice to her Swiss pension clients, Jensen should most likely adhere to the stricter Swiss regulations requiring ESG assessments prior to the pension funds making an investment. Jensen would not likely be required to adhere to Irish legislation, because she is not directly associated with the Fund nor are her clients based in Ireland. In this instance, the CFA Institute Standards are less strict than Swiss regulations, because they do not require members to undertake ESG assessments prior to taking investment action or making an investment recommendation.

questions.q: Given O’Connor’s first statement about the asset allocation, expected returns, and strategy of the Step Up Social Impact Private Equity Fund, does O’Connor most likely violate the CFA Institute Standards?
options: No
Yes, with regard to Standard V(B): Communication with Clients and Prospective Clients
Yes, with regard to Standard III(A): Loyalty, Prudence, and Care
questions.why:
A. Correct because there is no indication O’Connor violated Standard III(A): Loyalty, Prudence, and Care or Standard V(B): Communication with Clients and Prospective Clients. With regard to Standard III(A), investors in this type of social impact fund are likely looking to achieve high levels of social impact as well as to obtain somewhat competitive investment returns. Consequently, returns may not be the primary focus so the Fund can still meet its fiduciary duty to clients. As long as this strategy is clearly indicated in the prospectus prior to entry into the Fund, O’Connor would not be in violation of Standard III(A). In addition, with regard to Standard V(B), since the investment strategy is clearly stated in detail in the prospectus and notifications of changes are sent to clients prior to changes being made, O’Connor, as part of the senior management team, would not be in violation of Standard V(B).
B. Incorrect because there is no indication the information contained in the prospectus is incorrect or misleading. Therefore, O’Connor, as part of the senior management team, is not in violation of Standard V(B): Communication with Clients and Prospective Clients.
C. Incorrect because there is no indication O’Connor violated Standard III(A): Loyalty, Prudence, and Care.

questions.q: Given O’Connor’s second statement to Jensen, which further action should O’Connor least likely take to comply with required or recommended procedures for the CFA Institute Standards of Professional Conduct?
options: Notify clients of the finder’s fee policy on a semiannual basis.
Monitor the consultants’ compliance policy execution.
Disclose the finder’s fee arrangement in the fund prospectus.
questions.why:
A. Correct. O’Connor should least likely notify clients of the finder’s fee policy on a semiannual basis. Recommended procedures to implement Standard VI(C): Referral Fees are to notify clients at least quarterly, not semiannually.
B. Incorrect. Make-a-Difference has made claims that it abides by the CFA Institute Code and Standards. O’Connor has a responsibility under Standard I(A): Knowledge of the Law to not knowingly participate or assist others in violating any CFA Institute Standards. Therefore, she must seek assurances that Make-a-Difference Consultants also disclose the receipt of finder’s fees to their clients where applicable as required by Standard VI(C): Referral Fees.
C. Incorrect. O’Connor should ensure that the potential use of paying finder’s fees to Make-a-Difference Consultants or any other third-party agents is disclosed in the prospectus to avoid violating Standard VI(C): Referral Fees.

questions.q: With regard to the asset management firm’s compensation arrangements for the investment analysts as mentioned in O’Connor’s final statement, does O’Connor most likely violate any CFA Institute Standards?
options: Yes, relating to the bonus pool
Yes, relating to the part-time policy
No
questions.why:
A. Incorrect because O’Connor has not violated any CFA Institute Standards relating to the firm’s bonus pool.
B. Incorrect because O’Connor has not violated any CFA Institute Standards relating to the hiring of part-time analysts.
C. Correct. O’Connor has not violated any CFA Institute Standards relating to the firm’s bonus pool or its part-time policy. With regard to the year-end bonus pool, Standard VI(A): Disclosure of Conflicts is not violated, because the participation in the bonus pool is not structured to provide immediate compensation or give returns based on short-term investment action with little or no long-term value creation. In compliance with Standard III(A): Loyalty, Prudence, and Care recommendations, the firm discloses all forms of management compensation arrangements. With regard to the part-time policy, O’Connor has also not violated any CFA Institute Standards. The Standards do not prohibit independent contractors. Standard VI(A): Disclosure of Conflicts is being upheld in that the firm discloses the part-time relationship with its clients and potential clients.

vignettes.body:
Martin Pasco is an analyst with the Hekla University Endowment. Pasco is evaluating opportunities to increase the alternative investments allocation in Hekla's portfolio.
Pasco considers Fund 1, a commodity managed futures fund, as a potential investment for Hekla. Current price data for the largest exposures in Fund 1 are presented in Exhibit 1.
Exhibit 1
# Item | Crude oil—Brent ($ per barrel) | Cocoa ($ per metric tonne) | Gold ($ per troy ounce)
Spot price | 75.02 | 3,318 | 1,919.4
3-month futures price | 74.25 | 3,264 | 1,929.3
6-month futures price | 74.25 | 3,233 | 1,935.6
Pasco reviews a previous cocoa trade for Fund 1. At inception of the trade, Fund 1 took a fully collateralized long position in a 3-month futures contract at a price of $3,294. Three months later, the entire position was rolled into a new 3-month futures contract. At that time, the price of the initial futures contract was $3,285 and the price of a new 3-month futures contract was $3,260. The collateral earned an annualized return of 5.0% during the three months.
Pasco also evaluates several equity hedge fund strategies for Hekla's portfolio.
First, Pasco reviews Fund 2, an event-driven hedge fund. The fund has a merger arbitrage trade involving a potential merger between two companies, Acquirer Company (AC) and Target Company (TC). AC has offered to buy TC in a stock-for-stock deal. The offer ratio is one share of AC for three shares of TC. AC was trading at $39 per share prior to the merger announcement, and its price decreased to $35 per share after the announcement. TC was trading at $10 per share prior to the merger announcement, and its price increased to $11 per share after the announcement. After the merger announcement, the hedge fund bought 30,000 shares of TC at $11 per share and sold 10,000 shares of AC at $35 per share.

questions.q: Based on the current price data of Fund 1's largest exposures, the most appropriate conclusion is that the:
options: cocoa market is in backwardation.
crude oil basis is zero.
gold market calendar spread is positive.
questions.why:
A. Correct. For cocoa the spot price (3,318) is above the 3-month futures price (3,264), which is above the 6-month price (3,233): the futures curve slopes down, so the market is in backwardation.
B. Incorrect. The crude oil basis = spot − near-term futures = 75.02 − 74.25 = 0.77, not zero. It is the calendar spread (near-term minus farther-term futures, 74.25 − 74.25) that is zero.
C. Incorrect. Gold: near-term futures 1,929.3 − farther-term futures 1,935.6 = −6.3, so the calendar spread is negative (gold is in contango).

questions.q: The 3-month total return of the past cocoa futures trade is closest to:
questions.why:
B. Correct. Total return = price return + roll return + collateral return.
Price return = (3,285 − 3,294) ÷ 3,294 = −0.2732%.
Roll return = (near-term contract price − new contract price) ÷ near-term contract price = (3,285 − 3,260) ÷ 3,285 = +0.7610%.
Collateral return for 3 months = 5.0% ÷ 4 = 1.25%.
Total = −0.2732 + 0.7610 + 1.25 = 1.7378%, about 1.7%.
A. Incorrect. 0.2% subtracts the roll return instead of adding it (−0.2732 − 0.7610 + 1.25).
C. Incorrect. 5.5% adds the annualised collateral return of 5.0% instead of the 3-month return of 1.25%.

questions.q: If the merger between AC and TC closes successfully, Fund 2's merger arbitrage trade will result in a gain closest to:
questions.why:
B. Correct. If the merger closes, the 30,000 TC shares bought at $11 (cost $330,000) convert into 30,000 ÷ 3 = 10,000 AC shares, which cover the short position sold at $35 (proceeds $350,000). Gain = 350,000 − 330,000 = $20,000.
A. Incorrect. It computes the payoff as ($35 ÷ 3 − $11) × 10,000 = $6,667, about $7,000.
C. Incorrect. It uses the pre-announcement prices: 10,000 × $39 − 30,000 × $10 = $90,000.

questions.q: The main risk of Fund 2's merger arbitrage trade is that:
options: the AC share price rises after the merger closes, which hurts the short AC position.
the merger is cancelled and the TC shares fall back toward their pre-announcement price.
the TC shares are converted into AC shares at the announced ratio, which locks in a loss.
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. After closing, the TC shares convert into AC shares that offset the short AC position, so a higher AC price does not hurt the closed trade.
B. Correct. The position is long TC and short AC; it earns the spread if the stock-for-stock deal closes. If the deal fails, TC falls back toward its pre-announcement price while the short AC hedge no longer offsets it, causing a loss.
C. Incorrect. Conversion at the announced ratio is the expected outcome that produces the gain, not a loss.

title: Mock 9
desc: 10 new vignettes from sub-topics different from Mock 8, plus 1 Ethics vignette

vignettes.body:
Lena Voss is valuing Hartwell Corporation common shares using a free cash flow approach. Voss gathered information about Hartwell from several sources. She begins her analysis by determining free cash flow to the firm (FCFF) and free cash flow to equity (FCFE) for the 2012 fiscal year, using the financial statements in Exhibits 1 and 2. Hartwell's fiscal year ends 31 December.

Exhibit 1
Hartwell Corporation Selected Financial Data ($ millions, except per share amounts)
# For Year Ending 31 December | 2012
Revenues | $6,102
Earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization (EBITDA) | 1,262
Depreciation expense | 231
Operating income | 1,031
Interest expense | 172
Pretax income | 859
Income tax (32%) | 275
Net income | $584
Number of outstanding shares (millions) | 395
2012 earnings per share | $1.48
2012 dividends paid (millions) | 142
2012 dividends per share | 0.36
2012 fixed capital investment (millions) | 502
Cost of equity | 11.5%
Weighted average cost of capital (WACC) | 8.5%

Exhibit 2
Hartwell Corporation Consolidated Balance Sheets ($ millions)
#   | 2012 | 2011
Cash and cash equivalents | $28 | $19
Accounts receivable | 398 | 404
Inventories | 655 | 601
Other current assets | 129 | 117
Total current assets | $1,210 | $1,141
Current liabilities | $2,640 | $2,545
Long-term debt | 2,105 | 2,305
Common stockholders' equity | 1,008 | 566
Total liabilities and stockholders' equity | $5,753 | $5,416

Voss plans to perform two different valuations of Hartwell, which she calls the "base case" valuation and the "alternative" valuation. Critical assumptions for each are given in the following lists.

Base case valuation

2013 FCFF will be $520 million.
Beyond 2013, FCFF will grow in perpetuity at 3.5% annually.
The market value and book value of Hartwell's long-term debt are approximately equal.

Alternative valuation

2013 earnings per share (EPS) will be $1.65.
EPS will grow forever at 5% annually.
For 2013 and beyond: Net capital expenditures (fixed capital expenditures minus depreciation) will be 35% of EPS. Investments in working capital will be 15% of EPS. Of future investments, 65% will be financed with equity and 35% will be financed with debt.

Greta Lindqvist, Voss's supervisor, reviews Hartwell's valuations. Specifically, Lindqvist makes the following three statements:

Statement 1: Because the company's capital structure seems unstable, the FCFE valuation approach is superior to the FCFF valuation approach.
Statement 2: If there is a change in control at Hartwell, the discounted dividend valuation approach would be superior to a free cash flow valuation approach.
Statement 3: The free cash flow valuation approach is superior to the discounted dividend valuation approach because the company's dividends have been substantially different from its FCFE.

questions.q: Hartwell's FCFF ($ millions) for 2012 is closest to:
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. It uses the tax rate instead of (1 − tax rate) on interest.
B. Incorrect. It ignores the working capital investment.
C. Correct. Working capital (current assets excluding cash − current liabilities) went from −1,423 to −1,458, so WCInv = −35 (an inflow). FCFF = 584 + 231 + 172 × (1 − 0.32) − 502 − (−35) = 465.

questions.q: Using Voss's base case valuation assumptions and the FCFF valuation approach, the year-end 2012 value per share of Hartwell common stock is closest to:
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. It discounts at the cost of equity instead of the WACC.
B. Correct. Firm value = 520 ÷ (0.085 − 0.035) = 10,400. Equity = 10,400 − 2,105 (debt) = 8,295. Per share = 8,295 ÷ 395 = $21.00.
C. Incorrect. It does not deduct the debt.

questions.q: Using Voss's alternative valuation assumptions and the FCFE valuation approach, the year-end 2012 value per share of Hartwell's common stock is closest to:
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. It is the FCFF-style calculation: 1.65 − 0.5775 − 0.2475 = 0.825 ÷ 0.065.
B. Correct. FCFE1 = EPS − (1 − DR) × net capex − (1 − DR) × WCInv = 1.65 − 0.65 × 0.5775 − 0.65 × 0.2475 = 1.11375. Value = 1.11375 ÷ (0.115 − 0.05) = $17.13.
C. Incorrect. It grows FCFE1 again by (1 + g).

questions.q: Which of Lindqvist's three statements pertaining to Hartwell's valuation is the most accurate? Statement:
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. FCFF, not FCFE, is preferred when the capital structure is unstable or changing.
B. Incorrect. With a change in control, the new owner has discretion over free cash flow and can change the dividend, so a free cash flow approach is superior to a dividend approach.
C. Correct. FCFE or FCFF is preferred to the dividend approach when dividends differ significantly from the capacity to pay them (and when control may change).

vignettes.body:
Leon Fischer is a fund manager with Summit Asset Partners, a fixed-income asset management firm. He actively manages his fund's holdings, duration, and yield curve exposure.

Fischer's fund currently has a large position in two option-free and default-risk-free zero-coupon bonds. The first bond has a 1-year maturity and the other bond has a 10-year maturity. Fischer's view is that the spot curve one year from today will reflect the current forward curve. Interest rate information for option-free and default-risk-free zero-coupon bonds is contained in Exhibit 1.

Exhibit 1
Maturity (years) | 1 | 2 | 3
Spot rate | 2.50% | 3.40% | 4.30%
1-year forward rate | f0,1 = 2.50% | f1,1 = 4.31% | f2,1 = 6.12%

Fischer next focuses his attention on the short end of the yield curve. He observes the US Treasury bill rate, the overnight indexed swap rate (OIS), and the secured overnight transactions market reference rate (MRR). He collects the current rate and spread information in Exhibit 2 and uses it to calculate the 3-month TED spread.

Exhibit 2
# 3-Month US Treasury Bill Rate | 3-Month OIS Rate | 3-Month MRR – 3-Month OIS Spread
7 bps | 9 bps | 12 bps

Later in the day, Fischer meets with another analyst to discuss the current fixed-income environment. This second analyst believes fixed-income markets are about to enter a period of high uncertainty. This analyst also expects a flight to quality and a bullish flattening of the yield curve. He recommends Fischer adjust the fund's exposure through the purchase and sale of option-free default-risk-free bonds.

questions.q: If Fischer's view of spot rates one year from today is accurate, the 1-year total return of the 10-year bond will be:
options: equal to the total return of the 1-year bond.
greater than the total return of the 1-year bond.
less than the total return of the 1-year bond.
questions.why:
A. Correct. If spot rates evolve as the current forward curve implies, bonds of every maturity earn the one-year (risk-free) rate over the year.
B. Incorrect. It would be higher only if spot rates fell below those implied by the forward curve.
C. Incorrect. It would be lower only if spot rates rose above those implied by the forward curve.

questions.q: Fischer's view that the spot curve one year from today will reflect the current forward curve is most consistent with:
options: the segmented markets theory.
the liquidity preference theory.
the pure expectations theory.
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Segmented markets: each maturity is priced by its own supply and demand; forward rates are not forecasts.
B. Incorrect. Liquidity preference adds a premium for longer maturities, so forward rates overstate expected future spot rates.
C. Correct. Pure expectations: forward rates are unbiased predictors of future spot rates, so the future spot curve equals today's forward curve.

questions.q: The 3-month TED spread that Fischer calculates should equal:
options: 5 bps.
14 bps.
19 bps.
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. It subtracts the T-bill rate from the MRR–OIS spread (12 − 7).
B. Correct. 3-month MRR = OIS + (MRR − OIS spread) = 9 + 12 = 21 bps. TED spread = MRR − T-bill rate = 21 − 7 = 14 bps.
C. Incorrect. It adds the T-bill rate to the MRR–OIS spread (12 + 7).

questions.q: The strategy best suited to exploit the second analyst's expected changes to the current fixed-income environment is to:
options: extend duration and construct a barbell portfolio.
keep duration constant and construct a barbell portfolio.
extend duration and construct a bullet portfolio.
questions.why:
A. Correct. Flight to quality: government yields fall, so extend duration. Bullish flattening: long rates fall more than short rates, so shift from a bullet to a barbell.
B. Incorrect. Duration should be extended when yields are expected to fall.
C. Incorrect. Extending duration is right (flight to quality lowers yields) but a bullet suits a parallel shift or a steepening, not a bullish flattening.

vignettes.body:
Helen Marsh is an analyst at Beacon Fund covering the real estate and energy sectors. She and her colleague are analyzing two companies that are currently held by the fund.

The first company is Mercury Corp., a publicly traded, national retail grocery store chain that has 3,100 physical stores. Mercury leases most of its grocery stores and all five of its office locations that help the company achieve its core business of operating 50,000 square foot stores in all markets of the United States. Mercury also owns the real estate (land and building) associated with 120 physical store locations. Mercury recently announced that its board of directors approved a strategic real estate plan to pursue a separation of all its owned assets. The company currently has a speculative-grade credit rating.

The separation would be achieved through a series of sale-leaseback transactions with real estate investment trusts (REITs) that specialize in owning retail properties. Under the plan, Mercury will sell its 120 owned grocery stores and lease them for 20-year terms with a combined annual rent expense of USD54 million. Mercury expects to receive cash proceeds of approximately USD1,000 million from the property sales, which will be used to retire approximately USD700 million of debt and repurchase 5 million common shares.

Mercury believes the pro forma capital structure following the transactions will enable it to receive an investment-grade credit rating. The sale-leaseback transactions value the 120 assets at an average capitalization rate of 5.40%. Based on Marsh’s colleague’s research, the 25th, 50th, and 75th percentile cap rates for sale transactions for similarly situated properties and similar lease terms in the last three years were 4.90%, 5.40%, and 5.90%, respectively.

The second company is Neptune Corp., a publicly traded US energy company. Marsh has been asked to assess the valuation of a potential spin off for this company. Neptune operates and reports three segments: Upstream, Midstream, and Downstream. In the last 12 months, the company reported the financial results shown in Exhibit 1.

Exhibit 1
# Segment | EBITDA (USD millions)
Upstream | 12,600
Midstream | 4,200
Downstream | 2,800
Consolidated | 19,600
Neptune is currently trading at an enterprise value of USD313,600 million, or an EV/EBITDA multiple of 16. A spin off of the Downstream segment has long been rumored because it has been under-invested in by the current management team, resulting in slower revenue growth than its peers. Marsh finds that the median Upstream, Midstream, and Downstream peers are trading at enterprise value-to-EBITDA multiples of 18, 15, and 12, respectively.

questions.q: Which of the following statements about Mercury's motivations for the strategic real estate plan is incorrect?
options: The expected change in Mercury's credit rating after the transactions will increase the firm's costs of capital.
The transactions will allow Mercury to unlock the value of its real estate assets.
The transactions will enable Mercury to sell a non-core business.
questions.why:
A. Correct. Retiring debt should improve the credit rating, which lowers (not raises) the cost of capital, so this statement is incorrect.
B. Incorrect. Sale-leasebacks unlock the value in the real estate: Mercury receives cash and records a lease liability.
C. Incorrect. Real estate ownership is not Mercury's core business (operating grocery stores), so this statement is correct.

questions.q: Which of the following statements best describes Mercury's average capitalization rate for the sale-leaseback transactions? Mercury's average capitalization rate:
options: is supported by the comparable transactions.
compares favorably to the comparable transactions.
compares unfavorably to the comparable transactions.
questions.why:
A. Correct. The average cap rate of 5.40% equals the median (50th percentile) of comparable transactions (4.90%, 5.40%, 5.90%), so it is supported.
B. Incorrect. 5.40% is not better than the median of comparable transactions.
C. Incorrect. 5.40% is not worse than the median of comparable transactions.

questions.q: Based on Exhibit 1 and the peer median EV/EBITDA multiples, Neptune's estimated enterprise value is closest to:
options: USD294,000 million.
USD313,600 million.
USD323,400 million.
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. It uses the average of the peer multiples (15) for every segment.
B. Incorrect. USD313,600 million is Neptune's current enterprise value, not the estimate.
C. Correct. Sum of the parts: Upstream 12,600 × 18 = 226,800; Midstream 4,200 × 15 = 63,000; Downstream 2,800 × 12 = 33,600; total 323,400.

questions.q: A spin-off of the Downstream segment would most likely:
options: distribute shares of the Downstream business to Neptune's existing shareholders.
sell the Downstream segment to another company for cash.
sell shares of the Downstream business to new investors in a public offering, giving Neptune cash.
questions.why:
A. Correct. In a spin-off the parent distributes the shares of the subsidiary pro rata to its own shareholders; no cash is raised.
B. Incorrect. That describes a divestiture (sale) of the segment, not a spin-off.
C. Incorrect. That describes an equity carve-out, which raises cash for the parent.

vignettes.body:
Daniel Ashworth is an equity analyst at an investment bank. He is preparing updated research reports on two companies, Zorin Incorporated and Harlan Company.
Zorin Incorporated
Ashworth indicates in his updated report that Zorin's profits are cyclical. Using the data for the past four years in Exhibit 1, he computes Zorin's normalized EPS based on the average ROE method. He determines that Year 1 through Year 4 (the most recent year) constitutes a full business cycle.
Exhibit 1
#   | Year 1 | Year 2 | Year 3 | Year 4
EPS | $2.84 | $1.96 | $0.52 | $2.31
Book value per share | $11.40 | $12.20 | $12.90 | $13.60
Harlan Company
Ashworth next reviews Harlan, which operates in a previously mature industry that now has high growth potential due to a recent technological innovation. Harlan's debt-to-equity ratio is significantly higher than the average of its competitors. Harlan spent heavily on advertising to create and maintain its brand, which is an important asset. The company is favored by many investors because its dividend payout ratio is the highest in its industry. Ashworth considers several potential metrics to use in valuing Harlan.
During the past year, Harlan's share price rose from $24.60 to $28.35 per share and the company paid an annual dividend of $1.10 per share. Over the same period, the market index rose from 488.30 to 521.90 and had an average dividend yield of 3.1%. Ashworth computes Harlan's relative strength compared to the index, which is a common technical indicator.

questions.q: Ashworth finds that Zorin's profits are cyclical. Compared with the latest reported EPS, normalized EPS is used because it:
options: uses forecast earnings, which are always available for cyclical companies.
adjusts reported earnings for the effect of share repurchases.
estimates the earnings Zorin would earn at mid-cycle, removing the effect of the business cycle.
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Forecast earnings give a forward P/E; normalized earnings are an estimate of average earnings over a full cycle.
B. Incorrect. Share repurchases are not what normalizing is for.
C. Correct. Normalized EPS removes the influence of the business cycle by estimating mid-cycle earnings (here average ROE over a full cycle times current book value per share).

questions.q: Zorin's normalized EPS based on the average ROE method is closest to:
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. $1.91 is the average EPS of Years 1 to 4.
B. Incorrect. $1.94 multiplies the average ROE (15.5%) by the AVERAGE book value per share ($12.525) instead of the current one.
C. Correct. ROE by year: 24.9%, 16.1%, 4.0% and 17.0%, average 15.5%. Normalized EPS = average ROE × current (Year 4) book value per share = 0.1550 × $13.60 = $2.11.

questions.q: Which of the following is the most appropriate metric for Ashworth to use in valuing Harlan?
options: Price to book ratio
Enterprise value to sales ratio
Dividend yield
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Book value ignores Harlan's brand, an internally generated intangible asset built by advertising that is not on the balance sheet.
B. Correct. EV/sales uses the total value of debt and equity, so it suits Harlan's high debt-to-equity ratio and diverse capital structures; sales are stable and hard to manipulate.
C. Incorrect. Dividend yield ignores capital gains, which are likely important with the industry's growth potential, and the highest payout in the industry may not be safe.

questions.q: Harlan's relative strength compared to the market index over the past year is closest to:
questions.why:
A. Correct. Relative strength = (Harlan price ÷ index) at the end divided by the same ratio at the start = (28.35 ÷ 521.9) ÷ (24.6 ÷ 488.3) = 0.054321 ÷ 0.050379 = 1.0782. Dividends are not included.
B. Incorrect. 1.0479 compares Harlan's price return with the index's total return (price change plus the 3.1% yield); relative strength uses prices only.
C. Incorrect. 1.0885 compares total returns (adds Harlan's $1.10 dividend and the index yield); relative strength uses prices only.

vignettes.body:
Marovia, a resource-abundant West African country, has a developing economy with low capital per worker available. Although the majority of its population is impoverished, Marovia has a long history of advanced education and is committed to technological progress. President Emmanuel Kessogo recently appointed Aminata Camara, PhD, as Economic Development Secretary. He asks her to help him develop economic policies to promote growth.

Last year, Kessogo attended a summit of international leaders, where he learned that developing countries typically face several factors that affect their growth prospects, such as enforcement of substantive laws, restrictions on imports, and low rates of saving.

Kessogo believes that the Marovia economy relies too heavily on the export of natural rubber. He is convinced that significant industrial capital investment will persuade foreign direct investors that he is serious about economic development. He announces that the Marovia government will construct a large tire factory to take advantage of the country’s rubber resources. Kessogo expects that as a result of this investment, per capita productivity will rise rapidly driving rapid growth in GDP.

Camara believes that according to the classical growth theory, gains in per capita GDP are temporary because the resulting population explosion will lower per capita GDP to subsistence real wage levels. She considers endogenous growth theory to be more realistic, believing that (1) investments, such as the new tire factory, will increase the rate of per capita output growth until the steady state rate of growth is achieved; and (2) investment in research and development will boost growth even further, thus extending the abnormal growth period before diminishing marginal returns eventually set in.

questions.q: Camara's understanding of the two growth theories is most accurate with regard to:
options: classical growth theory.
endogenous growth theory.
both classical growth theory and endogenous growth theory.
questions.why:
A. Correct. Her view of classical theory is right: gains in per capita GDP are temporary because the resulting population growth pushes income back to subsistence.
B. Incorrect. Her description of endogenous theory is wrong: a steady state of growth and diminishing marginal returns are features of neoclassical theory; endogenous theory has no diminishing returns to capital (R&D, human capital).
C. Incorrect. Her understanding of endogenous growth theory is incorrect.

questions.q: Which of the following factors favors economic growth?
options: Limited foreign capital and trade flows
Limited regulations in order to encourage entrepreneurial activity
Low rates of saving
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Foreign investment and trade can raise the capital stock, productivity, employment and wages.
B. Correct. Limited regulation encourages new companies, which are strongly correlated with higher productivity.
C. Incorrect. Low saving and investment limit growth.

questions.q: According to the neoclassical growth model, when trade barriers are removed, convergence of per capita income levels between developed and developing countries should:
options: occur more slowly.
remain unaffected.
occur more quickly.
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Opening up speeds up, not slows down, convergence.
B. Incorrect. Opening up affects the rate of growth and convergence.
C. Correct. With open trade and capital flows, capital moves to poorer countries and their capital-to-labor ratios rise faster, so productivity and per capita incomes converge more quickly.

questions.q: Opening an economy to trade and financial flows will most likely:
options: discourage domestic spending on research and development.
not impact domestic spending on research and development.
encourage domestic spending on research and development.
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Open trade encourages, not discourages, R&D spending.
B. Incorrect. Open trade affects innovation by encouraging R&D and human capital spending.
C. Correct. Open trade gives access to larger markets and a greater flow of ideas, so firms invest more in R&D and human capital, raising the return on new investment and growth (though small, lagging countries can lose domestic innovation).

vignettes.body:
Ethics: Standards of Professional Conduct
Four independent questions. Each one can be answered on its own.

questions.q: A firm that is a market maker comes into possession of MNPI. It should:
options: Stop trading in the security
Keep making the market for liquidity and confidentiality, but remain passive
Tell clients so that they can decide
questions.why: A trading prohibition may harm confidentiality and liquidity (stopping would itself signal something to others). Continue market making, passively.
